name: Aabenraa (Denmark)
summary: Aabenraa is a port city in Denmark, located at the head of Aabenraa Fjord, approx 61 km (38 mi) north of Schleswig (Germany's Schleswig-Holstein state), with population around 16,000. As cruise port, Aabenraa (port locode DKAAB) features a deepwater natural harbor allowing access to ships with max drought 7,5 m (25 ft).
description: Aabenraa is a port city in Denmark, located at the head of Aabenraa Fjord, approx 61 km (38 mi) north of Schleswig (Germany's Schleswig-Holstein state), with population around 16,000. As cruise port, Aabenraa (port locode DKAAB) features a deepwater natural harbor allowing access to ships with max drought 7,5 m (25 ft). Regular passenger ferries link Aabenraa with Kristiansand (Norway) and Goteborg (Sweden) . Aabenraa was first mentioned in the 12th century when the town was attacked by the Wends (slavic people). The settlement started growing around the bishop's castle Opnor Hus and received its merchant status in 1240. During the Middle Ages (13th-15th centuries), the town developed a fishing industry and hops production (flowers aka seed cones or strobiles). Town's glory days were in the period 1750s-1864 when the shipping traffic steadily grew, serving the trade routes linking Denmark with the Mediterranean, South America, China, Australia. Aabenraa had a good harbor providing safe navigation and shelter for large-sized sailships. The port had Denmark's 3rd-largest trade fleet - following only Copenhagen and Flensborg ( Flensburg ). The town also had several renowned shipbuilding yards. Among the town's most popular tourist attractions are Sanct Nicolai Kirke (13th-century church) and Brundlund Slot (15th-century castle, currently housing an Art Museum). Aabenraa is also a popular bathing resort vacation destination. Aabenraa is a compact port town where the historic centre, museums and waterfront are close enough to combine in a few hours. For most cruise visitors, sightseeing is easy independently once passengers have exited the secure port area . Aabenraa is primarily a commercial port rather than a purpose-built cruise terminal, so the exact berth, passenger gate and any ship-provided transport should be confirmed onboard.
getting_from_port: Aabenraa Havn is an active commercial and ISPS-controlled port with several basins and quays rather than a dedicated cruise terminal. Cruise ships have previously berthed at Sønderjyllandskajen , but berth assignments can change between calls. The port's secure areas are fenced and access-controlled, so passengers should follow the route specified for their particular ship rather than attempting to leave by an industrial gate. No permanent cruise shuttle service should be assumed; any shuttle or escorted transfer is call-specific. From the inner harbor area, central Aabenraa is very close. Depending on the berth and passenger exit, expect roughly 0.5–1 km (0.3–0.6 mi) to the pedestrianised old town. The Aabenraa bus station is also within the central area and is useful mainly for longer trips outside town.
terminal_notes: Aabenraa is primarily a commercial port rather than a purpose-built cruise terminal, so the exact berth, passenger gate and any ship-provided transport should be confirmed onboard.

things_to_do.name: Explore Aabenraa Old Town
things_to_do.description: Allow 1.5–2.5 hours. This is the simplest choice for a shorter call. Storetorv and Storegade form the pedestrianised heart of town, while narrow lanes such as Jomfrugangen, Persillegade and the Pottergade streets retain much of Aabenraa's older street pattern. Useful stops include the Old Town Hall at Storegade 30, Vægterpladsen and Sct. Nicolai Church. The tourist office at the Old Town Hall is also the starting point for an official self-guided audio walk, although the audio content is currently offered in Danish and German.

things_to_do.name: Brundlund Castle and the Historic Centre
things_to_do.description: Allow 2.5–3.5 hours for a combined walk. Brundlund Slot is close enough to add to an old-town visit without transport. The castle houses an art museum devoted largely to artists associated with Southern Jutland, while its moat, gardens and exterior are worthwhile even for passengers not planning a long museum visit. Another option is Museum Sønderjylland's Cultural History Aabenraa on H.P. Hanssens Gade. Its displays focus strongly on Aabenraa's sailing-ship, shipbuilding and trading heritage. Museum opening days and hours can be more limited than the outdoor attractions, so check them for the date of the call.

things_to_do.name: Sønderstrand City Beach
things_to_do.description: Allow about 2–3 hours for a relaxed beach visit, or add it to a longer walking day. Sønderstrand lies south of the central harbor and is Aabenraa's main city beach. It has Blue Flag status, a bathing jetty, toilets, changing facilities, a playground and seasonal refreshments. The beach is roughly 1–1.5 km (0.6–0.9 mi) from the central harbor area, depending on the passenger exit. The route is generally flat. It works particularly well in warm weather when sightseeing time is limited and a longer regional excursion is unnecessary.

things_to_do.name: Gråsten, Dybbøl and Sønderborg
things_to_do.description: Allow at least 4–5 hours. Passengers with a longer call can use Aabenraa as a base for Southern Jutland. Gråsten is about 22 km (13.7 mi) away by road, while Sønderborg is about 32 km (20.0 mi) away. Normal driving time is roughly 20–25 minutes to Gråsten and around 30–35 minutes to Sønderborg before allowing for traffic and stops. Gråsten Palace and its surroundings can be combined with the Dybbøl battlefield area and Sønderborg. Public buses connect Aabenraa and Sønderborg, with a typical journey taking around 50 minutes each way, but this consumes considerably more of a port call. An organized excursion, taxi or pre-arranged vehicle is preferable when combining several regional sights or when the ship has an early departure.

things_to_do.name: Old Town and Brundlund Castle
things_to_do.description: Distance: approximately 3 km (1.9 mi), depending on the passenger gate. Pure walking time: about 45 minutes. Recommended total time: 2–3 hours. Difficulty: Easy. Mostly level streets, with some cobbles and a gentle rise around the church. Passenger exit / inner harbor – Leave the secure port by the official passenger route. Gammelhavn and Skibbrogade – Walk toward the old town along the historic connection between the harbor and merchant quarter. Old Town Hall, Storegade 30 – A useful orientation point and the starting location for the town's official audio walk. Storegade and Storetorv – Follow the pedestrianised main street through Aabenraa's historic commercial centre. Vægterpladsen and the Pottergade lanes – Detour into the smaller streets for some of the best-preserved old houses. Sct. Nicolai Church – Visit the medieval church on its slight rise above the surrounding streets. Brundlund Castle – Walk south to the castle, moat and park; add the art museum if time and opening hours permit. Return to the port – Head back toward the harbor, allowing additional time to reach the correct security gate and gangway.

things_to_do.name: Old Town, Castle and Sønderstrand
things_to_do.description: Distance: approximately 4.5–5 km (2.8–3.1 mi). Pure walking time: about 1 hour 10 minutes. Recommended total time: 3–4 hours. Difficulty: Easy to moderate because of the additional distance; terrain remains mostly flat. Follow the old-town route through Sct. Nicolai Church and Brundlund Castle, then continue southeast to Sønderstrand. Spend time on the beach or bathing jetty before returning along the waterfront toward the cruise berth. This is a good option for passengers who prefer walking to indoor museum visits.
things_to_do.difficulty: Easy to moderate because of the additional distance

Aalborg is a North Sea port city in Denmark, located on Jutland Peninsula's north-eastern coast. By population (around 112,000) it is ranked the country's 4th largest - after Copenhagen , Aarhus and Odense . By road, the city is approx 65 km (40 mi) southwest of Frederikshavn , approx 120 km (73 mi) north of Aarhus and approx 410 km (255 mi) northwest of Copenhagen (Denmark's capital). Port Aalborg handles over 60% of Denmark's shipping trade with Greenland. The port has 4 harbours - Marina Fjordparken (closest to downtown), Skudehavnen (used mainly by fishing boats and Sejlklubben Limfjorden / sailing club), Vestre Badehavn (adjacent to Skudehavnen / ~1 km from downtown) and Ostre Havn (Eastern Harbor, residential and commercial district, site of the former Aalborg Shipyard). Private ports are Aalborg Portland (serving the cement plant) and Vattenfall (serving the power station). The town was established in the early-11th century, making it one of Denmark's oldest. Its strategic location (at Limfjorden's narrowest point) made it an important harbor port which later developed into a major industrial centre. The town is best-known for its half-timbered houses. Aalborg's current economy is based mainly on export shipping (grain, cement, coal, feedstuffs, fertilizers, spirits, oil cargoes), green-energy sectors (including production of rotors for wind turbines), information technologies, health support systems. City's largest companies and employers are Siemens Wind Power (turbine rotors), Aalborg Industries (manufacturer of marine boilers, burners, heat exchangers, inert gas systems), Aalborg Portland (cement producer), Telenor Denmark (telecommunications), Danisco (Danish Distillers, owned by Arcus ASA / Norway's largest wholesaler of wine and liquor). Tourism is another fast-growing industry, with an increasing number of overnight tourists. The city is served by Aalborg Airport (civilian/military) located in Norresundby, approx 7 km (4 mi) northwest of Aalborg. The airport serves domestic and international flights linking to Amsterdam, UK ( London ), Norway ( Oslo ), Spain ( Barcelona , Malaga ). Seasonal flights connect to Turkey ( Antalya ), Greece ( Crete , Cyprus ), Spain ( Mallorca , Gran Canaria ), Faroe Islands (Vagar), Sweden ( Bornholm ). Among city's most popular landmarks are Budolfi Catedral (15th-century), Aalborg Kloster (15th-century monastery), Alborghus Slot (16th-century castle), Aalborg Historiske Museum (with Viking relics), marine museum, military museum, Kunsten Museum (modern art), zoo, large nature parks, Tivoliland (theme park). 2019 was Aalborg cruise port's record season with handled 35 ship calls and ~30,000 tourists. For 2020 were projected min 45 ship calls and ~36,000 tourists. In July 2019, Port Aalborg introduced a new policy that limits the number of daily visiting cruise ships (calls) to one per day. The new rule was prompted by the increasing number of cruise vessels and their passengers-crew to Denmark's only inland cruise port. In the period 2014-2018, cruiser numbers increased from ~1000 (2014) to ~40,000 (2018). For 2019 were scheduled 34 ship calls and for 2020 were booked 45. In 2019, Aalborg's Royal Cruise Berth was deepened/dredged to allow docking of vessels with max LOA length 255 m (837 ft). Aalborg is one of the easier Danish cruise ports to explore independently. Most cruise calls use Honnørkajen, the Royal Cruise Berth directly on the city waterfront beside Aalborghus Castle. From here, the historic center, pedestrian streets and main waterfront sights are only a few minutes away on foot.
getting_from_port: Honnørkajen is directly in front of Aalborghus Castle and forms part of Aalborg's public waterfront. Passengers can normally start sightseeing immediately after leaving the ship. Nytorv, Østerågade and the pedestrian shopping streets are around a 5-10 minute walk away, while the Utzon Center is also only a few minutes from the berth. Not every ship necessarily uses Honnørkajen. The Port of Aalborg's current cruise schedule occasionally assigns vessels to Berth 4110, a commercial quay roughly 2 km (1.2 mi) from the central sightseeing area. If your ship uses an alternative berth, follow the onboard instructions for the passenger exit and any shuttle or transfer arrangements rather than assuming that the city-center walking route applies. Taxis are most useful for attractions outside the center. Aalborg also has a local bus network, with several routes serving central stops such as Nytorv and Vesterbro.
terminal_notes: In 2019, Aalborg's Royal Cruise Berth was deepened/dredged to allow docking of vessels with max LOA length 255 m (837 ft). Most cruise calls use Honnørkajen, the Royal Cruise Berth directly on the city waterfront beside Aalborghus Castle.

things_to_do.name: Historic Aalborg and the Waterfront
things_to_do.description: Allow: 2-3 hours. Transport: Walk. Independent sightseeing: Very easy. This is the most practical choice for a first visit. From the ship, combine Aalborghus Castle, Jens Bang's Renaissance house, Budolfi Cathedral and the small historic streets around Hjelmerstald with the modern Limfjord waterfront. The Utzon Center and Musikkens Hus provide a strong contrast to the older city and are still within easy walking distance of the ship.

things_to_do.name: Lindholm Høje Viking Site and Museum
things_to_do.description: Allow: about 2.5-3.5 hours. Distance: approximately 4.5 km (2.8 mi) from central Aalborg. Independent sightseeing: Practical with some planning. Lindholm Høje, across the Limfjord in Nørresundby, combines a large Iron Age and Viking burial ground with a museum explaining the site and Viking life around the fjord. A taxi generally takes around 10-15 minutes. Public buses from central Aalborg can also reach the Lindholm Høje area in roughly 15-20 minutes, but check the current timetable before leaving the city center. The outdoor archaeological site is on a hill and includes grass and uneven ground. Visitors with limited mobility may find the museum easier than the burial field itself.

things_to_do.name: Kunsten Museum of Modern Art
things_to_do.description: Allow: about 2-3 hours including transport. Distance: roughly 2 km (1.2 mi) from Honnørkajen. Independent sightseeing: Easy. Kunsten is particularly worthwhile for passengers interested in modern art and Scandinavian architecture. The building was designed by Alvar Aalto, Elissa Aalto and Jean-Jacques Baruël. It can be reached in around 25-30 minutes on foot from the waterfront or more quickly by taxi or local transport. Check the museum's opening hours for the day of your call before making it the main part of your visit.

things_to_do.name: Rebild Bakker and Rold Skov
things_to_do.description: Allow: at least 4-5 hours. Distance: about 30 km (18.6 mi) south of Aalborg. Independent sightseeing: Possible by car; organized excursion recommended for most cruise visitors. The heath-covered hills of Rebild Bakker and the neighboring Rold Skov forest are around a 30-minute drive from Aalborg. They suit passengers wanting countryside rather than city sightseeing, but public-transport connections consume considerably more port time. A ship excursion, private tour or pre-arranged taxi is more practical when the call is short.

things_to_do.name: Old Town and Waterfront Loop
things_to_do.description: Start: Honnørkajen/Royal Cruise Berth. Distance: approximately 3 km (1.9 mi). Pure walking time: about 40-45 minutes. Recommended total time: 2-3 hours. Difficulty: Easy, with some cobbled streets. Aalborghus Castle: Begin immediately beside the cruise berth. Walk through the grounds and view the half-timbered castle buildings. Nytorv and Jens Bang's House: Walk into the historic center to see one of Aalborg's best-known Renaissance buildings on Østerågade. Budolfi Cathedral and Gammeltorv: Continue through the pedestrian area to Aalborg's cathedral and the surrounding historic square. Hjelmerstald: Detour into this small cobbled street of low historic houses. The paving here is less even than the main pedestrian streets. Utzon Center: Return toward the Limfjord and follow the waterfront to Jørn Utzon's architecture and design center. Musikkens Hus: Continue east along the promenade to Aalborg's modern concert hall and cultural waterfront. Return to Honnørkajen: Retrace the waterfront promenade west to the ship. The route is largely flat and keeps you close to the ship throughout most of the day. It can easily be shortened by turning back at the Utzon Center or extended with cafés, shopping streets or an indoor museum visit.

Aappilattoq is a port village in Kujalleq municipality (Southern Greenland) with population around 200. Aappilattoq is located east of Nanortalik , approx 50 km (31 mi) north of Greenland's Cape Farewell. It is also close to some of world's most scenic fjords, including the 100 km (62 mi) long Prince Christian Sund. Town's name is translated as "sea anemone". The area has been inhabited since 19th century, but the current-day village was established in 1922. Locals' main occupations are hunting and fishing. The boat service house is operated by Kujalleq municipality. The general store is operated by KNI AS (Greenland Trade company, successor to Denmark's Royal Greenland Trading Department. The village also has a general repairs workshop and a fire station (served by Nanortalik fire department). It also has an elementary school and its own church. Main transportation routes are via sea or air. The village is inaccessible by land due to the surrounding mountain region and its remote location. Aappilattoq has a heliport (helicopter landing facility) served by Air Greenland (domestic airline) which operates (predominantly cargo helicopter) flights as part of a government contract. Every summer a number of large or very large ships cruise through Prince Christian Sound and en-route stop at Aappilattoq. Aappilattoq is a tiny, isolated settlement in South Greenland near Prince Christian Sound. Cruise visits are usually expedition-style calls rather than conventional port stops. Ships typically anchor offshore and passengers come ashore by tender or Zodiac at the small village harbor. Independent sightseeing: Easy within the village; organized excursion recommended for hiking beyond it. The settlement is compact enough to explore on foot, but there are no road connections to neighboring communities and little conventional tourist infrastructure. Aappilattoq does not have a cruise terminal for large ships. Expedition vessels and other visiting cruise ships generally anchor and transfer passengers ashore by tender or Zodiac. The exact landing arrangement can change with the ship, sea conditions and expedition plan. The small harbor is already inside the settlement, so there is no meaningful transfer into town. Once ashore, most village points of interest are within a short walk. There are no roads connecting Aappilattoq with other settlements. Reaching other communities, fjords or more distant wilderness requires a boat, helicopter or a substantial backcountry hike and is not realistic as an improvised cruise-day trip.
terminal_notes: Aappilattoq does not have a cruise terminal for large ships.
tender_evidence: Ships typically anchor offshore and passengers come ashore by tender or Zodiac at the small village harbor.

things_to_do.name: Walk Through Aappilattoq
things_to_do.description: Allow 1–1.5 hours. Wander through the compact settlement between the harbor and the houses scattered over the rocky ground. The church, cemetery, local football field, working waterfront and views across the surrounding fjords provide the main points of interest. This is easy to arrange independently after landing, although visitors should remember that Aappilattoq is a residential community rather than an open-air attraction. Keep clear of working areas and respect private homes.

things_to_do.name: Join a Local Cultural Visit
things_to_do.description: Allow about 1–2 hours. Local tourism activities can include guided village walks, kaffemik-style visits and singing performances. These are best arranged through the cruise line, expedition team or local operator rather than expected as walk-up activities.

things_to_do.name: Hike to a Viewpoint Above the Settlement
things_to_do.description: Allow around 1.5–3 hours depending on the route. Low hills around Aappilattoq provide elevated views of the colorful settlement, mountains and surrounding waterways. Some expedition itineraries include guided hikes through the village and onto higher ground. Organized or expedition-led hiking is recommended. Trails outside the settlement may be unmarked, and Greenlandic terrain can become steep, wet and slippery quickly. Do not treat surrounding mountains as a casual extension of the village walk.

things_to_do.name: Explore Prince Christian Sound by Zodiac
things_to_do.description: If offered by the ship, a Zodiac cruise can be more rewarding than spending the entire call ashore. The waterways around Aappilattoq are enclosed by steep mountains, with glaciers and floating ice possible elsewhere in the Prince Christian Sound system. This is an organized activity rather than something passengers should attempt independently. Conditions, ice and weather determine where small boats can operate.

things_to_do.name: Harbor, Church and Village Loop
things_to_do.description: Distance: roughly 1–1.5 km (0.6–0.9 mi), depending on the lanes and viewpoints used. Pure walking time: about 20–30 minutes. Recommended time: 60–90 minutes with stops. Difficulty: Easy to moderate because of uneven and occasionally sloping ground. Village harbor: Start from the tender or Zodiac landing and look back across the sheltered water toward the mountains. Working waterfront: Walk through the lower part of the settlement, keeping clear of boats and operational areas. Village lanes: Continue among the brightly painted houses toward the central part of Aappilattoq. Church and cemetery: Visit the church area and surrounding viewpoints while treating the cemetery respectfully. Football field: Continue toward the northern part of the settlement, where the local football field provides another glimpse of everyday village life. Low viewpoint: If conditions and your ship's instructions permit, use an obvious nearby path or rocky rise for a higher view rather than heading into the mountains. Return to the harbor: Retrace the village lanes to the landing area in good time for your tender or Zodiac departure.
things_to_do.difficulty: Easy to moderate because of uneven and occasionally sloping ground

Aarhus is Denmark's largest seaport and city on Jutland Peninsula's eastern coast. It is located approx 187 km (116 mi) northwest of Copenhagen (country's capital) and approx 290 km (180 mi) north of Hamburg Germany . The city has population around 275,000 (metro around 340,000), ranking it Denmark's second-largest (after Copenhagen). Among the well-known tourist attractions are ARoS Art Museum, Old Town Museum, Tivoli Friheden (amusement park), Moesgård Museum, Kvindemuseet (Women's Museum), The city is also a great shopping destination. Most foreign tourists are from Norway, Sweden, Germany and the UK. Overall annual tourist spending in the city is around USD 540 million. The average hotel stay is 3 days. Port Aarhus (locode DKAAR) is Denmark's largest and also one of northern Europe's biggest cargo ports (ranked 1st among the 200+ Baltic Sea cargo ports). It has the country's largest containership terminal handling over 1/2 of the country's container shipping traffic, 60% of the bulk cargo traffic and capacity to berth world's largest boxships . The port is located at the mouth of Aarhus River in Kattegat Sea, facing Helgenæs peninsula (east), Samso Island (southeast) and Riis Skov forest park (north). The seaport is self-governing and financially independent company managed by the municipality. Here are handled around 9,5 million cargo tons per year. The principal export is grain. Main imports include stone, cement, coal. The port has all 6 terminals - containership , multi-use, for bulk carriers, for oil tankers, ferries and cruise liners. Aarhus Ferry Terminal is used mainly by MOLSLINJEN ferries, serving annually ~1 million vehicles and ~2 million passengers. Aarhus Cruise Terminal serves cruise ships with Baltic Sea itineraries, operated between March and November. The Container Terminal is operated under concession by APM Terminals Aarhus - part of APM Terminals (2001-founded, The Hague Holland -based port and terminals management company, one of the world's largest). In 2020, APM Aarhus handled 593,670 TEU-containers (13% increase over 2019). APM Aarhus handles ~60% of Denmark's boxship traffic. In 2016 was inaugurated a regular flight service (via floatplanes) from Aarhus to Copenhagen, with fly time ~40 min (train travel time is ~3 hours). Aarhus Ferry Terminal is currently the only alternative to Storebæltsforbindelsen (Great Belt Fixed Link) that crosses the strait between the islands Zealand and Funen. The route is served with regularly scheduled ferries since 1830. The current main ferry operator is MOLSLINJEN, with annual traffic ~2 million passengers and 1 million vehicles. Ro-Ro ships (cargo ferries) link Aarhus to Kalundborg and Finland (regular weekly service). Aarhus is also becoming a cruise port destination for companies operating on Baltic Sea itineraries. In 2010, it was visited by just 2 ships and ~4300 tourists. In 2012 it handled 18 ship calls and over 38,000 passengers. In 2013 were handled 13 cruise calls. In 2018 were booked 41 cruise ship berthings with estimated nearly 100,000 passengers. In March 2022, Port Aarhus contracted Shore Link OU ( Tallinn Estonia -based engineering company specializing in port shorepower solutions) and PowerCon AS (Hadsund Denmark-based manufacturing company specializing in wind turbines) to design, supply and install a shore-power system. Shoreside power capabilities allow berthed vessels to turn off their diesel engines and instead use the city's power-grid electricity for onboard operations and services. The new system (inaugurated in June 2023) has a separate "CMS Cruiser"/smaller capacity unit designed exclusively for cruise liners. The other Danish cruise port with shore power capabilities is Copenhagen . Aarhus Port's shore-power facility was inaugurated on June 20, 2023, with AIDAmar ship . The system's total cost was EUR 7 million, of which 5M from the Port, 1M from the city and 1M from the European Union. The energy provider is the local company KONSTANT Net AS. Port Aarhus welcomes cruise ship passengers with live performances by Den Jyske Pigegarde (orchestra and dance girls aged 8-25) - usually a folk dance show. The terminal is located across the street from downtown. The quay was extensively improved in 2012. Since 2018, cruise passengers in Aarhus are welcomed by local hosts. These are around 1300 volunteers serving as hosts for cruisers. They all wear blue t-shirts and badgets signed "ASK ME", and assist the disembarking tourists with various cultural events in the city. Aarhus cruise port is located 3 hours from Copenhagen by bus. There are bus connections to Hamburg too. The closest airport is Tirstrup (45 min by bus). Independent sightseeing: Easy independently from the main cruise quay. Aarhus is one of the more convenient Scandinavian cruise calls for exploring on foot. Ships normally dock rather than tender, and the main cruise quay at Balticagade is close to the historic centre. Port of Aarhus also uses the more distant Omni Terminal for some calls, so check your ship's berth before planning a walking day.
getting_from_port: The usual cruise quay is at Balticagade in the harbour immediately southeast of central Aarhus. From here, DOKK1 on the waterfront is approximately 0.7 km (0.4 mi) away, while Aarhus Cathedral and the central pedestrian streets are about 1 km (0.6 mi) from the cruise area. Walking is normally the simplest option. The route into town is largely level, and once in the centre most major sights are close enough to combine without transport. Some cruise ships can instead berth at the Port of Aarhus Omni Terminal, which is farther inside the commercial harbour. If your ship is assigned there, do not use walking times from the Balticagade cruise quay; follow the transfer and passenger-exit arrangements announced for your particular call. Aarhus has city buses and the Letbanen light rail. DOKK1 is a useful transport point near the waterfront. Tickets for Aarhus city buses and light rail should be purchased before boarding, so passengers planning to use public transport should arrange a ticket through the available ticketing apps or other official sales channels before travelling.
terminal_notes: It has the country's largest containership terminal handling over 1/2 of the country's container shipping traffic, 60% of the bulk cargo traffic and capacity to berth world's largest boxships . Aarhus Ferry Terminal is used mainly by MOLSLINJEN ferries, serving annually ~1 million vehicles and ~2 million passengers. Aarhus Cruise Terminal serves cruise ships with Baltic Sea itineraries, operated between March and November. The Container Terminal is operated under concession by APM Terminals Aarhus - part of APM Terminals (2001-founded, The Hague Holland -based port and terminals management company, one of the world's largest). Aarhus Ferry Terminal is currently the only alternative to Storebæltsforbindelsen (Great Belt Fixed Link) that crosses the strait between the islands Zealand and Funen. The terminal is located across the street from downtown. Port of Aarhus also uses the more distant Omni Terminal for some calls, so check your ship's berth before planning a walking day.
tender_evidence: Ships normally dock rather than tender, and the main cruise quay at Balticagade is close to the historic centre.

things_to_do.name: Historic Centre, Cathedral and Latin Quarter
things_to_do.description: Allow: about 2–3 hours. Independent: very easy. For a short call, walking into central Aarhus gives the best return for your time. Continue from DOKK1 toward Store Torv and Aarhus Cathedral, then explore the small streets of the Latin Quarter, Lille Torv, the Aarhus River and the pedestrian shopping area. Salling Rooftop can be added for an elevated city view when accessible. This option needs no transport and can easily be shortened if the ship has an early departure.

things_to_do.name: ARoS Aarhus Art Museum
things_to_do.description: Allow: about 2–3 hours including the walk. Independent: easy. ARoS is approximately 2 km (1.2 mi) from the main cruise quay and is practical on foot in roughly 25 minutes. Its best-known feature is the rooftop Your rainbow panorama, but allow enough time for the galleries if art is your main priority. ARoS combines particularly well with the cathedral, Møllestien and the riverfront on the walk back toward the ship.

things_to_do.name: Den Gamle By – The Old Town Museum
things_to_do.description: Allow: about 3–4 hours. Independent: easy with a longer walk or local transport. Den Gamle By is an extensive open-air museum recreating Danish town life in different periods. It is roughly 2.5 km (1.6 mi) from the main cruise area, around a 30–35 minute walk depending on the route and pace. Because the museum itself deserves at least a couple of hours, passengers with limited time may prefer to walk there through the centre and use a taxi or public transport for one direction. Much of the attraction is outdoors, so ARoS may be the more practical museum choice in poor weather.

things_to_do.name: Moesgaard Museum
things_to_do.description: Allow: about 3–4 hours including transport. Independent: practical with planning and public transport. Moesgaard is outside central Aarhus and should be treated as a separate excursion rather than added casually to a city walk. It lies approximately 9 km (5.6 mi) south of central Aarhus and focuses on archaeology, prehistory and anthropology. City bus 18 runs from the central Park Allé/Banegårdspladsen area directly to Moesgaard, with the bus journey taking about 25 minutes. A taxi is simpler when time ashore is tight. Combining Moesgaard, Den Gamle By and a thorough visit to ARoS in one normal cruise call would usually make the day unnecessarily rushed.

things_to_do.name: Southern Coast and the Infinite Bridge
things_to_do.description: Allow: about 2–3 hours with transport. Independent: possible, but transport is advisable. The coastline south of central Aarhus combines beaches and Marselisborg woodland. The Infinite Bridge at Varna/Ballehage is a circular wooden walkway extending over Aarhus Bay and makes a good alternative for passengers more interested in scenery than museums. The bridge is seasonal and is normally installed from spring until late October. It is better reached by local transport, taxi or bicycle than by walking all the way from the cruise ship during a limited port call.

things_to_do.name: Harbour, Old Aarhus and ARoS Loop
things_to_do.description: Distance: approximately 5.5 km (3.4 mi). Pure walking time: about 70–80 minutes. Recommended total time: 3–4 hours with sightseeing stops. Difficulty: easy to moderate. Mostly level streets, with some cobbles and gentle gradients around ARoS and the western centre. Balticagade cruise quay: leave the main cruise area and walk toward central Aarhus along the harbour. DOKK1: pass the distinctive waterfront library and continue toward the historic centre. Store Torv and Aarhus Cathedral: explore the cathedral square and surrounding old streets. ARoS Aarhus Art Museum: continue southwest through the centre. Visit the museum if time allows, or simply use it as the turning point of the walk. Mølleparken and Møllestien: descend toward the Aarhus River and detour through the small cobbled street of Møllestien. Latin Quarter: continue via Vestergade and Lille Torv into the narrow streets north of the cathedral. Salling Rooftop and central pedestrian streets: add the rooftop viewpoint if time permits, then head back toward DOKK1. Return to Balticagade: follow the waterfront back to the cruise quay. This route closely follows a locally recommended central Aarhus walk and works particularly well for cruise passengers because it begins and ends at the harbour. Skip the ARoS interior if you have less than three hours available ashore.

The port's schedule lists all ships (in links) with cruises going to or leaving from Aasiaat, Greenland. To see the full itineraries (ports of call dates and arrival / departure times) and their lowest rates – just follow the corresponding ship-link.
description: Port Aasiaat cruise ship schedule shows timetable calendars of all arrival and departure dates by month. The port's schedule lists all ships (in links) with cruises going to or leaving from Aasiaat, Greenland. To see the full itineraries (ports of call dates and arrival / departure times) and their lowest rates – just follow the corresponding ship-link. Aasiaat (port locode GLJEG) is a town in western Greenland (Aasiaat Archipelago) located at Disko Bay's southern end. By population (around 3,000) it is Greenland's 5th-largest town. Its name means "Spiders" in Greenlandic. Sometimes, Aasiaat is referred to as "the Town of the Whales", because marine mammals such as seals and whales are a common sight. Aasiaat is a ferry port for Arctic Umiaq Line (freight and passenger shipping company). Arctic Umiaq serves the south-western Greenland route roundtrip from Nuuk . Next are listed route's ports of call (with arrival-departure times in brackets) - Nuuk (departure 8 pm)- Maniitsoq (6-630 am)- Kangaamiut (10-10:15 am)- Sisimiut (5-7 pm)-Aasiaat (6-6:15 am)-Qeqertarsuaq (10-10:15 am)- Ilulissat (3:30-5 pm)-Aasiaat (9:30-10 pm)-Sisimiut (9-11 am)-Kangaamiut (5:45-6 pm)-Maniitsoq (9:30-10 pm)-Nuuk (7-9 am)-Qeqertarsuatsiaat (4:30-4:45 pm)- Paamiut (11:45-12 midnight)-Arsuk (6:45-7 am)- Qaqortoq (4-7 pm)- Narsaq (9:9:30 pm)-Arsuk (6:45-7 am)-Paamiut (2-2:30 pm)-Qeqertarsuatsiaat (10:15-10:30 pm)-Nuuk (arrival 7:30 am). Aasiaat is a compact Greenlandic town on the southern edge of Disko Bay, surrounded by a low archipelago of islands, channels and open water. For cruise visitors, the main attractions are the historic waterfront, Aasiaat Museum, local art and short boat trips into the archipelago. Most central sightseeing is straightforward on foot.
getting_from_port: Aasiaat has a working commercial and ferry harbour rather than a purpose-built cruise terminal. Cruise ships may anchor offshore and tender passengers into the harbour. Follow the ship's instructions for the exact landing point and final tender time, as arrangements can change with the vessel and conditions. Once ashore, walking is the most practical way to explore. The museum, church, old colonial buildings, shops and other central sights are clustered around the harbour. Taxis exist, but they are generally unnecessary for a normal town visit.

things_to_do.name: Explore the Historic Harbour and Aasiaat Museum
things_to_do.description: Allow: about 1.5–2 hours. This is the simplest choice for a short port call. Walk through the harbour and preserved colonial area to Aasiaat Museum, housed in the former colonial manager's residence. The collections concentrate on local and Greenlandic history, including hunting, kayaking, sledding and traditional life. The nearby sod house, historic waterfront buildings and Aasiaat Church make this a compact cultural circuit. Museum access and opening times should be checked on the day of the visit.

things_to_do.name: Follow Aasiaat's Art Around Town
things_to_do.description: Allow: about 1.5–2.5 hours. Aasiaat has an unusually strong collection of public art for a town of its size. Murals decorate several apartment blocks, while stone sculptures by local artist Jens Erik Kjeldsen are scattered through the town. The assembly house also contains a large group of paintings created by Danish artist Per Kirkeby. Destination Disko Bay publishes an Art'n'Walk self-guided route and a separate guide to Aasiaat's historic houses. These are useful additions to a cruise-day walk because the sights are dispersed through the central streets rather than concentrated in a single attraction.

things_to_do.name: Take a Sea Safari through the Aasiaat Archipelago
things_to_do.description: Allow: around 2 hours for a typical local boat excursion, plus time to reach the departure point and return to the tender. The surrounding archipelago is one of Aasiaat's main attractions. Local boat trips may combine island scenery, icebergs and the historic whale graveyard, with the possibility of seeing whales. Summer is the main whale-watching season, although wildlife sightings are never guaranteed. Organized excursion recommended: Boat departures are weather-dependent and may not align with a short cruise call. A cruise-line excursion or a locally pre-booked trip specifically timed around the ship is safer than trying to arrange one after arrival.

things_to_do.name: Short Nature Walk
things_to_do.description: Aasiaat Island is relatively low compared with many Greenland destinations, and marked hiking routes lead beyond the town into open Arctic terrain. For passengers with a longer call, a short section of one of these routes can provide coastal and archipelago views without committing to a full hike. The established longer routes are not ideal for a typical short cruise visit. For example, the Tele Mast/Top 90 route is roughly 4.4–5 km (2.7–3.1 mi) and may require 2–4 hours, while the Nuggoq route is about 8 km (5.0 mi) and takes roughly 2–4 hours. Only attempt them when the port schedule leaves a substantial margin for the return.

things_to_do.name: Harbour, History and Art Circuit
things_to_do.description: Distance: approximately 1.5–2 km (0.9–1.2 mi). Pure walking time: about 30–40 minutes. Recommended total time: 1.5–2 hours. Difficulty: Easy to moderate, with some gradients and uneven surfaces. Tender landing / tourist pontoon: Start in the central harbour area and take a few minutes to look across the working waterfront. Old colonial harbour: Walk through the historic cluster of traditional wooden buildings near the waterfront. Aasiaat Museum: Visit the local-history collections if the museum is open. Sod House: See the traditional turf-house reconstruction beside the museum area. Aasiaat Church: Continue uphill to the church overlooking the harbour. Assembly House: Pass the building known for its collection of Per Kirkeby paintings. Harbour and local shops: Loop back toward the waterfront, passing the commercial centre and Brættet, the traditional local provisions market area. Tender landing: Return directly to the harbour with plenty of time before the final tender. This route keeps you close to the ship throughout and can easily be shortened if tender operations or weather reduce your time ashore.
things_to_do.difficulty: Easy to moderate, with some gradients and uneven surfaces

name: Abashiri (Japan Okhotsk)
summary: Abashiri (port locode JPABA) is a port city in Japan's Okhotsk Subprefecture (on Hokkaido Island) with population around 40,000. The city is served by trains (Abashiri Station) and domestic flights (Memanbetsu Airport, near Ozora).
description: Abashiri (port locode JPABA) is a port city in Japan's Okhotsk Subprefecture (on Hokkaido Island) with population around 40,000. The city is served by trains (Abashiri Station) and domestic flights (Memanbetsu Airport, near Ozora). Port Abashiri is in Okhotsk's eastern part, approx 50 km (31 mi) east of Kitami. The surrounding scenery lacks tall mountains and instead is marked by numerous low hills, the Abashiri River (flowing through the town), 3 lakes (Abashiri, Notoro, and Tofutsu) inside the city. The lakes and Mt Tento (height 207 m / 680 ft) are part of the Abashiri NP. Because of the short growing season, crops in the region (oats, potatoes, beans) are required to be hardy. Hay is also grown as fodder for cows, horses, and sheep. The city's economy is also heavily dependent on commercial fishing, oysters farming and seaweed. Despite the reputation for its extremely cold weather, Abashiri is not among Japan's coldest cities. It is actually less cold in the winter months than Obihiro and warmer during the summer than Kushiro or Nemuro. Abashiri obtains less precipitation than any other Japanese city because of its location on the drift-ice-affected Okhotsk Sea. Fogs are common during winter when Lake Abashiri freezes. On Mt Tento is located the "Okhotsk Ryu-hyo Museum". The facility offers extensive information and real drift ice experience. The museum's basement level has the "Drift Ice Illusion Gallery" (with 5 large LED screens) featuring 3D drift ice show. The museum's "Drift Ice Experience Terrace" boasts a 100-ton ice pack preserved at temperature -15 C. From Abashiri as cruise shore excursions are offered bus tours to Shiretoko National Park (on Hokkaido Island's northeastern tip). The National Park (NP) has land area approx 386 km2 (149 mi2), covers most of the Shiretoko Peninsula (one of Japan's most remote regions), and is the home of the country's largest population of brown bears. From the Peninsula can be seen Kunashir Island - part of Russia's Kuril Islands archipelago. Often in the winter, Abashiri harbour closes due to ice-cover. Aurora 1 and Aurora 2 are Abashiri port-based icebreaker cruise ships offering sightseeing tours. Tourists can not only see but get closer and even touch the ice on the locally famous "Abashiri Drift Ice Sightseeing" Icebreaker cruises around the city's ice sea. During the icebreaker cruise, passengers can hear the actual cracking of ice. Other option available on these tours are taking break on ice floes (ice floats / large packs of floating ice) and wildlife viewing (seals, Steller's sea eagles). These cruise tours are operated each year in the period late-January through early April. Abashiri is a compact eastern Hokkaido port with several distinctive attractions close to the city, but the cruise berth is not directly in the sightseeing centre. Ships normally dock alongside at Abashiri Port rather than tender. Independent sightseeing is practical with a taxi or local bus, especially for the museums around Mt. Tento, while longer trips toward Shiretoko are better suited to organized excursions.
getting_from_port: Japan's official cruise-port guide lists No. 4 Wharf #2 as Abashiri's cruise berth. It is within the commercial port at Minatomachi, and the exact berth arrangements can vary with the ship. JR Abashiri Station and Abashiri Bus Terminal are both approximately 10 minutes from the cruise berth by car. Walking from the ship into the sightseeing centre is not the most practical choice because the route begins within a working harbour area and uses ordinary port roads. No permanent cruise shuttle should be assumed. Check the ship's information for any transfer provided on the day. Otherwise, a taxi is the simplest way to reach the city centre, Roadside Station Ryuhyo Kaido Abashiri or the Mt. Tento museums. The GO taxi-dispatch app also operates in Abashiri. Once in central Abashiri, local buses become useful. The Tourist Facility Tour Line links Abashiri Bus Terminal and JR Abashiri Station with Abashiri Prison Museum, Okhotsk Ryu-hyo Museum and the Hokkaido Museum of Northern Peoples.
terminal_notes: Abashiri is a compact eastern Hokkaido port with several distinctive attractions close to the city, but the cruise berth is not directly in the sightseeing centre.
tender_evidence: Ships normally dock alongside at Abashiri Port rather than tender.

things_to_do.name: Abashiri Prison Museum
things_to_do.description: Allow 2–3 hours including transfers. This open-air museum is Abashiri's best-known attraction and preserves historic buildings from the former prison, including the distinctive five-wing wooden cell block. A quick visit takes about one hour, while roughly two hours is better for exploring the site properly. The museum is on the lower slopes of Mt. Tento. From JR Abashiri Station, the sightseeing-facilities bus takes roughly 7–9 minutes. Taxi travel from the cruise port is also straightforward and is particularly useful when port time is limited. Do not confuse the museum with the modern Abashiri Prison nearby, which remains an active correctional facility.

things_to_do.name: Mt. Tento and Okhotsk Ryu-hyo Museum
things_to_do.description: Allow 2–3 hours. The Okhotsk Ryu-hyo Museum stands on Mt. Tento, roughly 5 km (3.1 mi) from JR Abashiri Station. Its exhibits explain the Sea of Okhotsk's drift ice and marine life, including a chilled room containing real drift ice. The rooftop observatory provides panoramic views toward the Sea of Okhotsk, Lake Abashiri and, in clear weather, the Shiretoko mountain range. The sightseeing bus from Abashiri Station normally takes about 12–14 minutes. The Hokkaido Museum of Northern Peoples is nearby and focuses on the cultures of northern peoples including the Ainu and other Arctic and sub-Arctic communities. It can be added when the ship has a longer stay, but visiting all three major museums in detail can consume most of a port day.

things_to_do.name: Combine the Prison Museum and Mt. Tento
things_to_do.description: Allow about 4 hours. This is arguably the best independent itinerary for a normal Abashiri cruise call. Take a taxi or the Tourist Facility Tour bus to Abashiri Prison Museum, spend 1.5–2 hours there, then continue to the Okhotsk Ryu-hyo Museum for another 1–1.5 hours. The sightseeing bus serves both locations, but its timetable should be checked before leaving the ship. A taxi gives greater flexibility and reduces waiting time when the port stay is short.

things_to_do.name: Lake Tofutsu and the Okhotsk Coast
things_to_do.description: Allow about 3–4 hours. Lake Tofutsu is approximately 12 km (7.5 mi) from central Abashiri and around 15 minutes away by car. The lake is a protected wetland known for migratory birds, with a Waterfowl and Wetland Center providing an easy introduction to the area. Public buses serve the area, followed by a short walk from the nearest stop, but a taxi, private vehicle or organized excursion is more efficient for cruise passengers. This option works particularly well for visitors more interested in landscapes and wildlife than museums.

things_to_do.name: Waterfront, Moyoro and Downtown
things_to_do.description: Distance: approximately 2 km (1.2 mi). Pure walking time: about 35–45 minutes. Recommended total time: 1.5–2.5 hours with stops. Difficulty: Easy. Mostly level urban streets and waterfront paths. Take a taxi from the cruise berth to Roadside Station Ryuhyo Kaido Abashiri rather than beginning the walk inside the commercial port. Roadside Station Ryuhyo Kaido Abashiri: Start at the waterfront tourism centre, where local information, food and souvenirs are available. The Aurora sightseeing boat also uses this complex during the winter drift-ice season. Abashiri River Mouth: Walk along the waterfront where the river enters the Sea of Okhotsk, with views across the fishing harbour. Moyoro Shell Mound Museum: Continue roughly 15 minutes to this archaeological museum built beside the remains of an important Okhotsk-culture settlement. Abashiri River: Cross back toward the central city and follow the river into the downtown area. Central Abashiri: Explore the compact shopping and restaurant streets around Minami 2-jo. Abashiri Bus Terminal: Finish near the bus terminal, from where a taxi can return directly to the cruise berth or a sightseeing bus can continue toward Mt. Tento. This route works particularly well as a short independent visit or as an addition after one of the museums. Allow additional time for the taxi or other authorized transfer back through the port.

things_to_do.name: Drift-Ice Sightseeing
things_to_do.description: Abashiri is famous for sea ice arriving from the Sea of Okhotsk during winter. The Aurora drift-ice sightseeing vessel normally operates from the Roadside Station Ryuhyo Kaido Abashiri area from late January through March. The presence and density of drift ice depend entirely on weather, winds and sea conditions, so it cannot be guaranteed. Cruise passengers visiting during the operating season should also make sure the boat timetable leaves sufficient time to return to their ship.

things_to_do.name: Summer and Early Autumn
things_to_do.description: During the warmer cruise season, the surrounding wetlands, coastal scenery and flower areas become more relevant than actual drift ice. The Okhotsk Ryu-hyo Museum still provides a drift-ice experience year-round, making it a useful alternative outside winter.

name: Aberdeen (Scotland)
summary: Port Aberdeen cruise ship schedule shows timetable calendars of all arrival and departure dates by month. The port's schedule lists all ships (in links) with cruises going to or leaving from Aberdeen, Scotland. To see the full itineraries (ports of call dates and arrival / departure times) and their lowest rates – just follow the corresponding ship-link.
description: Port Aberdeen cruise ship schedule shows timetable calendars of all arrival and departure dates by month. The port's schedule lists all ships (in links) with cruises going to or leaving from Aberdeen, Scotland. To see the full itineraries (ports of call dates and arrival / departure times) and their lowest rates – just follow the corresponding ship-link. Aberdeen is a North Sea port city in Scotland located between the rivers Dee and Don. By population (around 230,000) the city is ranked the UK's 37th. The company Northlink Ferries provides regularly scheduled crossings connecting Aberdeen with the Northern Isles, Lerwick (Mainland Shetland) and Kirkwall (Orkney Island) . Founded as a fishing port on Dee River's estuary, Aberdeen Harbour (locode GBABD) has continually been improved. It is currently a major cargo port for export goods shipped from UK to Scandinavia (Baltic Sea in general). Major exports include granite, chemicals, fertilizers. By cruise liners, the Port is usually visited on "Around Britain" itineraries, as well as on some Scandinavian (Baltic Sea) itineraries. Port's cruising season is early-May through early-September. Harbour's water depth (max draft) is 10,5 m (35 ft). In 2017, the cruise port handled 25 ship calls and 2095 passengers. In 2018, at Aberdeen Harbour were handled 27 cruise ship calls and 3387 passengers (61% increase over 2017). In 2018, NorthLink ferry traffic increased by 5% (to 151,000+ passengers). The total number of ship calls increased from 6775 (2017) to 9266 (2018). The Port's total ship tonnage increased 5%. In 2018 were continued the works on the harbor's north breakwater - part of GBP 350 million port expansion project at Nigg Bay (completed in 2020). The Harbour's expansion allowed docking of larger passenger ships , also ranking Port Aberdeen as Scotland's largest by berth capacity. On May 29, 2019, Aberdeen Harbour welcomed its ever-longest vessel - the 175-m/574-ft MV Beltnes (IMO 9432206). The Self Discharging Bulk Carrier arrived to discharge 35000 tons of Norway-quarried fill material at South Harbour (behind the concrete caissons). The operation was part of the GBP 350 million South Harbour construction project, and particularly for creating the two new quays (Dunnottar and Castlegate). Both docks are designed to support activities associated with the booming renewable energy industry. In late September 2020, Aberdeen Harbour Board awarded Royal Van Oord (1868-founded Dutch company specializing in dredging, land reclamation, and artificial islands construction) with two contracts for Aberdeen South Harbour's expansion. The project included rock removal and revetment (coastal engineering/shore protection) works. South Harbour's expansion (budgeted ~GBP 400M) became the UK's largest marine infrastructure project and was completed in April 2023. In 2023, cruise ships were handled at three quays, representing over 40% of Aberdeen's cruise calls. A short, restriction-free channel provides straightforward harbor access (entry and egress/exiting) and allows vessels to quickly navigate the pilot buoy. In November 2021, the Port received GBP 0,4 million (~EUR 0,48M) in Government funding for a demo "Feasibility Study for Shore Power" (via a partnership with Connected Places Catapult) for a shoreside power supply facility within North Harbour. The technology allows berthed ships to turn off their engines/diesel generators and instead use electricity from the port's/city's power grid. In 2023 (May through October) the cruise port handled a total of 43 ship calls (~33000 tourists). For season 2024 were scheduled/booked 55 calls. Stats for 2023 showed that each cruise ship visit resulted in an average of GBP 134 (EUR 154/USD 163) per person in passenger expenditure. In 2024, the Port had scheduled 60 cruise ship calls (+150% over 2022). In 2025 (April to September) were booked 63 ship berthings with estimated ~40,000 passengers. Aberdeen is Scotland's oil industry center, university center, as well as one of the country's largest seaside resorts. Best-known tourist attractions include St Machar's Cathedral (15th-century), Mercat Cross (17th-century), Brig o' Balgownie (14th-century, Scotland's oldest bridge), and Winter Garden (Europe's largest indoor garden). Old Town Aberdeen is the "students' quarter", also housing the campuses of two 15th-century universities - King's College (est 1495) and Marischal College (est 1500) - now combined into the University of Aberdeen. The city is perfect as a base for touring the nearby castles Crathes, Dunnotar, and Slains, as well as the whisky distilleries Glenlivet, Glenfiddich, Speyside Cooperage. Other popular sites include the Royal Family's summer residence Balmoral Castle, and the Braemar Castle, which hosts the Highland's largest games every September. During the mid-18th-mid-20th centuries, the town's buildings incorporated locally quarried grey granite, that sparkles like silver due to its high mica content. In 2017, Port Aberdeen started building a new deepwater harbour to attract larger-sized cruise liners (with max capacity 5000 passengers and crew). The new facility is scheduled for completion in 2020. Currently, Aberdeen is a tender cruise port and handles annually around 30 smaller-sized vessels. After the vessel anchors, its passengers are transported ashore via the ship's tender boats. The new / deeper harbor will allow direct (quayside) disembarkation. Aberdeen is a practical cruise port for independent sightseeing, but the experience depends strongly on the ship's berth. Larger cruise ships normally use the expanded South Harbour, several kilometres from the city centre, while smaller vessels may use berths in the older North Harbour much closer to central Aberdeen. Ships normally dock alongside rather than tender.
getting_from_port: Port of Aberdeen has two principal harbour areas. South Harbour, completed in 2023, has deep-water berths capable of handling ships up to 300 m (984 ft) long and now receives many of the larger cruise vessels. Cruise ships have used berths including Balmoral Quay and Castlegate Quay. South Harbour is roughly 4–5 km (2.5–3.1 mi) by road from the central Union Square area, depending on the berth and port exit used. Walking from these berths into central Aberdeen is not a good use of limited port time because the route passes through and around working harbour and industrial areas. Transfers arranged by the cruise line may operate on individual calls, but passengers should check the ship's daily information rather than assume a shuttle is provided. Taxis or pre-arranged vehicles are another practical option, with the journey into central Aberdeen normally taking around 10–15 minutes in ordinary traffic. Smaller ships can sometimes berth in North Harbour, where some quays are much closer to Union Square, the Maritime Museum and the city centre. If the ship is assigned a North Harbour berth, walking may be practical after passengers leave the controlled port area. Union Square is a useful starting point for independent travel. Aberdeen railway station and bus station are together here, providing easy connections for trips to Stonehaven and other parts of Aberdeenshire.
terminal_notes: The Harbour's expansion allowed docking of larger passenger ships , also ranking Port Aberdeen as Scotland's largest by berth capacity. Aberdeen is a practical cruise port for independent sightseeing, but the experience depends strongly on the ship's berth.
tender_evidence: Currently, Aberdeen is a tender cruise port and handles annually around 30 smaller-sized vessels.

things_to_do.name: Aberdeen City Centre and Maritime Museum
things_to_do.description: Allow 2–4 hours. This is the simplest independent option and works well even on a relatively short call. Aberdeen Maritime Museum overlooks the old harbour and covers the city's shipbuilding, fishing and offshore-energy connections. From the museum, continue on foot through the historic centre to Castlegate, Marischal College, Provost Skene's House, Aberdeen Art Gallery and Union Terrace Gardens. Most of these sights are within a compact central area, so very little transport is required once passengers reach Union Square.

things_to_do.name: Old Aberdeen
things_to_do.description: Allow about 3 hours. Old Aberdeen is approximately 4 km (2.5 mi) north of Union Square and has a very different character from the commercial city centre. Highlights include King's College, the University of Aberdeen's historic campus, St Machar's Cathedral and the Cruickshank Botanic Garden. Take a local bus or taxi from the city centre rather than walking the entire distance. Between April and September, the seasonal Aberdeen Adventurer sightseeing bus also serves Old Aberdeen. Once there, the principal sights are close enough to explore on foot.

things_to_do.name: Stonehaven and Dunnottar Castle
things_to_do.description: Allow about 4–5 hours. This is one of the best independent excursions from Aberdeen when the ship has a comfortable port call. Trains from Aberdeen to Stonehaven average about 17 minutes, making rail considerably more practical than many cruise-port day trips. Stonehaven station is around a 15-minute walk from the town and harbour. From the harbour, a scenic coastal path continues to Dunnottar Castle, approximately 2.6 km (1.6 mi) south of Stonehaven. The clifftop walk takes roughly 20–30 minutes in each direction. Dunnottar itself is considerably more demanding than the approach suggests. Entry involves a long descent and climb, including more than 200 steps, and there are no lifts or ramps into the castle. Passengers with limited mobility can still reach the clifftop viewpoint without entering the ruins. For a quicker visit, use a taxi between Stonehaven and the castle rather than walking the coastal path. Leave additional time for the train back to Aberdeen and the final transfer from Union Square to the ship.

things_to_do.name: Royal Deeside and Crathes Castle
things_to_do.description: Allow about 4–6 hours. Crathes Castle is approximately 26 km (16.2 mi) west of Aberdeen and combines a 16th-century tower house with gardens and woodland. Banchory and the surrounding River Dee countryside can be added on a longer call. Organized excursion or pre-arranged transport is preferable. Regional buses run along Royal Deeside, but using several local connections consumes valuable port time. A coach excursion or private driver makes it much easier to visit a castle and countryside stops while retaining a sensible return margin. Balmoral Castle is much farther west, near Ballater, and its public opening arrangements are seasonal and can change during the year. Cruise passengers should only plan a Balmoral visit after checking that the estate is open on the date of their call.

things_to_do.name: Union Square to Aberdeen's Historic Centre
things_to_do.description: Distance: approximately 2.5 km (1.6 mi). Pure walking time: about 35–45 minutes. Recommended total time: 2–3 hours with stops. Difficulty: Easy. Mostly paved city streets with some gentle gradients. Union Square: Start here after arriving from South Harbour, or use it as the reference point if walking from a nearby North Harbour berth. Aberdeen Maritime Museum: Walk to Shiprow for views over the historic harbour and, if time permits, visit the museum. Castlegate and Mercat Cross: Continue through the lower end of Union Street to one of the city's main historic public spaces. Marischal College: Walk north to the large granite Gothic building that is one of Aberdeen's most recognizable landmarks. Provost Skene's House: Visit Aberdeen's oldest surviving townhouse, immediately beside Marischal Square. Check the day's opening arrangements if planning to go inside. Aberdeen Art Gallery: Continue west through the city centre to the gallery and surrounding cultural district. Union Terrace Gardens: Finish with a walk through the landscaped gardens before following Union Street or Guild Street back toward Union Square. Passengers returning to a South Harbour berth should allow additional time for the transfer from Union Square or the city centre back to the ship.

things_to_do.name: Torry Battery and Greyhope Bay
things_to_do.description: Allow about 2 hours. Torry Battery overlooks the entrance to Aberdeen Harbour and is one of the city's best locations for watching bottlenose dolphins. Dolphins are seen throughout the year, although sightings can never be guaranteed. Greyhope Bay Centre provides a sheltered viewpoint and café at the battery. The area is geographically close to South Harbour but is best reached by taxi or pre-arranged transport rather than trying to find a pedestrian route through the working port. This is a useful choice for passengers who prefer wildlife and coastal scenery to museums, and it can also be combined with central Aberdeen when the call is long enough.

Abidjan (port locode CIABJ) is the principal seaport, the largest city and the economic capital of the Ivory Coast (Cote d'Ivoire). It is also one of Africa's most populous French-speaking cities. The city has population around 4,4 million. Considered Africa's cultural crossroad, Abidjan is characterized by a high level of urbanization and industrialization. The city quickly expanded after a new dock/wharf was built in 1931, and in 1933 it was designated as the capital of the then-French colony. Abidjan City remained Ivory Coast's capital after the country gained its independence from France in 1960. After the Vridi Canal was completed in 1951, the city also became a major seaport. In 1983, Yamoussoukro was designated as Cote d'Ivoire's official capital. However, nearly all foreign embassies and political institutions remained in Abidjan City (designated as the country's "economic capital"). The encompassing Abidjan Autonomous District (plus some city suburbs) is one of Ivory Coast's all 14 districts. By shipping traffic volumes, Port Abidjan is ranked West Africa's largest seaport and Africa's second-largest, after Lagos (Nigeria). The containership /cargo port was opened in 1951. The largest ships dock in the Vridi Canal which has draft 15 m (50 ft). Abidjan City is the economic center of the Ivory Coast and as well as of the inland countries Mali and Burkina Faso. The city's road infrastructure effectively increased the seaport's activities as ~50% of the businesses based in Burkina Faso, Niger and Mali pass through it. Port Abidjan receives ~60% of ivory park industry. It also serves the region's oil production (especially refining and distribution) and cargo exports (cocoa, coffee, bananas, pineapples, cashew, mango, manganese, timber). In August 2020 was signed a contract with CHEC (China Harbour Engineering Company) for the construction of the new Cote d’Ivoire Terminal - port’s second container terminal. Works started on October 5, 2020, and are scheduled for completion by the end of 2021. The new facility is adjacent to Abidjan Terminal (port's first) and both are operated by a joint venture company formed by Bollore Ports (port infrastructure operator and logistics company ) and APM Terminals ( The Hague Holland -based port and container terminal operator/one of the world's largest). Abidjan's new container terminal will increase seaport's annual capacity with 1,2 million TEU-containers (annually). Cote d’Ivoire Terminal covers total area 37,5 hectares (93 acres/~0,4 km2) and is w ell-connected with the city. On November 2, 2022, was officially opened/became fully operational Port Abidjan's Cote d'Ivoire Terminal. The facility is a joint venture between APM Terminals (Netherlands) and Bollore Ports (South Africa/part of Bollore Group). The new terminal's first vessel was the 6000-TEU boxship CMA CGM ROSSINI (2004-built, IMO 9280639). Abidjan is primarily an excursion-oriented cruise port rather than a walk-off destination. Ships dock alongside inside the large commercial Port of Abidjan, and recent cruise calls have frequently used the new Grain Terminal. The port is an industrial, controlled area, so passengers should not expect to walk directly from the ship into the city. For most visitors, a cruise excursion or a pre-arranged vehicle with driver is the practical way to explore.
getting_from_port: Abidjan does not have a conventional downtown cruise terminal surrounded by tourist facilities. Recent large cruise ships have used the port's Grain Terminal, a 700 m (0.4 mi) quay commissioned in 2023, although the exact berth can vary between calls. The port complex is separated from Abidjan's main sightseeing areas by industrial roads and the Ébrié Lagoon. Le Plateau, the central business district, is roughly 5 km (3.1 mi) from the port area, but driving time can vary considerably with traffic. Do not assume that taxis or ride-hailing vehicles can collect passengers directly beside the ship. Cruise-line coaches and locally arranged tours commonly meet inside the controlled port area. Independent visitors should confirm the authorized meeting point with the ship before arranging a driver. For independent travel, a pre-arranged private car or reputable ride-hailing service is preferable to shared taxis or minibuses. Abidjan traffic can be heavy and unpredictable, particularly around bridges and major junctions.

things_to_do.name: Le Plateau and Central Abidjan
things_to_do.description: Allow 3–4 hours. This is the most realistic introduction to Abidjan during a shorter call. Le Plateau contains the city's high-rise business district and several notable modern buildings, including St Paul's Cathedral with its distinctive concrete bell tower and stained glass. A driver or guided city tour is preferable to trying to reach the district by public transport. Once dropped in Le Plateau, short sections can be explored on foot during daylight, but it is better to have transport available between stops rather than plan a long city walk. The Musée des Civilisations de Côte d'Ivoire is also in Le Plateau, but it is currently listed as temporarily closed. Check locally before including it in a port-day itinerary.

things_to_do.name: Banco National Park
things_to_do.description: Allow about 4–5 hours including transfers. Banco National Park protects tropical forest within the Abidjan metropolitan area and offers walking through dense vegetation close to the city. It has repeatedly featured in sightseeing programs arranged for visiting cruise ships. This is not a practical destination to approach casually from the port. Arrange a vehicle and preferably a guide in advance. Trails can be hot, humid and muddy after rain, so closed footwear, water and insect protection are useful.

things_to_do.name: Historic Grand-Bassam
things_to_do.description: Allow at least 5–6 hours. Grand-Bassam is approximately 35 km (21.7 mi) by road from the Treichville side of Abidjan. In light traffic the drive can take around 30–40 minutes, but cruise passengers should plan for substantially longer when congestion is possible. The UNESCO-listed historic quarter preserves the former colonial administrative town between the lagoon and Atlantic Ocean. Typical visits include the historic streets, old administrative buildings and the National Costume Museum. The town also has Atlantic beaches, although a cruise visit is better focused on the historic district unless plenty of time is available. Organized excursion recommended. The distance and variable road traffic make a ship excursion or pre-arranged private tour more appropriate than local public transport.

things_to_do.name: Bingerville Botanical Garden
things_to_do.description: Allow about 4 hours. The botanical garden at Bingerville is another established cruise-excursion destination and provides a quieter alternative to central Abidjan. Its mature tropical vegetation makes it suitable for passengers interested in nature without committing to a longer forest walk. Use organized or pre-arranged transport. It can be combined with a limited Abidjan city tour on a longer call, but attempting to combine Bingerville, Banco and Grand-Bassam in one normal port day would involve too much road travel.
