Abu Dhabi is an Arabian Gulf cruise port part of the UAE (United Arab Emirates). Prior to the discovery of oil 1958, Abu Dhabi was a poor, rural wasteland. Now the city has one of the world's highest per-capita incomes. The city is the capital of the UAE, with population around 250,000. Traditionally for the UAE, the city is modern, clean, featuring high rise buildings and numerous palm trees. Tourist attractions include souks (marketplaces), Petroleum Exhibition, palaces owned by local sheiks. The walled coastal road (corniche) runs for about 13 km (8 mi) along Persian/Arabian Gulf. The city has an attractive park with flower gardens and 2200-year-old tomb ("Round Structure"). Abu Dhabi accounts for nearly 2/3 of the USD 400-billion UAE economy. It is the 4th most expensive city for expatriate employees in the area, and in 2014 was the world's 68th most expensive large city. The city features numerous modern amenities and attractions, like hotels, shopping, tours/excursions, also Abu Dhabi Grand Prix, Ferrari World, Falcon Hospital. The more popular Dubai is only a short ride away. A popular tourist destination, Dalma Island is located approx 42 km (26 mi) off Abu Dhabi's coast, as well as at 116 km (72 mi) away from Qatar's capital city Doha . On Dalma Island are identified 20+ archaeological sites from the Late Stone Age. Dalma's population is around 10,000, most of whom are from Qatar but granted UAE nationality. The only way of accessing the island is by sea and mainly by Ro-Pax ships ( car and passenger ferries ) leaving from Marsa Jebel Al Dhanna (Abu Dhabi). Abu Dhabi Ports Company was established in 2006 and formed as part of the UAE's commercial ports restructuring. The company replaced the old Abu Dhabi Seaports Authority. It manages a total of 11 ports (commercial, logistic, leisure), including Khalifa Port (deep-water), Zayed Port (deep-water, operational since 1972, also serving cruise vessels), Free Port, Musaffah Port and 5 ports in Al Gharbia. "Khalifa Industrial Zone Abu Dhabi" is adjacent to Khalifa Port and serves logistics and manufacturing companies. On November 5, 2017, the Chinese company COSCO SHIPPING Ports Ltd (CSP, Hong Kong-based subsidiary of COSCO Group, China) held at Khalifa Port the ground-breaking ceremony for the new "CSP Abu Dhabi Terminal". The USD 430 million CSP Abu Dhabi Terminal was officially inaugurated on December 10, 2018. Khalifa Port was opened in September and inaugurated on December 12, 2012. In 2016 it was ranked the world's second-fastest-growing global container port - following Shanghai China . As of 2019, the seaport is ranked world's 25th largest container port. It features 8 km (5 mi) long breakwater and 4 km (2,5 mi) total quay wall length (of which 2,4 km main berth, 800 m West Quay, 800 m Emal Quay). Pilotage is compulsory and available 24-7. Max vessel draft is 13 m (43 ft). The Port serves 20 containership lines, offers 60 direct links to international ports and is equipped with a total of 52 automated ship-to-shore (stacking) cranes (rail-mounted). In late-March 2018, Abu Dhabi Ports signed an MoU with CCPIT ("China Council for the Promotion of International Trade"). The Memorandum of Understanding was for promoting commercial shipping opportunities to potential Chinese investors in KIZAD ("Khalifa Industrial Zone Abu Dhabi") and KPFTZ ("Khalifa Port Free Trade Zone"). In April 2018, Emirates Global Aluminium (EGA) and Abu Dhabi Ports opened a container freight station to reduce aluminum trucking mileage within KIZAD, by over 290,000 km per year. The new facility is used to load aluminum into TEU containers for export shipping. Purpose-built near EGA’s Al Taweelah smelter site (world's largest), the new station reduces the trucking distance by approx 17 km for each consignment. EGA's annual aluminum volume for 2017 was nearly 600,000 tons, which (from Khalifa Port) required over 17,000 truck movements from Al Taweelah to the quayside. Total annual CO2 emissions savings are over 2000 tons. As of 2018, KIZAD (region's largest free zone) comprises 410 km2 (160 mi2), has over 200 tenants, attracted total investments of AED 65 billion (USD 17,7 billion). Since August 2017, 19 Chinese companies signed land lease agreements within Khalifa Port Free Trade Zone. Port Abu Dhabi is part of the "Cruise Arabia" alliance, which also includes Dubai and Sharjah (both in UAE), plus ports in Oman, Qatar and Bahrain. Since December 2016, Abu Dhabi has Arabian Gulf's only dedicated desert cruise island port - Sir Bani Yas island . Many regular holiday tourists visit Yas Island as a day trip or overnight vacation destination. Abu Dhabi is also gaining popularity as a wedding destination for guests from India, Europe, the USA. Zayed Port's cruising season is October through July. The cooperation with the UAE's national carrier Etihad Airways resulted in a relatively steady annual increase in visiting cruise tourists from India (around 10% per year) and also in tourists flying to Abu Dhabi from Delhi or Mumbai (around 30% per year). The Etihad Airways has additionally partnered with Jet Airways for connecting cheap flights to all major airport cities in India. The option for cruises to UAE leaving from ports in India is expected to become reality in the following years. During season 2014-2015, the cruise port handled a total of 94 ship calls and ~190,000 passengers. During season 2015-2016, these numbers grew to 113 ship visits and 232,600 passengers (increase 22% / 16%). For comparison, Zayed Port during season 2006-2007 handled a total of 35,366 cruise ship tourists. During season 2016-2017, the cruise port's business increased by 15% (over 2015-2016) with nearly 345,000 passengers. The estimated number of cruise tourists by the year 2020 is 450,000 and by the year 2025 - 808,000. Ship numbers increased from 115 (2015-2016) to 161 (2016-2017). In 2017, the port reported 48% increase in passenger volumes at its cruise terminals - about 6 times the 8% increase in 2016. In 2016, Abu Dhabi and other UAE cities introduced a new (multi-entry) visa system allowing cruise passengers to visit various UAE tour destinations with 1 permit. Previously, UAE visas were only for tourists arriving and leaving the UAE on a cruise ship. The new visas allow tourists to fly to Dubai Airport, embark on a cruise vessel in Mina Rashid and cruise to Abu Dhabi and also to other Persian Gulf countries with a single visa rather than obtaining 2 or 3 separate visas. The new visas are also cheaper (AUD 59) in comparison to Dubai's 96-hours visa (AUD 44). In mid-February 2020, Abu Dhabi Ports and MSC Cruises signed a long-term agreement for preferential berthing at Abu Dhabi Cruise Terminal and Sir Bani Yas Island. The Abu Dhabi Ports-MSC deal is expected to bring around 1,3 million cruise ship tourists over the agreement period. For 2019, the cruise port reported 47% growth in passenger numbers and 45% increase in cruise ship calls over 2018. During season 2021-2022, the Port handled 130 cruise ship calls and 177,639 tourists. During season 2022-2023, the cruise port's schedule listed a total of 184 ship calls and handled 600,000+ tourists (including ~82000 homeporting). For season 2023-2024, the Port had booked a total of 126 cruise ship berthings. The 2023-Q1 showed remarkable growth, with 363,494 visitors and 120 ship calls, surpassing 2022-Q1's numbers of both visitors (89,953) and calls (60). Cruise ships to Abu Dhabi dock in Zayed Port. The following photo shows Abu Dhabi cruise ship terminal with a docked Costa ship. Ferries to Dalma Island depart from homeport Marsa Jebel Al Dhanna. Before August 2019, these passenger vessels were homeported at Mugharag. The new Port Zayed cruise terminal in Abu Dhabi has exclusive check-in facilities (operated via partnership with Etihad Airways). Since its inauguration on December 13, 2015, the number of visiting tourists was significantly increased. The terminal is also in close proximity to popular city attractions, such as Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque (at just a 20-min drive) and Saadiyat (city's cultural district featuring the Louvre Abu Dhabi / opened in 2017). The Abu Dhabi cruise terminal's building became an Arabian Gulf tourism landmark. The construction project underlined the UAE's ambitions for a leading position in the South Asian tourism sector. The building as design is a fusion of traditional Arabic ornaments and modern architecture. The roof's design is a lattice work inspired by the UAE’s national tree Ghaf (flowering tree in the pea family). Inside the terminal building, the wooden beams design was inspired by the country's traditional sailing boats. The terminal is sized approx 800 m2 (8600 ft2) and has capacity to handle 3 cruise vessels (7000+ passengers) at a time. The building include as facilities tourist info counters, check-in counters, security checks. On the mezzanine floor are located souvenir shops, bars and restaurants, offices, and cruise ship crew/staff waiting areas. Abu Dhabi is straightforward to explore during a cruise call, but it is not primarily a walk-off sightseeing port. Ships normally dock alongside at Abu Dhabi Cruise Terminal in Zayed Port, while the major sights are spread across the city and nearby islands. Metered taxis are usually the most practical way to move between attractions, making independent sightseeing quite manageable without booking a tour.
getting_from_port: Cruise ships normally berth directly at Abu Dhabi Cruise Terminal in Zayed Port rather than tendering passengers ashore. A second cruise-terminal facility was added in 2022. The terminal complex has passenger services including shops, restaurants, currency exchange and airline check-in facilities. Marsa Mina, a waterfront area with casual dining and retail, is immediately beside the cruise-terminal area and is suitable for passengers who have very little time ashore. The main tourist sights, however, are farther away and walking from the port is generally not a good use of a cruise call. Metered taxis are widely available in Abu Dhabi and are the simplest option for most cruise visitors. Uber and Careem also operate in the city. Depending on traffic, many central attractions can be reached in approximately 10–20 minutes. Public buses are air-conditioned, but passengers need a Hafilat smart card purchased and topped up before travel; cash and ordinary bank cards are not accepted on board. This makes buses less convenient for occasional cruise visitors. The free Experience Abu Dhabi tourism shuttle has been temporarily paused while its routes and schedules are being updated, so passengers should not rely on it without checking its current status.

things_to_do.name: Louvre Abu Dhabi and Saadiyat Island
things_to_do.description: Allow 3–4 hours. Louvre Abu Dhabi is one of the easiest major attractions to visit from the cruise port. It is on Saadiyat Island, roughly 6 km (3.7 mi) from the terminal, and the taxi journey is usually around 10–15 minutes. Allow at least two hours for the museum itself. The galleries are normally closed on Mondays, so check the operating day before leaving the ship. A public water-taxi connection also links Marsa Mina with Louvre Abu Dhabi. It can provide an attractive alternative to a road transfer, but cruise passengers should confirm the day's schedule before relying on it for the return journey.

things_to_do.name: Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque
things_to_do.description: Allow 3–4 hours including transfers. The Grand Mosque is approximately 20 km (12.4 mi) from Zayed Port and normally around a 20–25-minute taxi ride each way, depending on traffic. Entry is free, although advance visitor registration is useful. Visitors must follow the mosque's dress requirements. Shoulders and knees must be covered, and women are required to wear appropriate full-length clothing and a head covering. Because it remains an active mosque, tourist access can be restricted around prayers; on Fridays the main prayer hall is closed to visitors between noon and 3 pm.

things_to_do.name: Qasr Al Hosn and Central Abu Dhabi
things_to_do.description: Allow 2.5–4 hours. Qasr Al Hosn is the city's principal historic fort and a good choice for passengers who want Emirati heritage without spending much of the day in taxis. It is roughly 5–6 km (3.1–3.7 mi) from the cruise terminal. The fort can be combined with the adjacent House of Artisans and then a taxi to the Corniche. This is a more compact and flexible plan than trying to visit several widely separated headline attractions.

things_to_do.name: Qasr Al Watan and the Corniche
things_to_do.description: Allow 4–5 hours. Qasr Al Watan, the working Presidential Palace open to visitors, is approximately 13 km (8.1 mi) from Zayed Port. A taxi usually takes around 20 minutes, depending on traffic. The palace combines easily with the western Corniche, Founder's Memorial or a brief exterior stop at Emirates Palace. Because Qasr Al Watan is an official state venue, access can occasionally change or close for official events, so check its status on the day of the call.

things_to_do.name: Corniche Beach
things_to_do.description: Allow 2–4 hours. Passengers wanting a relaxed port day can take a taxi to the Corniche, approximately 8–9 km (5.0–5.6 mi) from the cruise terminal depending on the section visited. The waterfront has broad pedestrian paths, landscaped areas and a 2 km (1.2 mi) public beach. This is one of Abu Dhabi's better areas for walking. Beach facilities vary by section, and some areas are free while gated sections may charge for additional facilities. In the hotter months, a beach visit or promenade walk is much more comfortable in the morning than around midday.

things_to_do.name: Qasr Al Hosn and House of Artisans
things_to_do.description: Distance: approximately 1 km (0.6 mi) including walking around the complex. Pure walking time: around 15–20 minutes. Recommended total time: 1.5–2 hours. Difficulty: Easy and mostly level. Take a taxi from the cruise terminal directly to Qasr Al Hosn. Explore the fort and its courtyards, then continue on foot through the surrounding Al Hosn cultural complex to the House of Artisans, where traditional Emirati crafts are presented. After the visit, take a taxi onward to the Corniche or directly back to Zayed Port. A longer port-to-city walking tour is not recommended. Abu Dhabi's major sights are widely separated, several roads are designed primarily for vehicles, and high temperatures can make even moderate distances uncomfortable.

things_to_do.name: Grand Mosque and Qasr Al Watan
things_to_do.description: Allow about 5–6 hours. This is a practical independent combination using taxis. Visit the Grand Mosque first, then continue across the city to Qasr Al Watan before returning to Zayed Port. It gives a strong overview of modern Abu Dhabi without attempting too many stops.

things_to_do.name: Yas Island
things_to_do.description: Allow at least 6 hours for a theme park visit. Yas Island is approximately 30 km (18.6 mi) from Zayed Port and normally around 30 minutes away by taxi. Ferrari World, Warner Bros. World and Yas Waterworld are substantial attractions, so choose one rather than trying to combine several during an ordinary port call. Independent travel by taxi is straightforward, but the distance from the ship means passengers should allow a generous return margin.

things_to_do.name: Desert Safari
things_to_do.description: Organized excursion recommended. A desert experience normally involves a transfer beyond the city followed by activities such as dune driving and a desert camp visit. Timing and location vary considerably between operators. For cruise passengers, a pre-arranged excursion with clearly defined port pickup and return timing is more practical than attempting to organize separate transport after arrival.

Abu Simbel is a Lake Nasser cruise port and a complex of two in-rock temples located in Nubia (Upper Egypt), near the Egypt-Sudan border. The temples are on Lake Nasser's western bank, approx 300 km (190 ml)) by road southwest of Aswan . Abu Simbel temples (aka Nubian Monuments) are designated UNESCO site, running from Abu Simbel downriver to Philae (Aswan). The temples (originally carved out of the rock in 13th-century BC) served as a mausoleum to King Ramesses II and his Queen Nefertari. They also commemorated king's victory at Battle of Qadesh (1274 BC). In 1968, the entire Abu Simbel temple complex was relocated on a man-made hill located above Aswan High Dam. Their relocation was necessary as they would have been submerged in Lake Nasser - an artificial water reservoir on Nile River, which formed in 1970 after the inauguration of Aswan High Dam. Abu Simbel is an unusual cruise stop rather than a conventional port town. Lake Nasser cruise vessels call primarily so passengers can visit the Abu Simbel temple complex, and shore arrangements are commonly coordinated by the cruise operator. There is no large cruise terminal with a predictable walk-off route, and the exact mooring or passenger landing point can vary by vessel and itinerary. Lake Nasser cruise ships operate between Aswan and Abu Simbel, but Abu Simbel does not function like a conventional ocean-cruise terminal. Operators may use different docking or landing arrangements, so passengers should follow the transfer instructions provided aboard their particular vessel rather than assuming they can simply walk from the ship. The temples stand directly beside Lake Nasser, and some cruise itineraries approach them from the water before passengers go ashore. Guided visits to the complex are commonly incorporated into Lake Nasser cruise programs. If you intend to separate from the organized group, first confirm where and when you must meet the ship again. Local transport is much less extensive than in Aswan or Luxor, making an improvised return to the vessel a poor option.
terminal_notes: There is no large cruise terminal with a predictable walk-off route, and the exact mooring or passenger landing point can vary by vessel and itinerary. Lake Nasser cruise ships operate between Aswan and Abu Simbel, but Abu Simbel does not function like a conventional ocean-cruise terminal.

things_to_do.name: Visit the Great Temple of Ramesses II
things_to_do.description: This is the essential Abu Simbel experience. The monumental façade is dominated by four colossal seated figures of Ramesses II. Inside, a sequence of halls leads toward the sanctuary, with reliefs and statues throughout the temple. Allow roughly 45-60 minutes if you want time for both the exterior and interior rather than rushing through with a group.

things_to_do.name: See the Temple of Hathor and Nefertari
things_to_do.description: The smaller temple stands close to the Great Temple and should be included in the same visit. It is dedicated to Hathor and Queen Nefertari and is particularly notable for the prominent representation of the queen on its façade. Allow another 20-30 minutes, depending on queues and how much time you spend examining the interior reliefs.

things_to_do.name: Allow Time for the Lake Nasser Setting
things_to_do.description: Do not use the entire shore visit inside the temples. The approach paths and lakeside side of the complex provide useful views of the monuments in their present setting above Lake Nasser. The temples were relocated to higher ground during the 1960s to protect them from the rising reservoir. A complete temple visit with photographs, both interiors and some time beside the lake normally fits comfortably into about 1.5-2 hours.

things_to_do.name: Abu Simbel Village
things_to_do.description: The modern settlement is separate from the archaeological visit and is not a major sightseeing destination during a short cruise call. Consider it only if your vessel has a long stay and transport has been arranged. The temples should take priority.

Aburatsu is a small port town and natural harbor serving Nichinan City in Japan's Miyazaki Prefecture (Kyushu Island). In 1952, the port was designated Special Major Port. In 1955 started construction works that resulted in building breakwaters and mooring (ship docking) facilities. In 1998 was inaugurated Higashi Wharf (berth), where cargo and passenger ships ( container carriers , RO-RO ships, ferries , and cruise liners) can dock. In 1999 was completed a 12-meter-long wharf at the Port's eastern head. Port Aburatsu is considered one of the gateways for cruise tourism to Miyazaki 's southern regions. Nichinan City was founded in 1950 as a merger of three towns - Agata, Aburatsu, and Obi. The current-day city was officially established in 1956 when were amalgamated also several nearby villages. Its population is around 55,000. Among the cruise ships that often dock in Aburatsu are the large Japan-flagged liner Asuka 2 . The port was also visited by Legend of the Seas (now Marella Discovery 2) - the largest passenger vessel that has called here so far. In 2019 (for June 26) was booked the 1900-passenger ship Costa neoRomantica ( Costa Asia ). Aburatsu is the cruise gateway to Nichinan and the southern Miyazaki coast. The port itself is not beside the main sightseeing areas: central Aburatsu is about 3 km (1.9 mi) from the berth, while the strongest attractions are farther away at Obi and along the Nichinan Coast. Overall: Independent sightseeing is practical with some planning. Aburatsu can be explored on foot, Obi works well by taxi or train, while Udo Jingu and the more distant coastal sights are easier with a taxi, private vehicle or organized excursion.
getting_from_port: Cruise ships normally dock directly at the East Area No. 9 and No. 10 berths, so tendering is not normally required. The berths are within a working port rather than the sightseeing center. Central Aburatsu: about 3 km (1.9 mi) from the port, officially listed at roughly a 30-minute walk. Allow longer at a relaxed pace or in hot weather. Aburatsu Station: about a 5-minute drive from the port. The station is useful for trains toward Obi. Shuttle buses: shuttles are used on some cruise calls, but routes, fares and operating times are call-specific. Check the information provided onboard before assuming one will operate. Taxis: the simplest independent option for Obi, Udo Jingu and coastal sightseeing. For a multi-stop trip, arranging a vehicle in advance is safer than relying on finding another taxi at an outlying attraction. Public transport: JR trains and Miyazaki Kotsu buses can be useful, but services are not frequent enough to treat them like city transit. Check the return timetable before leaving the port area.

things_to_do.name: Aburatsu Old Port and Horikawa Canal
things_to_do.description: Allow 1.5–3 hours. Easy independently once in town. This is the lowest-risk option for a short call. The main sights are the historic Horikawa Canal, stone Horikawa Bridge, Yumemi Bridge, Aburatsu Red Brick Hall and the traditional streets around the shopping arcade. Restaurants in the area are also a practical place to try Nichinan seafood or bonito. The main drawback is the approach from the cruise berth. Walking from the ship adds about 3 km (1.9 mi) each way, so a shuttle or short taxi ride greatly improves this option when available.

things_to_do.name: Obi Castle Town
things_to_do.description: Allow 3–4 hours. Independent with some planning. Obi is generally the best independent excursion from Aburatsu. The preserved castle town is about 8 km (5.0 mi) from the berth and around 15–20 minutes by car. Its compact historic district includes Otemon Gate, moss-covered castle walls, former samurai residences, traditional streets, Shintokudo domain school and several small museums and houses. A taxi is the easiest option. Alternatively, reach Aburatsu Station and take the JR Nichinan Line to Obi; the train journey itself is around 10 minutes. From Obi Station, allow another 15–20 minutes on foot to reach the core of the castle district. Train frequency is limited, so plan around a specific return service rather than arriving at the station and waiting.

things_to_do.name: Udo Jingu and the Nichinan Coast
things_to_do.description: Allow about 2.5–3.5 hours for Udo alone, or 3–4 hours combined with another nearby coastal stop. Independent transport required. Udo Jingu is about 12 km (7.5 mi) from the port. The main shrine stands inside a sea cave beneath the cliffs, making it one of the most distinctive sights near Aburatsu. The visit involves walking, slopes and stairs, so it is less suitable for passengers with limited mobility. Scheduled buses connect the Aburatsu area with Udo Jingu and points farther north, but departures are relatively limited. A taxi, prearranged car or excursion gives substantially more flexibility. Sun Messe Nichinan, known for its coastal setting and Moai replicas, can be combined with Udo Jingu because the two are a short drive apart.

things_to_do.name: Aoshima and the Northern Nichinan Coast
things_to_do.description: Allow at least 4–5 hours. Organized excursion or prearranged transport recommended. Aoshima is about 30 km (18.6 mi) from Aburatsu Port and approximately 40 minutes away by road under normal conditions. The small island, Aoshima Shrine and the unusual coastal rock formations known as the Devil's Washboard make a good scenic destination, but the transfer consumes a significant part of a cruise call. Public transport is possible but introduces more schedule risk. A cruise excursion or prearranged taxi is usually the more practical choice, particularly if combining Aoshima with Udo Jingu or other stops along the coast.

things_to_do.name: Cape Toi
things_to_do.description: Best for a long port call. Organized excursion recommended. Cape Toi lies roughly 45 km (28.0 mi) south of the port, around 50 minutes by road each way. The cape is known for its coastal landscape and free-ranging Misaki horses. Public transport is not convenient for a cruise-day visit, so this is primarily a guided tour or private-car destination. Avoid combining it with distant northern sights such as Aoshima unless the ship has an unusually long stay.

things_to_do.name: Easy Aburatsu Town Loop
things_to_do.description: Distance: about 2.5–3 km (1.6–1.9 mi) within town Pure walking time: about 40 minutes Recommended time: 1.5–2 hours Difficulty: Easy; generally level urban walking This route works best if your ship provides a shuttle into central Aburatsu or you take a taxi from the berth. Horikawa Bridge – begin beside the historic canal and stone bridge. Horikawa Canal waterfront – follow the waterside through the old port district. Yumemi Bridge – a wooden bridge built with local Obi cedar and traditional joinery. Aburatsu Red Brick Hall – a preserved early-20th-century brick warehouse beside the canal. Sugimura Hardware Store – a distinctive historic wooden commercial building on the old route toward the port. Aburatsu Shopping Arcade – finish with cafés, local shops or a meal before returning to your shuttle or taxi. If you walk all the way from the cruise berth instead of using transport, the complete outing becomes roughly 8–9 km (5.0–5.6 mi). Allow around 2.5–3 hours and extra time in warm or humid weather.

things_to_do.name: Obi Castle Town Walk
things_to_do.description: Distance: about 3.5–4 km (2.2–2.5 mi) from Obi Station and back Pure walking time: about 50–60 minutes Recommended time: 2–3 hours in Obi Difficulty: Easy to moderate; mostly gentle streets with stone steps around the castle JR Obi Station – walk toward the historic center. Traditional merchant streets – follow the preserved townscape and waterways toward the castle area. Yoshokan – a former samurai residence and garden close to the castle entrance. Otemon Gate – the reconstructed main gateway into the former castle. Obi Castle grounds – explore the stone walls, steps and cedar-shaded former enclosures. Matsuo-no-Maru or the Historical Museum – choose one if time is limited rather than trying to visit every paid building. Shintokudo – the former domain school, then return through town to Obi Station. Before starting the walk, note the departure time of your return train. If the schedule leaves an uncomfortable margin, use a taxi back to Aburatsu instead.
things_to_do.recommended_time: 2–3 hours in Obi Difficulty: Easy to moderate

Abydos is a Nile River cruise port and an Ancient Egyptian city in Upper Egypt's Sohag Governorate, located approx 11 km (7 mi) west of the river (near the towns El Balyana and El Araba El Madfuna). Abydos is one of Egypt's most important archaeological sites, with numerous temples and tombs (burial sites for the pharaohs of the 1st to 13th dynasties). As cruise port, Abydos is visited for the temple of Menmaatre Seti I, where can be seen the Abydos King List (aka Abydos Table) which has listed the names of 76 Egyptian pharaohs (from Menes to Ramesses I). Other important sites are the Umm El Qa'ab necropolis, Great Osiris Temple, Ramesses II Temple. Most cruises to Abydos start from Cairo (with hotel stay and domestic flight to Aswan (ship embarkation port) from where starts the cruise itinerary to Luxor . Abydos is an archaeological port call rather than a place for casual waterfront sightseeing. Long Nile cruises normally stop at El Balyana, while the ancient site lies about 10-11 km (6.2-6.8 mi) inland. The main reason to visit is the exceptionally well-preserved Temple of Seti I, usually reached by coach or private vehicle from the river.
getting_from_port: Nile cruise vessels visiting Abydos generally stop at or near El Balyana rather than beside the archaeological complex itself. This is a river mooring rather than a conventional sea-cruise terminal, and arrangements can vary between ships. Abydos is approximately 10-11 km (6.2-6.8 mi) from El Balyana and the Nile. Allow roughly 20-30 minutes each way by road depending on the exact mooring and local traffic. Walking from the vessel is not practical. Most passengers should use the cruise line's included or organized transfer. A prearranged private car with driver can work if the ship remains at El Balyana long enough, but confirm both the departure deadline and the exact place where the vessel will be waiting. Some long Nile itineraries continue sailing while passengers are ashore and arrange a later road transfer to rejoin the ship.

things_to_do.name: Temple of Seti I
things_to_do.description: Allow about 1.5-2 hours at the site, plus the road transfer. This is the essential Abydos visit and is practical during almost any cruise call that includes an official transfer. The temple is particularly notable for its surviving roof, finely carved reliefs and unusual L-shaped plan. Inside, the route passes through columned halls to seven sanctuaries dedicated to Seti I and major Egyptian gods. Do not miss the Gallery of the Ancestors, containing the famous Abydos King List. The Osireion lies behind the main temple. What visitors can access or view may vary with archaeological and conservation conditions, so do not plan the visit around entering particular restricted areas.

things_to_do.name: Add the Temple of Ramesses II
things_to_do.description: If the schedule allows another 30-45 minutes, continue to the smaller Temple of Ramesses II, about 0.4 km (0.2 mi) northwest of the Temple of Seti I. It is much less complete but preserves interesting carved and painted reliefs and gives a useful contrast with the larger temple. The two temples together make the most practical extended visit at Abydos. Allow roughly 2-2.5 hours on site.

things_to_do.name: Focus on the Reliefs and King List
things_to_do.description: For a shorter stop, concentrate entirely on the interior of Seti I's temple rather than trying to cover the wider archaeological area. The second hypostyle hall, sanctuaries and King List are the highest-value sights and can form a worthwhile visit in about 60-90 minutes.

things_to_do.name: Seti I Temple and Ramesses II Temple Route
things_to_do.description: Distance: approximately 1.5-2 km (0.9-1.2 mi), depending on how extensively you explore the interiors. Pure walking time: about 25-35 minutes. Recommended total time: 2-2.5 hours with sightseeing. Difficulty: Easy to moderate. Distances are short, but expect uneven stone, occasional steps and strong sun outside the temples. Temple of Seti I entrance and forecourts: Start from the archaeological-site entrance and approach the surviving covered section of the temple. First Hypostyle Hall: Enter the columned interior and follow the temple's main axis toward the better-preserved inner rooms. Second Hypostyle Hall: Slow down here for some of the temple's finest relief work. Seven Sanctuaries: Explore the chapels dedicated to Seti I, Osiris, Isis, Horus and other principal deities. Gallery of the Ancestors: Continue into the southern section to see the Abydos King List. Osireion area: Walk around toward the rear of the temple for whatever exterior or designated visitor views are available. Temple of Ramesses II: If time permits, walk roughly 0.4 km (0.2 mi) northwest to the second temple before returning to your vehicle. Return to the transfer vehicle rather than attempting to walk back to the Nile. Keep the ship's stated meeting time as the controlling deadline.

Acajutla is a municipality and seaport in Sonsonate Department, El Salvador. It is the principal seaport of El Salvador from which a large portion of the exports of sugar, coffee and Balsam of Peru are shipped. Acajutla, as a municipality, is one of 17 such districts in Sonsonate. In 1992, the population of the town was 18,000 and in 2012 it reached 29,700 people. The total city area of Acajutla is 166.59 km2 (64.32 ml2). The inhabitants of Acajutla have their traditional celebrations between the last days of May and June 2 as the main day. One of the major celebrations is between March and April: then, they celebrate the passion of Christ, clean the roads and create decorative images in the sand brought from the beach. At noon they start the simulation of passion from San Francisco de Asis church close to Barrio La playa ending in the early hours of the next day in the same location. On October 24 they make celebrations of fishermen, in honor of San Rafael Arcangel. The port of Acajutla was constructed in its initial phase at a cost of 25M colones. The wave breaker of 338m inaugurated operations in August 1961. It is managed by CEPA (the Executive Commission of Autonomous Port). The deepwater harbor of Acajutla is the principal port. For some types of shipping, two operational ports exist in El Salvador. The port cargo loading facilities allow marine shipment of large portions of Acajutla's major exports of coffee (40%) and sugar. Its oil refinery is the largest in the country and mainly refines petroleum that is imported from Venezuela. The following photo show's Acajutla port's cruise ship docking pier (no terminal building). Acajutla is primarily a gateway port rather than a walk-off sightseeing destination. Cruise ships normally dock at the working commercial port, where there is no conventional cruise terminal building and passenger movement through the industrial area is controlled. The most practical choices are a short transfer into Acajutla or to a nearby beach, or an organized/private excursion into western El Salvador. :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}
getting_from_port: Because Acajutla is a working cargo port, passengers should not plan to leave the ship and simply walk through the port gates. Cruise excursion vehicles can collect passengers inside the port, and shuttle arrangements to Acajutla or nearby coastal areas have also been provided on some cruise calls. Shuttle destinations and operation can vary, so check the arrangements announced aboard your ship. :contentReference[oaicite:4]{index=4} Taxis or pre-arranged private vehicles are the most useful option for independent travelers. Local buses exist, but their indirect routes and transfers can consume too much of a short port call; for example, the approximately 11 km (6.8 mi) trip between Acajutla and Los Cóbanos can require well over an hour by public transport despite being only a short drive. :contentReference[oaicite:5]{index=5}

things_to_do.name: Acajutla Waterfront and Local Life
things_to_do.description: Allow about 2–3 hours. This is the simplest option if you prefer not to spend much of the call traveling inland. Take the ship's transfer, if provided, or a taxi into the town and waterfront area. Acajutla has a local beach, seafood restaurants, the artisanal fishing wharf and a municipal market rather than a concentrated group of major tourist sights. :contentReference[oaicite:6]{index=6} This option is practical independently once you have transport out of the port. It works particularly well on a short call or for passengers who want a low-key look at the destination rather than a full-day excursion.

things_to_do.name: Los Cóbanos Beach
things_to_do.description: Allow about 3–5 hours. Los Cóbanos is approximately 11 km (6.8 mi) from Acajutla and is one of the easiest worthwhile coastal destinations from the port. The fishing community is surrounded by beaches with unusually light-colored sand, volcanic rock and reef areas. :contentReference[oaicite:7]{index=7} A taxi, private transfer or cruise-arranged beach transfer is much more practical than public buses. Allow additional time if you arrange a boat, snorkeling or other marine activity locally, and confirm conditions before entering the water.

things_to_do.name: Ruta de las Flores
things_to_do.description: Allow about 6–8 hours for a useful visit. This highland route links towns including Nahuizalco, Juayúa, Salcoatitán, Apaneca and Concepción de Ataco, with markets, murals, coffee-growing scenery and cooler mountain landscapes. :contentReference[oaicite:8]{index=8} Trying to cover the entire route is unrealistic during most cruise calls. A better plan is two or three towns, usually starting with Nahuizalco and continuing toward Juayúa, Apaneca or Ataco. A private driver is possible, but an organized shore excursion is generally preferable because the itinerary involves substantial road travel and several stops.

things_to_do.name: Cerro Verde and the Volcanoes
things_to_do.description: Allow about 5–6 hours. Cerro Verde is one of the most practical nature excursions from Acajutla. The park has viewpoints toward the surrounding volcanic landscape and relatively easy interpretive trails through cloud forest. Typical cruise-oriented excursions from Acajutla take around 5–5.5 hours, with road travel taking roughly an hour or more each way depending on conditions. :contentReference[oaicite:9]{index=9} This is better suited to an organized excursion or private vehicle than independent public transport. A visit to Cerro Verde's viewpoints and short trails is much more realistic on a cruise call than attempting a demanding volcano summit hike.

things_to_do.name: Tazumal and Santa Ana
things_to_do.description: Allow about 7 hours. Tazumal Archaeological Park in Chalchuapa contains Maya temples, a ceremonial complex and a ball court. Cruise excursions commonly combine it with nearby archaeological sites and the historic center of Santa Ana. :contentReference[oaicite:10]{index=10} Tazumal is around 70 km (43.5 mi) from the port area and the journey can take approximately 1.5 hours each way, making this an excursion-oriented choice rather than a casual independent trip. :contentReference[oaicite:11]{index=11}

Acapulco (port locode MXACA) is a large port city and Mexico's fun capital and largest Pacific resort. As destination, it offers superb weather with an average 360 days of sunshine a year and amazing beaches. City's urban area is approx 85 km2 (33 mi2), and its population - around 700,000 (metro over 800,000). In April 2026, Acapulco Cruise Port was leased by Global Ports Holding (GPH). The 24-year concession agreement marked GPH’s first Mexican port concession. The deal was signed with the ASIPONA Acapulco (National Port System Administration) and includes the operation and development of the cruise terminal (within a concession period) through phased investments by GPH (Turkey-based, family-run corporation, ranked the world's largest cruise port operator). Located on a deepwater, semicircular bay, the city has the best harbour waterway on Mexico's Pacific coast. Acapulco runs along a narrow land strip between the bay and surrounding mountains. The most popular beaches and hotels are to the east and around the bay - Condesa, Icacos, Playas Hornos, Hornitos. A very popular cliff diving destination is Le Quebrada. Acapulco harbor was discovered in 1531 by Hernan Cortes (1485-1547, Spanish conquistador/conqueror) and the settlement was established in 1550 as an important seaport for Spanish galleons (large wooden warships) sailing between Spain and the American territories. Sea traffic dwindled following Mexico gaining independence in 1821. Local tourism started to develop since 1927 when a paved road over mountains connected Pacific Mexico's first resort city. Today, tourism is the largest economic contributor, with most of it centred on Acapulco Bay. Over 70% of Acapulco's population is involved in commerce, and most of it relates to tourism and the cruise port. Manufacturing and mining employ nearly 1/5. Under 5% is agriculture. Acapulco is one of Mexico's oldest coastal tourist destinations, booming during the 1950s as a vacation destination for US millionaires and Hollywood stars. In recent years, tourists face problems with corrupt police stealing money by extortion and threatening tourists with jail. Sadly, once a premium resort vacation destination, current-day Acapulco is largely associated with crime and corruption. The city is also plagued by violence from drug cartel wars. In 2015 were reported 903 murders - more than in any other Mexican city. The US State Department issued travel warnings for some Mexican areas, and Acapulco was also listed as risky. In 2016, the cruise port handled a total of 18 ship calls. In 2017, the number grew to 32 (a 78% increase). The list of cruise companies with scheduled ships to Acapulco included Crystal , Hapag Lloyd , NCL , Oceania , RSSC-Regent , Saga UK , Silversea . In 2017-2018, the cruise port had scheduled a total of 30 ship calls. For season 2017-2018, Holland America pulled from its Mexican Riviera cruise itineraries Port Acapulco due to concerns about violent crime in the region. The company (Carnival Corporation subsidiary) had scheduled 8 different itineraries to Pacific Mexico ports, but the popular resort destination Acapulco was scrapped and replaced with alternative Mexican ports. The changed Itineraries included 7 Panama Canal transits and 7 South American voyages. During winter 2018-2019, the UK-based company CMV (Cruise and Maritime Voyages) homeported here the 1500-passenger liner Magellan . CMV's Acapulco roundtrip program included itineraries visiting the most popular Mexican Riviera ports Ixtapa-Zihuatanejo , Manzanillo , Puerto Vallarta , Cabo San Lucas (Baja California) . A USD 1 billion development plan (2017-2022) includes cruise port upgrades, major resorts renovations (Pierre Mundo Imperial, Princess Mundo Imperial), building new airport terminal, new hotels, shops, restaurants, amusement park, tennis stadium, medical center. The project includes: In April 2017 was opened the USD 200 million macro-tunnel connecting Golden and Diamond districts. The 3,3 km long tunnel is Mexico's longest. The 3-line tunnel allows locals and tourists just 3 min commute travel (compared to the 1-hour drive via Avenida Escenica). The tunnel is monitored 24-hours via CCTVs, has modern fire protection system, temperature control (with 14 large fans), LED lighting, sound system (broadcasting important messages), emergency stations, 100% cell phone coverage, and can resist 8-Richter scale earthquake. Macro-tunnel passing costs around US$1.60 (residents) and US$3 (tourists). During 2017's holiday season (Dec 20 - Jan 7) the city was visited by around 573,000 tourists, with average hotel occupancy over 81%. The port reported 3 cruise ship calls (Oceania Sirena, MS Europa, Norwegian Star) during the holidays and 40% increase in passenger shipping over 2016. For season 2019, the cruise port had scheduled 30 ship calls (25 in 2018). Among the booked cruise companies were NCL-Norwegian , Oceania , RSSC-Regent , Ponant , Fred Olsen , Phoenix Reisen , CMV. The Terminal Marítima Acapulco is a mid-tier cruise port primarily used as a call port rather than a homeport. It has the ability to accommodate one to two large cruise ships (up to ~300 m) at dedicated alongside berths with adequate draft. Terminal facilities are functional but relatively basic, providing essential passenger services such as restrooms, small retail outlets, and tour dispatch, without the scale or modern amenities of major cruise hubs. Its standout advantage is its central location in Acapulco, allowing cruise tourists to easily access the historic downtown, waterfront, and nearby attractions on foot, which significantly enhances its appeal despite infrastructure limitations. The port operates as a multi-purpose facility shared with cargo traffic, which constrains scalability, but planned investments under a 24-year concession by GPH (2026-2050), including a new extended pier and upgraded terminal infrastructure. In 2027 Q1 is planned the completion and inauguration of Acapulco's new cruise pier (length 350 m/1148 ft), allowing the berthing of larger cruise ships. Independent sightseeing: Independent with some planning or transport. Acapulco is unusually convenient for a large resort city because cruise ships normally berth at the waterfront cruise terminal beside the historic center. Fuerte de San Diego, the malecón and Zócalo are all close enough for a short independent visit. La Quebrada and the traditional beaches are also nearby but are more practical by taxi. For destinations farther around the bay or outside central Acapulco, an organized excursion or prearranged transport is preferable. Government travel advisories for Guerrero are restrictive because of security concerns, so passengers should check their own government's latest advice and follow guidance provided onboard.
getting_from_port: Cruise ships normally dock directly at Acapulco Cruise Port, officially the Puerto Transatlántico Internacional Teniente José Azueta. Tendering is not the normal arrangement. The terminal is directly on the downtown waterfront, opposite the Fuerte de San Diego area and close to the old center. The port is undergoing phased redevelopment under a new cruise-terminal operator, so the precise passenger exit and terminal facilities can change. Follow the route marked for your ship rather than relying solely on the mapped berth position. Fuerte de San Diego: directly beside/opposite the cruise-terminal area and reachable in a few minutes on foot. Zócalo and Acapulco Cathedral: roughly 0.7 km (0.4 mi) from the terminal, normally around 10 minutes on foot. La Quebrada: roughly 2 km (1.2 mi) from the port. A taxi is preferable, particularly in the heat. Caleta and Caletilla: approximately 3.5 km (2.2 mi) from the port; use a taxi rather than walking. Capilla de la Paz: approximately 6 km (3.7 mi) away in the hills above the bay and requires road transport. Taxis are the simplest option for attractions beyond downtown. Confirm the destination and fare before leaving. Acabús and local buses operate in the city, but for a short cruise call they are less convenient than walking or a taxi because routes, waiting times and traffic can reduce sightseeing time.

things_to_do.name: Fuerte de San Diego and Old Acapulco
things_to_do.description: Allow 2–3 hours. Easy independently. This is the simplest option for passengers who prefer to stay close to the ship. Start with the star-shaped Fuerte de San Diego, Acapulco's principal historic monument, then continue along the waterfront to the Zócalo and the Cathedral of Our Lady of Solitude. The fort houses the Museo Histórico de Acapulco, although individual galleries can occasionally be temporarily unavailable. Check admission conditions at the entrance before planning a long museum visit.

things_to_do.name: La Quebrada Cliff Divers
things_to_do.description: Allow 2–3 hours. Independent by taxi with some planning. La Quebrada is Acapulco's signature attraction, where divers leap from cliffs approximately 35 m above the narrow Pacific inlet. The local tourism authority normally lists an early-afternoon performance around 13:00 as well as evening shows, but passengers should confirm the day's schedule before leaving the ship. A taxi from the cruise port is the practical choice. There are steps and uneven sections around the viewing areas. Sinfonía del Mar, an open-air amphitheater overlooking the Pacific, is nearby and can easily be combined with the divers.

things_to_do.name: Caleta, Caletilla and Isla La Roqueta
things_to_do.description: Allow 3.5–5 hours. Independent with transport and careful timing. Take a taxi approximately 3.5 km (2.2 mi) from the cruise terminal to the traditional Caleta/Caletilla beach area. These protected beaches generally have calmer water than Acapulco's exposed Pacific beaches. Boats leave from this area for Isla La Roqueta. The crossing takes only a few minutes, and some boats have glass-bottom viewing sections. On the island, passengers can swim, snorkel or walk through the vegetation. The longer island trail is about 3 km (1.9 mi) and requires suitable footwear. Do not make the island trip late in the port call. Boat departures, sea conditions and the taxi ride back to the terminal all need to be included in the return margin.

things_to_do.name: Scenic Bay Drive and Capilla de la Paz
things_to_do.description: Allow 3–4 hours. Taxi/private driver or organized excursion recommended. A drive around Acapulco Bay provides a broader impression of the resort than the historic center alone. Capilla de la Paz sits approximately 6 km (3.7 mi) from the cruise port on the hillside above Las Brisas and has extensive views across the bay. This is not a practical walking destination. Combining the chapel, panoramic viewpoints, the Costera and La Quebrada works particularly well with a private driver or organized city tour. Traffic on the main coastal roads can be slow, so avoid an itinerary that returns close to sailing time.

things_to_do.name: Easy: Fort, Waterfront and Zócalo
things_to_do.description: Distance: approximately 1.5–2 km (0.9–1.2 mi) round trip. Pure walking time: about 25–35 minutes. Recommended total time: 1.5–2.5 hours. Difficulty: Easy, although heat and busy road crossings can make the walk more tiring. Cruise terminal exit – begin on the downtown waterfront. Fuerte de San Diego – visit the fort and its historical museum if open. Malecón – continue along the waterfront toward central Acapulco. Zócalo / Plaza Álvarez – the traditional main square. Acapulco Cathedral – immediately beside the Zócalo. Return along the waterfront to the cruise terminal. The route is concentrated close to the ship and is the most practical independent option for a short call. Allow extra time for the fort rather than extending the walk unnecessarily into unfamiliar neighborhoods.
things_to_do.difficulty: Easy, although heat and busy road crossings can make the walk more tiring

things_to_do.name: Moderate: Old Acapulco to La Quebrada
things_to_do.description: Distance: approximately 4–5 km (2.5–3.1 mi) if walked as a round trip from the terminal. Pure walking time: about 70–90 minutes. Recommended total time: 3–4 hours including the diving show. Difficulty: Moderate, with hills, steps, strong sun and limited shade. Cruise terminal Fuerte de San Diego Zócalo Acapulco Cathedral La Quebrada Sinfonía del Mar This longer route is suitable only for confident daytime walkers who have checked current local and ship guidance. A more practical version is to walk through the historic center and then take a taxi to La Quebrada, returning to the terminal by taxi after the show.

name: Addu Atoll Maldives (Gan Island)
summary: Addu Atoll (port locode MVADU), fka Seenu Atoll, is the Maldives' southernmost atoll, located approx 541 km (336 ml) south of Male (Kaafu Atoll) . In this atoll is located Addu City, one of the country's only two cities (together with Male).
description: Addu Atoll (port locode MVADU), fka Seenu Atoll, is the Maldives' southernmost atoll, located approx 541 km (336 ml) south of Male (Kaafu Atoll) . In this atoll is located Addu City, one of the country's only two cities (together with Male). Addu City comprises of all Addu Atoll's inhabited areas, which are on the islands Feydhoo, Hithadhoo, Hulhudhoo, Maradhoo, and Meedhoo, plus several uninhabited islands, among which is Gan Island, where the atoll's only airport (Gan International Airport) is located. Addu Atoll features a natural anchorage, as its waters are protected by large islands surrounding it. The result is a natural, calm and safe at all times harbor waterway, not affected by seasonal climate changes. The atoll has 4 channels, all leading into its lagoon. Barrier reefs protect the atoll's islands from the Indian Ocean's storms and high waves. This allows coconut palms to grow everywhere on the isles. The islands also feature small lakes, wetlands, marshy fields and white terns (small tropical seabirds) which in the Maldives can be found only in this atoll. The fauna is also represented by whales and dolphins, with a great variety of species. Atoll's inhabited islands are named (alphabetically listed) Feydhoo, Hithadhoo, Hulhudhoo, Maradhoo, and Meedhoo. These islands also form Addu City's 5 districts. All these islands are natural and well-connected. Atoll's uninhabited islands are named (alphabetically listed): Most cruise ships to Addu Atoll dock (anchor) at Gan Island, where is located the Gan International Airport. Independent sightseeing: Independent with some planning or transport. Cruise ships calling at Addu Atoll normally anchor near Gan Island rather than berth at a conve:contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}efore go ashore by tender or local boat, with the exact landing point arranged for the individual call. Gan itself is suitable for a short independent visit, particularly for its former British military sites. For the more interesting wetlands, local communities and scenery of the western islands, a taxi or pre-arranged vehicle is much more practical. Gan, Feydhoo, Maradhoo-Feydhoo, Maradhoo and Hithadhoo are connected by road.
getting_from_port: There is no conventional walk-off cruise terminal. Most large cruise ships remain at anchor near Gan, so allow additional time for tendering in both directions and confirm the day's landing point and last-tender arrangements on board. Once ashore on Gan, taxis or arranged vehicles are the most useful transport for a cruise visit. The road connection continues through the neighboring islands to Hithadhoo. Gan International Airport to central Hithadhoo is roughly 13 km (8.1 mi) by road, while the full road corridor between Gan and the northern part of Hithadhoo is about 16 km (9.9 mi). Local buses operate on the connected islands, but cruise passengers should not depend on an unfamiliar timetable for the return journey. A taxi or pre-arranged driver provides substantially more control over the day.

things_to_do.name: Gan and the Former RAF Base
things_to_do.description: Allow 1.5–2.5 hours. Easy independently if the tender lands on Gan. Gan was used as a British military base, and surviving reminders include the Addu Atoll Memorial, former RAF buildings and other remnants around the old base area. Equator Village occupies part of the former military complex. The airport runway itself also developed from the former airfield. This is the simplest choice for passengers who do not want a long transfer. Most sightseeing is on level terrain, although shade can be limited and the tropical heat makes even modest walks tiring.

things_to_do.name: Drive the Connected Islands to Hithadhoo
things_to_do.description: Allow about 2.5–4 hours. Practical independently with a taxi or arranged vehicle. A drive from Gan through Feydhoo and Maradhoo to Hithadhoo is one of the best ways to see how Addu differs from a resort island. The causeways and coastal road pass local neighborhoods, mosques, small shops, cafés and stretches of lagoon shoreline. Rather than treating Hithadhoo as a single major attraction, use the journey as a scenic local-island tour and combine it with Addu Nature Park. Agree with the driver on waiting time and the return to the tender point before setting out.

things_to_do.name: Addu Nature Park
things_to_do.description: Allow 2.5–3.5 hours including transport from Gan. Independent with pre-arranged transport. At the northern end of Hithadhoo, Addu Nature Park protects the Eydhigali Kilhi wetlands and Koattey area. Visitors can see mangroves, freshwater wetlands, birdlife and coastal vegetation from roads, paths and viewing structures. White terns are a characteristic sight in Addu. The park is around a 20–30 minute drive from the Gan area under normal conditions. Walking, cycling, buggy rides and canoeing have been offered within the park, but activity availability should be confirmed locally rather than assumed for a cruise call.

things_to_do.name: Diving and Lagoon Trips
things_to_do.description: Allow at least 3–4 hours. Organized excursion recommended. Addu is particularly strong for scuba diving, with reefs, manta encounters and the British Loyalty wreck among its best-known underwater attractions. The wreck is reached by boat and is a scuba-diving site rather than a casual shore-snorkeling stop. For a cruise call, use a ship excursion or an established local dive operator that understands the ship's departure time. Boat transfers, equipment preparation and sea conditions make this a poor activity to improvise after arriving ashore.

name: Adelaide (South Australia)
region: Australia - New Zealand - Pacific Ocean Islands

description: Port Adelaide cruise ship schedule shows timetable calendars of all arrival and departure dates by month. The port's schedule lists all ships (in links) with cruises going to or leaving from Adelaide, South Australia. To see the full itineraries (ports of call dates and arrival / departure times) and their lowest rates – just follow the corresponding ship-link. Adelaide is the capital city of South Australia. It is located on Torrens River, between Mt Lofty Ranges (to the east) and Gulf St Vincent (to the west). By metro population (over 1,3 million), the city is ranked Australia's 5th largest - after Sydney (New South Wales) , Melbourne (Victoria) , Brisbane (Queensland) and Perth (Western Australia) . Adelaide is named after Queen Adelaide of Saxe-Meiningen (1792-1849), consort of William lV (1765-1837, King of Hanover). City's layout was planned in 1836 as a square-mile grid of wide boulevards surrounded by gardens and nature parks. Once known as "City of Churches", Adelaide has become celebrated for its arts festival, alfresco lifestyle, manageable size and pace, enhanced by a climate in which hot summers and warm autumns are separated by mild winters and springs. There is a free city-loop bus service running along North Terrace and going to the south through Victoria Square. Shopping can be found close to North Terrace, at Rundle Mall off King William Str. Have in mind that shops and most attractions close at 5 pm. Beyond North Terrace is Torrens River with boat tours and tree-lined promenades, ovelooked by Festival Centre, Convention Centre and Adelaide Oval across the river. Port Adelaide is located on Port River (officially Port Adelaide River) which is part of an estuary north of downtown. Since 1837, Port River is used as a shipping channel that serves cargo and passenger ships. Harbour Terminal (serving passenger / ferry and cruise ships) is at Outer Harbour (on Gulf St Vincent). Port Adelaide is approx 14 km (9 mi) northwest of downtown and is also a city suburb (Outer Harbor, industrial suburb). Port's first wharf (Maclaren Wharf) was built in 1840. It had length 102 m (336 ft) and low tide draft/water depth 4,6 m (15 ft). Initially, the port had capacity to handle vessels with max displacement 539 tons. By mid-19th-century, the increasing shipping trade resulted in building new wharves and expanding the harbour facilities. Outer Harbor's construction started in early-20th-century in order to accommodate larger vessels and reduce the time for navigation up Port River to Inner Harbour. In 2002, Newport Quays (consortium) was contracted by state's Government for the AUD 1,5 billion port development project covering 51 hectares (130 acres) of land. Land sales began in 2005. This project included the building of 2000 residential homes, with construction works creating ~4000 local jobs. In 2008, the now budgeted AUD 2 billion project was nearing completion (2 of 3 phases completed). Phase 3 included building a boat/yacht marina (capacity 100 slots/berths) and a building over the water. In 2016 was proposed a project for Inner Harbor's Dock One transformation into a premium 23-hectares (0,23 km2) waterfront complex with residential and commercial buildings. The project included 1250 homes to be built across 4 precincts - 750 by Starfish Developments (at precincts Dock One, and Port Approach) and 500 by Cedar Woods (in precincts North West and Fletcher's Slip). The project included also constructing an esplanade (waterfront promenade) around Inner Harbor, a dockside piazza and refurbishment of Marine and Harbors (old building) into apartments. The 7-year project (estimated to generate ~AUD 280 million in investments) was officially launched on February 10, 2019. Inner Harbor is approx 13 km / 8 mi from downtown's CBD (central business district). Port's cruising season runs from late-October through early-April. Trends show that the Australian cruising market is growing at a rapid pace. It has some of the industry's highest penetration rates nationally. Currently, Australian cruise ports' strongest competition comes from Singapore and Hong Kong (China) . (statistics) Between season 2004-2005 and season 2009-2010, there were an over 450% increase in cruise ship visits and over 685% increase in cruise passengers. During season 2011-2012, MS Athena (renamed CMV Astoria , back then owned by Classic International Cruises / 1985-2012 defunct) was the first-ever cruise ship with long-term homeporting in Adelaide (regularly-scheduled roundtrips). (statistics) season 2015-2016 (Nov 2015 - May 2016) had scheduled 38 cruise ship calls. Of those, 23 to Adelaide, 10 to Kangaroo Island , 4 to Port Lincoln and 1 to Robe (Limestone Coast). On February 4-5, 2012 (over the weekend) at the port docked 4 cruise liners with total ~10000 passengers and crew. At that time, the largest cruiser that ever visited Australia ( Cunard 's RMS Queen Mary 2 ) berthed in the morning (Feb 4) carrying 2620 pax plus 1200 crew. On the next day (Feb 5), at "Outer Harbour 2" docked Celebrity Century (2150 pax, now Marella Explorer 2 ), Crystal Serenity (1100 pax) and MS Athena (550 pax, now Astoria ). Due to all ship calls, business hours in Rundle Mall were extended and live band music entertainment was provided. Weekend's 4 ship visits injected AUD 1,35+ million into the state's economy, with AUD 360,000+ to the city and its surrounding regions. Rundle Mall was visited by 60,000+ people (35,000-45,000 on regular weekend days). During season 2015-2016, inaugural calls at Port Adelaide were made by Explorer of the Seas ( RCI-Royal Caribbean ), Pacific Eden ( P&O Australia ), Superstar Virgo ( Genting Star Cruises ) and Queen Elizabeth (Cunard). Princess Cruises ' 2015-2016 program for the first time ever included a roundtrip departure from Adelaide. The 9-night itinerary visited Melbourne, Burnie (Tasmania) , Kangaroo Island, Port Lincoln and Portland (Victoria) , with prices starting from AUD 1200 pp (quad cabin rates). The company's 2015-2016 program had scheduled 80+ departures out of Australian ports (Sydney, Brisbane, Melbourne, Adelaide) and also from Auckland NZ . On December 11, 2016, the port was visited by its ever-largest cruise ship - RCI's Ovation of the Seas . The vessel docked at Port Adelaide Passenger Terminal (at 7 am) bringing nearly 6000 passengers and crew. At 4 pm, it departed for Hobart Tasmania . Australia's cruise industry worth for 2016 was estimated at ~USD 5,95 billion. Princess Cruises' 2018 program (based on Golden Princess ) offered roundtrips to New Zealand. The first departure was January 8, 2018 (ports of call Melbourne, Dunedin, Akaroa, Wellington, Gisborne, Tauranga, Auckland, Fiordland Park). During season 2017-2018 (October-March), the cruise port handled 65 ship calls (16 more than 2016-2017) and a total of 159,513 passengers. For season 2019-2020, the port had scheduled 86 ship calls (nearly 1/4 increase). On February 12, 2018, P&O Australia started the company's longest homeporting season in Adelaide. The 8-night cruise (themed "A Taste Of Tasmania") was operated by MS Pacific Eden. The voyage had twice the number of nights of the traditional 3-day Cruises to Nowhere and featured scenic passage through Wineglass Bay (Freycinet National Park) and Great Oyster Bay (Tasman Sea). The available for booking shore excursions were 56, including sampling oysters at Coffin Bay and exploring South Australia's first lighthouse at Cape Willoughby Conservation Park. During season 2018, P&O had scheduled 5 turnarounds/roundtrips from Adelaide with ~7000 passengers, injecting USD 5 million into the local economy. The 1500-passenger ship Pacific Eden started its first voyage from Adelaide (3-night "Comedy" cruise to nowhere) on February 9. The last roundtrip was on Feb 24 ( Food and Wine-themed ). In March 2019, the Dutch company Royal Boskalis Westminster NV won the contract for widening Outer Harbor's shipping channel. The EUR 40 million project was awarded by Flinders Ports (port owner/operator) and includes Boskalis to widen the channel from 130 to 170 m (427-558 ft) and also to extend port's swinging/turning basin to allow access to larger container ships (Post Panamax-sized boxships) and larger cruise liners . Works include removing over 1,5 million m3 of material (sand and clay) via one trailing suction hopper dredger (ship) and one backhoe dredger (barge-mounted excavator). The dredged material will be moved to a designated area approx 30 km (19 mi) offshore. The project's completion was scheduled for 2019-H2. For 2020-2021 (October through May), Princess scheduled the company's ever-largest South Australian homeporting season, with five Adelaide-visiting liners and estimated ~USD 20 million revenue to state's economy - from port charges, ship supplies, passenger-crew spending ashore. Of the 5 Australia-based Princess ships, 2 were homeported in Adelaide (Sea and Sapphire). Follows a list of destinations visited by cruise ships leaving out of Adelaide port: Australia repositioning cruises are considered most of the one-way itineraries between Australia and Asia (mainly to Singapore and Hong Kong) and also when ships change their Australian home (turnaround) ports. The latter include short one-way cruises between Sydney, Brisbane, Fremantle, Melbourne. Adelaide to Fremantle-Perth cruises are 6-day (easbound relocation) coastal itineraries also visiting Kangaroo Island and Esperance . Cruise ships dock in Port Adelaide Outer Harbour nearly 12 mi (19 km) north of the city centre. Shuttle buses to the shopping area are normally provided, taking 40 minutes to make the journey. The most popular beach at Glenelg can be accessed by a tram from the centre of the city. Adelaide port, beside its passenger (cruise ship) terminal, also has facilities to handle oil tankers and cargo ships (vehicle carriers, bulk carriers and container vessels) and dry dock facilities for marine vessel refurbishments and repairs. Adelaide is not a walk-off city port: cruise ships normally dock at the Port Adelaide Passenger Terminal in Outer Harbor, about 23 km (14.3 mi) from central Adelaide. The good news is that Outer Harbor Railway Station is only about 200 metres from the terminal and trains take roughly 35 minutes to Adelaide Railway Station. For most passengers, sightseeing is easy independently once the transfer from the port is allowed for.
getting_from_port: The passenger terminal is on Oliver Rogers Road at Outer Harbor. After leaving the secure terminal area, passengers have easy access to trains, taxis and tour coaches. Outer Harbor Railway Station is about 200 metres from the terminal via a dedicated walkway. Outer Harbor line trains run through Port Adelaide and continue to Adelaide Railway Station in the city centre, with the full trip taking about 35 minutes. Adelaide Railway Station is well placed for North Terrace, Rundle Mall, the River Torrens and Adelaide Oval. Contactless payment is available on Adelaide Metro services. Check the live timetable before leaving the ship, particularly when planning the return journey. The City of Port Adelaide Enfield operates a free cruise-passenger shuttle on selected ship arrival dates . When operating, it connects the terminal with Semaphore and several Port Adelaide attractions, with departures generally about every 20–30 minutes. The journey is approximately 15 minutes to Semaphore and 20 minutes to central Port Adelaide. Do not assume the shuttle operates for every cruise call; confirm the service for your date. Taxis are available outside the terminal building. They are useful for Semaphore, Port Adelaide or passengers who prefer a direct transfer into Adelaide. Port Adelaide's town centre is about 10 km (6.2 mi) from the cruise berth. There is no direct regular public bus service from the passenger terminal, so the train is normally the simplest public-transport choice.

Adelaide port, beside its passenger (cruise ship) terminal, also has facilities to handle oil tankers and cargo ships (vehicle carriers, bulk carriers and container vessels) and dry dock facilities for marine vessel refurbishments and repairs. Adelaide is not a walk-off city port: cruise ships normally dock at the Port Adelaide Passenger Terminal in Outer Harbor, about 23 km (14.3 mi) from central Adelaide. The good news is that Outer Harbor Railway Station is only about 200 metres from the terminal and trains take roughly 35 minutes to Adelaide Railway Station.

Port Adelaide's town centre is about 10 km (6.2 mi) from the cruise berth. things_to_do.name: Central Adelaide: North Terrace, Rundle Mall and the Botanic Garden
things_to_do.description: Allow about 4–6 hours including port transfers. Easy independently. For a first visit, central Adelaide provides the best balance of sightseeing and simple transport. Take the train directly to Adelaide Railway Station and explore on foot. North Terrace contains Parliament House, the State Library, South Australian Museum and Art Gallery of South Australia, while Adelaide Botanic Garden is farther east. Rundle Mall is only a short walk south of North Terrace. If Adelaide Central Market is a priority, use the free city tram toward Victoria Square and walk from there. The market does not trade every day, so check its current opening day before making it the focus of your visit.

things_to_do.name: Historic Port Adelaide and Its Museums
things_to_do.description: Allow about 3–5 hours. Independent with some transport planning. Port Adelaide is a good alternative for passengers who do not want to spend much of the call travelling into the CBD. The historic waterfront area has old commercial buildings, street art, cafes and several major maritime and transport attractions. The South Australian Maritime Museum and National Railway Museum are close enough to combine on foot, while Port River cruises may also be possible if their departure time fits the ship's schedule. The cruise-day local shuttle, when operating, is particularly convenient because it serves several Port Adelaide visitor stops. Otherwise, use a taxi or the Outer Harbor train line and allow additional walking from the station.

things_to_do.name: Semaphore Beach and Foreshore
things_to_do.description: Allow about 2.5–4 hours. Easy with a shuttle or taxi. Semaphore is the simplest beach option for a cruise call at Outer Harbor. The broad sandy beach, jetty, lawns and cafes around Semaphore Road make it suitable for a relaxed few hours rather than a full sightseeing day. The local cruise shuttle takes about 15 minutes when operating; a taxi is the more dependable option when it is not. Semaphore is preferable to travelling across Adelaide to Glenelg when the main goal is simply beach time and the port call is relatively short.

things_to_do.name: Barossa Valley or Adelaide Hills
things_to_do.description: Allow most of the port call. Organized excursion recommended. Adelaide is a gateway to major wine regions, but these are not beside the cruise terminal. The Barossa is roughly 50–60 minutes from central Adelaide by road, while the Adelaide Hills and Hahndorf are around 20–30 minutes from the CBD. Travel from Outer Harbor adds additional time. For cruise passengers, a ship excursion or pre-arranged tour with port pickup is generally more practical than trying to combine trains, regional buses and winery visits independently. Choose one region rather than attempting several wine areas during a normal port call. Organized transport is also the sensible choice when wine tasting is part of the day.

things_to_do.name: North Terrace and City Centre Loop
things_to_do.description: Distance: about 4 km (2.5 mi). Pure walking: about 50–60 minutes. Recommended total time: 2.5–4 hours with sightseeing stops. Difficulty: Easy; predominantly flat city streets and paved paths. Adelaide Railway Station – start immediately after arriving from Outer Harbor. Parliament House – directly beside the station area on North Terrace. State Library of South Australia – continue east through the main cultural precinct. Art Gallery of South Australia – next to the library and suitable for either a brief look or a longer indoor visit. Adelaide Botanic Garden – continue east along North Terrace and spend 30–60 minutes walking through the gardens. Rundle Mall – return west through the city for pedestrianized shopping, cafes and Adelaide Arcade. King William Street and Adelaide Railway Station – walk north to complete the loop and catch the train back to Outer Harbor. The route is flexible: museum or gallery visits can easily turn it into a half-day outing, while passengers short on time can omit the Botanic Garden. For Adelaide Central Market, extend the outing south using the free CBD tram rather than adding a long walk.

name: Admiralty Island (Alaska)
summary: Port Admiralty Island cruise ship schedule shows timetable calendars of all arrival and departure dates by month.
