To see the full itineraries (ports of call dates and arrival / departure times) and their lowest rates – just follow the corresponding ship-link.
description: Port Admiralty Island cruise ship schedule shows timetable calendars of all arrival and departure dates by month. The port's schedule lists all ships (in links) with cruises going to or leaving from Admiralty Island, Alaska. To see the full itineraries (ports of call dates and arrival / departure times) and their lowest rates – just follow the corresponding ship-link. Admiralty Island is located in the Alaska's Alexander Archipelago. The island has length of 90 mi (140 km) and width of 25 mi (56 km), with a total land area of 1646 mi2 (4264 km2), ranking it the USA's 7th-largest and the word's 132th-largest. Its total population is around 700. The island is nearly cut in two by the Seymour Canal - an inlet with two large islands within it - Swan Island (north) and Tiedeman Island (south). Admiralty is the second largest of Alaska's ABC Islands Alaska (Admiralty, Baranof , Chichagof ). All three are located in the Alexander Archipelago and are part of the Tongass National Forest. Most of the islands' area is protected wilderness, with a minimal human presence on them. Most of the island is occupied by the "Admiralty Island National Monument" (protected wilderness). Another protected area is the Kootznoowoo Wilderness (rainforest). Both are among the world's best habitats for species like bald eagles, brown bears, Sitka deer (black-tailed). This island has North America's highest density of brown bears (over 1600). The only settlement on the island is named Angoon (on the western coast). On the island, there are several public-use cabins maintained by the US Forest Service for recreational purposes. Cross Admiralty Canoe Route links all the island's lakes through a series of portages (carrying cargo or watercrafts over land). Greens Creek is an underground mine (for gold, silver, zinc, lead) located on the island's northwest end (within the Admiralty Island National Monument). Mining operations started in 1989. Pack Creek Brown Bear Viewing Area (open during summer months) offers the opportunity to observe the bears in their natural habitat. Permits are required and can be obtained through the US Forest Service. Point Retreat Light (on the Mansfield Peninsula - the island's northern tip) is a lighthouse providing navigation aid through the Lynn Canal - a 90 mi (140 km) long artificial canal from Chilkat River to Chatham Strait and Stephens Passage. The other (in the "USA top 10") largest Alaskan islands are Kodiak , Prince of Wales, Chichagof , St Lawrence, Admiralty, Nunivak, Unimak, and Baranof . Chatham Strait is a narrow waterway (passage) in the Alexander Archipelago that separates Baranof Island and Chichagof Island (to the west) from Kuiu Island and Admiralty Island (to the east). Chatham Strait has length 240 km (150 mi) and width 5-16 km (3-10 mi), extending southwards from the junction of Lynn Canal and Icy Strait to the open sea. Cruise ships to Admiralty Island dock (anchor) at Angoon - port town (and the island's only settlement) located on the western coast. Admiralty Island is primarily a wilderness expedition call rather than a conventional Alaska cruise port. There is no fixed cruise terminal with shops, taxis and tour desks. Small expedition ships normally anchor and use their own launches or skiffs, and the exact landing area can vary with the itinerary, tides, weather and wildlife conditions. Independent sightseeing: Limited; organized or ship-led activities recommended. The main reasons to come ashore are guided hiking, kayaking, skiff exploration and wildlife viewing. Much of the island is remote bear habitat with no road access or visitor infrastructure. Admiralty Island calls can differ substantially from one sailing to another. Expedition itineraries may use locations such as Whitewater Bay or another suitable sheltered bay rather than a permanent passenger pier. Captains may alter the day's destination according to sea conditions, tides and wildlife activity. At a wilderness landing there are no taxis, buses or rental cars. Transportation and equipment are normally provided as part of the ship's expedition program. Passengers should use the actual daily program rather than the mapped port position to determine where they will go ashore.
terminal_notes: There is no fixed cruise terminal with shops, taxis and tour desks. Expedition itineraries may use locations such as Whitewater Bay or another suitable sheltered bay rather than a permanent passenger pier.

things_to_do.name: Guided Wilderness Hike
things_to_do.description: A guided forest or shoreline walk is one of the most practical activities when conditions permit. Expect dense Tongass rainforest, streams, tidal shorelines and uneven ground rather than maintained urban paths. Routes are normally selected on the day by expedition staff. Allow: Roughly 1.5–3 hours, depending on the landing and route. Waterproof footwear and rain protection are important. Independent hiking away from the group is not advisable because Admiralty Island is major brown bear habitat.

things_to_do.name: Kayaking or Skiff Exploration
things_to_do.description: Sheltered bays and inlets are well suited to ship-operated kayaking and small-boat exploration. This gives passengers access to shorelines that cannot be reached by road and provides opportunities to look for eagles, marine mammals and other wildlife. Allow: Around 1.5–3 hours. Conditions can change quickly, so routes and even whether kayaking operates are normally decided by the expedition team on the day.

things_to_do.name: Wildlife and Bear Watching
things_to_do.description: Brown bears are the island's best-known wildlife attraction, particularly around salmon streams later in summer. Sightings remain unpredictable and should never be expected or approached independently. The safest and most practical option during a cruise call is wildlife observation with the ship's naturalists from a skiff, shoreline viewing position or the vessel itself.

things_to_do.name: Pack Creek Bear Viewing Area
things_to_do.description: Pack Creek is a regulated bear-viewing area elsewhere on Admiralty Island. It has no road connection and is reached by boat or floatplane. Visitor access is permit-controlled and there are no normal tourist facilities at the site. Although Pack Creek is one of Admiralty Island's major attractions, it should not be treated as an independent side trip from an expedition landing. Visit only when specifically arranged in advance as part of an appropriate permitted tour or cruise program.

things_to_do.name: Short Angoon Village Walk
things_to_do.description: Start at the ship's confirmed village landing or drop-off point. Follow the waterfront through the settled part of Angoon. Look for the community's clan totem poles and local artwork. Continue through the Front Street area. Pass the Angoon Trading Post and nearby village buildings. Return by the same local streets to the ship's designated pickup point. Distance: Approximately 2.1 km (1.3 mi) for the established audio-tour circuit. Recommended time: 1–1.5 hours with pauses. Difficulty: Easy to moderate, with local roads and potentially wet or uneven surfaces. Angoon is a living Tlingit community rather than a purpose-built cruise attraction. Respect private property, local activities and any areas identified as culturally sensitive or closed to visitors.
things_to_do.difficulty: Easy to moderate, with local roads and potentially wet or uneven surfaces

name: Adria (Italy)
summary: Adria (port locode ITARA) is a Po River cruise port and town in northern Italy, with a population of around 20,000. The town is between the mouths of the Adige and Po rivers.
description: Adria (port locode ITARA) is a Po River cruise port and town in northern Italy, with a population of around 20,000. The town is between the mouths of the Adige and Po rivers. Adria is very popular for the Etruscan city named Atria (3-4 m below the current town). There are even speculations that after Adria is named the Adriatic Sea, to which Adria is connected via channels. Local tourist attractions include Santa Maria Assunta Della Tomba (church built 7th-8th centuries and rebuilt in 1718), St Peter and Paul Cathedral, archaeological museum. Adria is a small inland river-cruise stop on the Canalbianco waterway in Italy's Veneto region. It is not a conventional seaport: river vessels and excursion boats use local pontoons along the canal, including centrally located landings close to the National Archaeological Museum. The exact landing can vary, but passengers arriving near central Adria can normally begin sightseeing on foot. Independent sightseeing: Easy independently. Adria is compact, flat and best explored on foot. The archaeological museum, canal-side streets, cathedral and historic center can comfortably fill a short call without organized transport.
getting_from_port: Dock or tender: River vessels berth alongside a landing or pontoon; a tender transfer is not normally required. Passenger landing: Adria has several Canalbianco landing points. Tourist navigation services use landings close to the town, and a central landing is only a few hundred metres from the National Archaeological Museum. Walking: The museum and central streets are readily accessible on foot. Most useful sights are within roughly 1 km (0.6 mi) of the historic center. Shuttle: A regular cruise shuttle is not needed for a centrally berthed river vessel and should not be assumed. Public transport: Adria has regional buses and a railway station, but they offer little advantage for sightseeing within town. Taxi/private transfer: More useful for the Po Delta, Rosolina Mare or other destinations outside Adria. Pre-arranging transport is preferable when the ship has a fixed departure time.

things_to_do.name: National Archaeological Museum and Historic Center
things_to_do.description: Allow about 2–3 hours. This is the most practical choice for a first visit. The National Archaeological Museum is Adria's principal attraction, with Etruscan, Greek and Roman material from the ancient river port, including ceramics, jewellery, Roman glass and the well-known chariot burial. After the museum, continue on foot toward the canal-side streets and Piazza Garibaldi, where the Cathedral of Saints Peter and Paul and Palazzo dell'Orologio form the main historic grouping. No transport is normally necessary.

things_to_do.name: Short Canal-Side and Town Walk
things_to_do.description: Allow about 1–1.5 hours. Passengers who do not want a museum visit can simply walk along the central waterways and through Piazza Cavour, Corso Vittorio Emanuele II and Piazza Garibaldi. Adria is a working provincial town rather than a major tourist center, so this option is best for a relaxed look at the town rather than intensive sightseeing.

things_to_do.name: Basilica of Santa Maria Assunta della Tomba
things_to_do.description: Allow about 2–3 hours when combined with the center. The basilica stands outside the tightest central cluster but remains practical on foot. It is one of Adria's most significant historic churches and can be added to a longer town walk without needing a taxi.

things_to_do.name: Po Delta Nature Excursion
things_to_do.description: Allow about 4–5 hours. Adria is a useful starting point for the Veneto section of the Po Delta, known for lagoons, wetlands, birdlife and boat excursions. Porto Tolle is around 31 km (19.3 mi) away by road, with a drive of roughly 30–35 minutes before continuing into the delta landscape. Organized excursion or pre-arranged private transport is recommended. The most interesting wetland areas are dispersed, and local public transport is not designed around cruise departure times. A guided boat or nature excursion also makes better use of a limited call than attempting to navigate the delta independently.

things_to_do.name: Rosolina Mare Beach
things_to_do.description: Allow at least 4 hours. For a warm-weather call, Rosolina Mare provides a straightforward beach alternative about 29 km (18.0 mi) from Adria, normally around 30–35 minutes by road. Regional buses connect the area, but services are not frequent enough to be ideal for a tight cruise schedule. A taxi or pre-arranged transfer is the more practical independent option. Confirm the return transport before leaving Adria.

things_to_do.name: Easy: Archaeological Museum and Historic Adria
things_to_do.description: Distance: approximately 2.5 km (1.6 mi) Pure walking time: about 35–40 minutes Recommended total time: 2–3 hours with museum and sightseeing stops Difficulty: Easy; mostly flat urban streets and pavements. Canalbianco passenger landing: Begin from the river landing used by your vessel and follow signs toward the museum or town center. National Archaeological Museum: Allow about 60–90 minutes if visiting the galleries. Canalbianco waterfront: Walk toward the older riverside streets that recall Adria's long connection with inland navigation. Piazza Cavour and Teatro Comunale: Continue into the compact central district. Corso Vittorio Emanuele II: Follow the main central street toward Piazza Garibaldi. Piazza Garibaldi: See the cathedral and Palazzo dell'Orologio before returning toward the canal and your landing. The route has no significant hills. Allow extra time for street crossings and for finding the precise pontoon used by your vessel.

things_to_do.name: Moderate: Historic Center and Basilica della Tomba
things_to_do.description: Distance: approximately 4 km (2.5 mi) Pure walking time: about 55–65 minutes Recommended total time: 2.5–3.5 hours Difficulty: Moderate only because of the additional distance; the terrain remains largely flat. Start at the Canalbianco landing. Visit or pass the National Archaeological Museum. Walk through the central canal-side streets toward Piazza Cavour. Continue along Corso Vittorio Emanuele II to Piazza Garibaldi. See the Cathedral of Saints Peter and Paul and Palazzo dell'Orologio. Continue south toward the Basilica of Santa Maria Assunta della Tomba. Return through the center to the river landing. This is a good option for passengers with several hours ashore who want to see more of Adria without arranging transport.
things_to_do.difficulty: Moderate only because of the additional distance

name: Aegina Island (Greece)
summary: Aegina Island (port locode GRAEG), aka Aigina/Egina, is in the Saronic Gulf and part of Greece's Saronic Islands group. The island is approx 27 km / 17 mi to the southwest of Piraeus-Athens . The island has total population around 13,000, and its largest settlements are the towns Aegina (west), Kypseli (northwest), Vathy/Souvala (north), Mesagros (northeast), and Perdika (south).
description: Aegina Island (port locode GRAEG), aka Aigina/Egina, is in the Saronic Gulf and part of Greece's Saronic Islands group. The island is approx 27 km / 17 mi to the southwest of Piraeus-Athens . The island has total population around 13,000, and its largest settlements are the towns Aegina (west), Kypseli (northwest), Vathy/Souvala (north), Mesagros (northeast), and Perdika (south). As a cruise port, Aegina is visited exclusively by smaller-sized ships and superyachts from the fleets of ultra-luxury travel company brands like Azamara , Silversea , Windstar , SeaDream . Regularly scheduled ferries connect Piraeus with the island's principal port (Aegina) as well as Souvala (the island's second-largest port, on the northern coast). The ferry service (daily crossings the whole year round) includes between 40-70 min of sea travel (depending on vessels) and is perfect for day-trippers from Greece's capital city. The Piraeus-Aegina ferry route is currently operated by four companies - two with conventional/large-capacity Ro-Pax ships (Blue Star Ferries, and ANES Ferries) and two with smaller-sized high-speed boats (Saronic Ferries, and Aegean Flying Dolphins/hydrofoil ships). The Athens-Aegina ferry route is operated by both direct crossings as well as with longer itineraries also visiting Methana (a resort town on the Peloponnese peninsula/mainland Greece) and the islands Agistri and Poros . Saronic Ferries connect Piraeus with the island's both ports (Aegina Town and Souvala). Egina is also popular as a vacation destination visited via luxury boats and yachts. By land area (~87 km2 / 34 mi2), Aegina is the largest in the Saronic Islands. Besides summer tourism, the island's economy is also based on agriculture (mainly the production of pistachios, as well as grain, cotton, vines, olives, figs, almonds) and sponge fishing. Aegina Island's main tourist attractions are its beaches, but it is also popular as a cultural destination housing the Temple of Aphaea/Afea (dedicated to the goddess Aphaia who was worshipped only on this island and later associated with Athena/Athene), the Zeus Hellanios Temple (13th-century church, built over an ancient greek temple), and the Agios Nectarios Monastery (dedicated to Saint Nectarios of Aegina). Aegina is a compact Saronic island where cruise visitors can combine a walkable harbour town with ancient sites, monasteries and beaches. Aegina Town is easy to explore independently ; reaching the Temple of Aphaia, Agios Nektarios, Agia Marina or Perdika is also practical, but requires a taxi or careful use of the island's limited bus timetable.
getting_from_port: Tender boats normally arrive in the main harbour of Aegina Town, putting passengers directly beside the waterfront. There is no lengthy transfer into town. Cafes, pistachio shops, the fish market and the historic streets are all within a few minutes' walk. The main bus stop is opposite the harbour, while taxis can normally be found near the port exit. Bus services cover the principal island destinations but departures are much less frequent than urban public transport. Check the current timetable and, especially, the return departure before relying on a bus for a cruise call.

things_to_do.name: Aegina Town and Kolona
things_to_do.description: Allow: 2–3 hours. Difficulty: Easy. Independent: Very easy. This is the safest choice for a short or tender-restricted call. Walk the harbour, browse the narrow streets behind the waterfront, see the Markellos Tower and buildings associated with Ioannis Kapodistrias, and continue to the archaeological site of Kolona and the Archaeological Museum. The site stands immediately north of the town, so no transport is required. Avra Beach lies beside Kolona and can be added for a swim without committing to an island transfer.

things_to_do.name: Temple of Aphaia and Agios Nektarios
things_to_do.description: Allow: About 3–4 hours. Difficulty: Easy to moderate. Independent: Practical by taxi; possible by bus with timetable planning. Agios Nektarios is about 6 km (3.7 mi) inland from Aegina Port. The Temple of Aphaia is approximately 12.5 km (7.8 mi) by road from the port and stands on a pine-covered hill on the eastern side of the island. Both are served by the bus corridor toward Agia Marina, but bus frequency makes a taxi the more flexible choice for cruise passengers. The archaeological site itself involves exposed, uneven ground, and summer shade is limited. A taxi itinerary linking the monastery, Aphaia and the return to Aegina Town is preferable if the port call is not long enough to accommodate waiting for scheduled buses.

things_to_do.name: Temple of Aphaia and Agia Marina Beach
things_to_do.description: Allow: 4–5 hours. Difficulty: Easy. Independent: Good with taxi or carefully timed bus transport. Agia Marina is around 14 km (8.7 mi) from Aegina Town on the island's east coast. Buses between Aegina Town and Agia Marina take roughly 35 minutes, while a taxi is considerably faster. Aphaia is close enough to combine with the resort, making this one of the best options for passengers who want both archaeology and beach time. Confirm the archaeological site's current opening schedule before making it the centerpiece of the day.

things_to_do.name: Perdika and Moni Island
things_to_do.description: Allow: At least 4–5 hours. Difficulty: Easy, but dependent on transport and boats. Independent: Practical in summer with careful timing. Perdika is approximately 9.5 km (5.9 mi) south of Aegina Town and can be reached by bus in around 20 minutes or more flexibly by taxi. The small fishing village has a waterfront lined with tavernas and is the usual departure point for local boats to nearby Moni Island. The crossing from Perdika to Moni takes about 10 minutes. Small boats operate primarily during the summer season and their frequency can depend on demand and weather. Cruise passengers should confirm the final return boat before crossing. A taxi back from Perdika provides more flexibility than relying on the last suitable bus connection.
things_to_do.difficulty: Easy, but dependent on transport and boats

things_to_do.name: Harbour, Historic Center and Kolona
things_to_do.description: Distance: Approximately 2.9 km (1.8 mi) round trip. Pure walking time: About 50–60 minutes. Recommended total time: 2–3 hours with sightseeing. Difficulty: Easy, with some uneven paving and rougher ground inside Kolona. Harbour and Agios Nikolaos Chapel: Start where the tender lands and walk along the waterfront toward the small white sailors' chapel at the harbour. Aegina Waterfront: Follow the quay past fishing boats, cafes, produce boats and shops selling local pistachio products. Markellos Tower: Turn into the compact streets behind the harbour to see the distinctive historic tower. Governor's House and Metropolis: Continue through the Kapodistrian quarter. Several historic government buildings are principally exterior sightseeing stops rather than conventional museums. Kolona Archaeological Site: Walk north toward the ancient acropolis, recognizable by the surviving column of the Temple of Apollo. Archaeological Museum: Visit the compact museum beside the archaeological site if its opening hours fit the port call. Avra Beach: Descend toward the beach immediately beside Kolona for a short swim or waterfront break. Return to the harbour: Follow the seafront directly back to the tender landing. The town section is mostly level and straightforward. The archaeological area has uneven surfaces and is less suitable for passengers with significant mobility limitations.
things_to_do.difficulty: Easy, with some uneven paving and rougher ground inside Kolona

name: Aero Island Denmark (Aeroskobing)
summary: Port Aero Island Denmark cruise ship schedule shows timetable calendars of all arrival and departure dates by month. The port's schedule lists all ships (in links) with cruises going to or leaving from Aero Island Denmark, Aeroskobing. To see the full itineraries (ports of call dates and arrival / departure times) and their lowest rates – just follow the corresponding ship-link.
description: Port Aero Island Denmark cruise ship schedule shows timetable calendars of all arrival and departure dates by month. The port's schedule lists all ships (in links) with cruises going to or leaving from Aero Island Denmark, Aeroskobing. To see the full itineraries (ports of call dates and arrival / departure times) and their lowest rates – just follow the corresponding ship-link. Aero Island (port locode DKARK) is one of Denmark's Baltic Sea islands, part of Southern Denmark (2007-established administrative region). The island covers a total area of approx 88 km2 (34 ml2) and has population around 7,000. Island's name comes from the Danish "aer" (maple) and "o" (island). Since January 1, 2006, Aero Island is a single municipality. Before 2006, it had 2 separate municipalities - Marstal (in the east) and Aeroskobing (in the west). Aeroskobing, with its narrow lanes and pretty 18th-century houses, was the island's main town and remains its principal port (and main cruise/ferry port), largest town, and commercial center. With its low traffic density, Aero Island is a popular travel destination for cycling and hiking. The beaches also attract numerous tourists, mainly from mainland Denmark. As one of the isles making up the South Funen archipelago, Aero is favored by fine weather, offering the most sunshine hours in comparison to the rest of Denmark. The year-round temperature is a few degrees above the country's average. Aero is the only Danish Baltic island not linked to mainland Denmark via a bridge. There are car ferries from Aero to Funen, Langeland and Als. The island's airport is near Marstal. On January 28, 2015, "Horizon 2020" (the EU's research and innovation program 2014-2020) administration confirmed the EUR 17 million application for a demonstration E-ferry project. The objective of Europe's "Green Ferry Vision" is to perform a study for the design, construction/building and operation of innovative low-weight ferries (for passengers and cars) powered only by green electricity stored in batteries. The world's currently most powerful all-electric (plug-in) ferryboat, "Ellen" was officially christened on June 1, 2019. It operates on the 22 nautical miles (25 ml / 41 km) crossing route between Aero and Fynshav. It is 7 times the length of any other route now served by an all-electric (plug-in) ferryboat. The vessel's naming ceremony was held at Soby Shipyard (in Soby, Aero Island's northernmost town). The E-ferry Ellen has LOA length 60 m, width 13 m, cruising speed 13-15,5 knots (max 29 kph/18 mph), passenger capacity 198 (during summer) and 147 (during winter months), cargo capacity 31 cars (or 5 trucks) parked on an open deck, battery pack 4,3 MWh. Ellen is also world's first electric ferry without an emergency back-up generator. Most cruise ships to Aero Island dock (anchor) in Aeroskobing - port town on the central-northern coast. SOme ships may also stop in Marstal - port town on the eastern coast. Ærø is a small island port where the main cruise attraction is the preserved town of Ærøskøbing itself. Most cruise calls anchor offshore and use tenders, normally landing close to Ærøskøbing harbour and the historic centre. Once ashore, independent sightseeing is straightforward: the old town, museums, marina and Vesterstrand beach are all within walking distance. Passengers wanting to see more of the island can use the free local bus or arrange a taxi.
getting_from_port: For a typical Ærøskøbing call, tenders bring passengers into the harbour area immediately beside the town. There is no long transfer into the sightseeing district: the first historic streets are only a few minutes away on foot. The free island bus stops at Ærøskøbing Havn . Under the published timetable, the ride from Ærøskøbing harbour to Marstal harbour takes about 25 minutes. The same bus network continues west toward Søby, making an independent island trip possible when the port call is long enough. If the ship instead lands passengers in Marstal , Marstal's harbour and maritime attractions are immediately accessible, while Ærøskøbing is about 25 minutes away by bus. Always base plans on the landing point and last-tender time announced aboard.
tender_evidence: Most cruise calls anchor offshore and use tenders, normally landing close to Ærøskøbing harbour and the historic centre.

things_to_do.name: Explore Historic Ærøskøbing
things_to_do.description: Allow: 1.5–2.5 hours. Best independently. The compact centre is the easiest choice for a short call. Walk from the harbour into Brogade and the small lanes around Torvet, looking for colourful old houses, cobbled streets and traditional doors. Ærø Museum on Brogade provides useful local context, while Hammerich's House preserves the interior and collections of an old Ærøskøbing home. The Bottle Ship Museum on Smedegade is another small maritime attraction if it is open during the visit. Because everything is close together, passengers can simply wander without committing to transport or a fixed schedule.

things_to_do.name: Walk to Vesterstrand and the Beach Huts
things_to_do.description: Allow: 1–2 hours from the harbour, or combine it with the old town for a 2–3 hour outing. Easy independently. Continue through the marina to Vesterstrand, a sandy beach lined with more than 70 traditional wooden beach huts. The waterfront is only a short walk beyond central Ærøskøbing, making this one of the most practical natural sights for cruise passengers. The water is shallow and the beach works equally well for a short coastal walk, photographs or a swim in suitable weather.

things_to_do.name: Take the Free Bus to Marstal
things_to_do.description: Allow: about 3–4 hours including transport and sightseeing. Independent with some planning. The free bus from Ærøskøbing Havn reaches Marstal Havn in roughly 25 minutes. Marstal has a distinctly maritime character, and the principal attraction is Marstal Maritime Museum, with ship models, vessels and exhibits on local seafaring. Eriksens Plads beside the harbour preserves elements of the town's shipbuilding heritage and can be visited as part of a harbour walk. If time permits, continue toward Eriks Hale for the beach and another group of Ærø's characteristic beach huts. Check the return bus before leaving Ærøskøbing and avoid relying on the final practical connection back to the tender landing.

things_to_do.name: See Voderup Klint and Rural Ærø
things_to_do.description: Allow: roughly 3–4 hours. Organized excursion or pre-arranged transport recommended. Voderup Klint is one of the island's principal natural sights, with a 33-metre-high terraced coastal cliff and open views across the Baltic. It is not a practical walk from Ærøskøbing. A pre-arranged taxi, guided island tour or suitable cycling plan is preferable, particularly if combining the cliffs with villages, churches or other countryside stops. This option is better for a longer call than for passengers with only a few hours ashore.

things_to_do.name: Easy: Ærøskøbing Historic Centre
things_to_do.description: Distance: about 1.5 km (0.9 mi). Pure walking time: about 25 minutes. Recommended total time: 1–1.5 hours. Difficulty: Easy, with some cobbles and uneven surfaces. Ærøskøbing Harbour: Start where the tender brings passengers ashore and walk directly toward the old town. Brogade: Follow one of the principal historic streets toward the centre. Ærø Museum: Visit if time and opening hours permit, or simply view the surrounding historic streets. Torvet: Cross the compact town square and explore the adjoining lanes. Ærøskøbing Church: Continue through the old centre to the church area. Hammerich's House: Pass the preserved house at Gyden before weaving back through the narrow streets. Smedegade: Pass the Bottle Ship Museum and return toward the waterfront. Harbour: Finish beside the tender landing.
things_to_do.difficulty: Easy, with some cobbles and uneven surfaces

things_to_do.name: Moderate: Old Town and Vesterstrand
things_to_do.description: Distance: about 3 km (1.9 mi). Pure walking time: about 45–50 minutes. Recommended total time: 2–3 hours. Difficulty: Easy to moderate, mainly because of the longer distance; the route is largely level. Begin at Ærøskøbing Harbour . Walk through Brogade to Torvet . Explore the lanes around Ærøskøbing Church and Hammerich's House . Return toward the waterfront and continue through Ærøskøbing Marina . Follow the waterfront to Vesterstrand . Walk along the line of colourful beach huts and spend time by the beach. Retrace the waterfront route through the marina to the harbour and tender landing . This is the most complete independent outing for passengers who want both Ærøskøbing's architecture and its best-known coastal scenery without depending on transport.
things_to_do.difficulty: Easy to moderate, mainly because of the longer distance

name: Agadir (Morocco)
summary: Port Agadir cruise ship schedule shows timetable calendars of all arrival and departure dates by month. The port's schedule lists all ships (in links) with cruises going to or leaving from Agadir, Morocco. To see the full itineraries (ports of call dates and arrival / departure times) and their lowest rates – just follow the corresponding ship-link.
description: Port Agadir cruise ship schedule shows timetable calendars of all arrival and departure dates by month. The port's schedule lists all ships (in links) with cruises going to or leaving from Agadir, Morocco. To see the full itineraries (ports of call dates and arrival / departure times) and their lowest rates – just follow the corresponding ship-link. Agadir is one of the major cities in Morocco, situated on the shore of the Atlantic near the foot of Atlas Mountains, and just north of the point where Sous River flows into the Atlantic Ocean. Agadir is at a distance of 508 kilometers to the south of Casablanca . It is also the capital of Agadir-Ida Ou Tanane Prefecture and of Souss-Massa economic region. The majority of Agadir's inhabitants speak Shilha as their first language (Berber language of Atlas branch). In 2012 the population of Agadir numbered 600,000 inhabitants. In 1960 the city of Agadir was destroyed by an earthquake. Later on, it was completely recovered with mandatory seismic standards. Today it is Morocco's largest seaside resort, where foreign tourists and lots of residents are attracted by the mild year-round climate. Agadir has been well served by cheap flights and a motorway out of Tangier since 2010. Over the decades, the city has had several ports: a major trading port, two fishing ports, and the recent port with marina for leisure boats. Avenue du Port is the main artery of Anza district. It is surrounded by canneries and offers many small restaurants that are adjacent to the fish market. Agadir's fishing port is one of the world's premier major sardine ports. The commercial port is famous for its exports of manganese, zinc, cobalt and citrus products. The economy of Agadir relies mainly on fisheries and tourism. Agricultural activities are based all around the city. Agadir boasts its Souk Al Ahad - one of the largest Souks in Morocco. The city also has its cement company named Ciments du Maroc (CIMAR), subsidiary of the Italian Italcementi. There is also a shipyard and Morocco's only Merchant Marine school. Some of the prettiest beaches in Morocco lie to the north of Agadir. Areas known for excellent surfing are situated close to the village of Taghazout to Cap Ghir. Many smaller and beautiful beaches are located along this coast between Agadir and Essaouira. Agadir is not a walk-off historic port. Cruise ships normally dock inside the working commercial port north of the resort center, where official port infrastructure includes berths used for cruise vessels. The main beach, marina and central sightseeing area are roughly 3–5 km (1.9–3.1 mi) from the cruise berths, depending on the berth and destination. For most passengers, a shuttle or taxi is the practical way to start sightseeing rather than walking through the port area. Independent sightseeing: Independent with some planning or transport. Once you reach the marina, beach or city center, Agadir is straightforward to explore independently. A taxi is useful for combining the waterfront, Agadir Oufella and Souk El Had; organized transport is preferable for longer trips into the mountains or countryside. Start with Agadir Oufella, the hilltop Kasbah overlooking the harbor and sweeping curve of Agadir Bay. The modern cable car provides an easy alternative to travelling up the hill by road; its route is approximately 1.7 km (1.1 mi) and the ride takes only a few minutes. After returning downhill, continue to the marina and Corniche for an easy waterfront walk. This combination is practical independently using a taxi between the port and the lower cable-car/waterfront area. Check locally that the cable car is operating before committing your day to it.
getting_from_port: Dock or tender: Cruise ships normally dock; Agadir is not generally a tender port. Walking: Do not rely on walking directly from the ship. The berth is inside a large commercial port, pedestrian access can depend on port arrangements, and the route toward town is industrial rather than scenic. Shuttles: Some cruise lines arrange transfers between the port and the tourist area. Availability and drop-off points vary by ship, so check the information provided onboard. Taxis: Usually the simplest option for independent visitors, especially if visiting several sights. Confirm the fare or use the meter where applicable before setting off. Public transport: Agadir has an extensive urban bus network, but stops accessible from a particular cruise berth are less predictable. For a short port call, taxis are normally more convenient.
terminal_notes: The main beach, marina and central sightseeing area are roughly 3–5 km (1.9–3.1 mi) from the cruise berths, depending on the berth and destination.

things_to_do.name: Agadir Oufella, Cable Car and Waterfront
things_to_do.description: Allow: about 3–4 hours. Best for: first-time visitors. Start with Agadir Oufella, the hilltop Kasbah overlooking the harbor and sweeping curve of Agadir Bay. The modern cable car provides an easy alternative to travelling up the hill by road; its route is approximately 1.7 km (1.1 mi) and the ride takes only a few minutes. After returning downhill, continue to the marina and Corniche for an easy waterfront walk. This combination is practical independently using a taxi between the port and the lower cable-car/waterfront area. Check locally that the cable car is operating before committing your day to it.

things_to_do.name: Souk El Had and Central Agadir
things_to_do.description: Allow: about 2–3 hours for the market, or 3–4 hours combined with the waterfront. Best for: shopping, food and local atmosphere. Souk El Had occupies more than 13 hectares and has thousands of stalls selling produce, spices, clothing, leather goods, household products and local specialties such as argan oil and amlou. Exploring independently is straightforward and a guide is not necessary. The market is roughly 4.5 km (2.8 mi) from Agadir Marina. Walking between the two takes about an hour, so a taxi is usually a better choice during a cruise call. Souk El Had is normally closed on Mondays for weekly cleaning.

things_to_do.name: Agadir Beach and the Corniche
things_to_do.description: Allow: 2–4 hours. Best for: an easy, low-stress port day. Agadir's broad sandy bay is the simplest option for passengers who do not want extensive sightseeing. Once transferred from the commercial port, the waterfront is easy to explore on foot. Combine time on the beach with the promenade and marina, leaving ample time for a taxi or shuttle back to the ship.

things_to_do.name: Taghazout
things_to_do.description: Allow: about 4–5 hours. Best for: coastal scenery, cafés and surf culture. Taghazout is approximately 20 km (12.4 mi) north of Agadir. The former fishing village has a compact waterfront, beaches, cafés and surf shops. It is realistic during a normal-length port call using a pre-arranged driver, taxi or organized transfer. Public transport is possible but less attractive for cruise passengers because waiting and connections reduce the safety margin for returning to the ship. If taking a surf lesson or travelling farther along the coast, arrange transport in advance.

things_to_do.name: Marina to Souk El Had
things_to_do.description: Start: Agadir Marina after arriving from the cruise port by taxi or shuttle. Distance: approximately 4.5 km (2.8 mi). Pure walking time: about 1 hour. Recommended total time: 2.5–3.5 hours including stops. Difficulty: Easy to moderate; mostly level urban walking. Agadir Marina – Walk around the yacht basin and waterfront before heading south. Agadir Corniche – Follow the broad seafront promenade with views across the bay toward Agadir Oufella. Agadir Beach – Continue beside the beach; this is the easiest section of the walk and can be shortened if the weather is hot. Place Al Amal area – Turn inland toward central Agadir. Jardin Ibn Zaidoun – Use the central garden area as a shaded pause on the way toward the market. Souk El Had – Finish with approximately 60–90 minutes in the market. Rather than walking the same route back, take a taxi from Souk El Had directly to the cruise port or to your ship's confirmed shuttle point. In hot weather, reversing the itinerary and walking only part of the waterfront is more comfortable.

things_to_do.name: Paradise Valley
things_to_do.description: Paradise Valley lies approximately 58 km (36.0 mi) from Agadir in the High Atlas foothills. The route includes winding mountain roads followed by walking through rocky terrain. Conditions at the pools and waterfalls vary considerably by season. Organized excursion recommended. Although independent travel using buses and shared taxis is technically possible, connections can involve waiting and transport becomes less frequent later in the day. That makes public transport unsuitable for most cruise schedules. Allow roughly 5–6 hours for a comfortable visit and use proper footwear.

things_to_do.name: Taroudant
things_to_do.description: Taroudant is approximately 80 km (49.7 mi) from Agadir, generally around 1–1.5 hours each way by road. Its walled medina, traditional souks and ochre ramparts provide a more traditional old-city experience than modern Agadir. Organized excursion or pre-arranged private driver recommended. The return journey consumes a substantial part of the port call, so this is best reserved for ships with a long day in Agadir. A visit combining Taroudant with additional distant attractions requires an especially generous schedule.

name: Agats (Asmat, Indonesia Papua)
region: Australia - New Zealand - Pacific Ocean Islands

To see the full itineraries (ports of call dates and arrival / departure times) and their lowest rates – just follow the corresponding ship-link. Agats (port locode IDAGA) is a port town and the administrative center of Asmat Regency (South Papua, Indonesia). The town has a population of around 1500. It is located near the Aswetsj River's estuary. As a cruise port, Agats is visited by smaller ships and mega-yachts operated by luxury travel brands, like Seabourn . Agats was established in the early 20th century (1938) as a Dutch outpost. It became the Agats District's capital and an administrative seat in November 2002, when the Asmat Regency (kabupaten) was formed by splitting off from the Merauke Regency . The Agats District consists of 12 villages (kampung). The Asmat Regency (1969-formed) is bounded by the Arafura Sea (to the southwest), the Mappi Regency (to the southeast and east), the Highland Papua Province (to the north), and the Central Papua Province (to the northwest). It became part of the South Papua Province in 2022. Asmat Regency's total population is around 120,000. The Asmat region is renowned for its cultural diversity, including wood carving practices and traditional ceremonies. Today, the Asmat Regency comprises 25 districts and 4 offshore islands. Agats is a remote expedition-style cruise call in South Papua and the gateway to the Asmat cultural region. The town itself is unusual: much of it stands above tidal swamp on raised wooden or concrete walkways, with electric motorcycles rather than conventional road traffic. Central Agats can be explored on foot, but the river journeys and village visits that are the main reason for calling here are best handled through the ship or an organized local guide. Agats has local ferry and sea-port facilities, but visiting cruise ships normally operate differently. Published expedition itineraries describe ships entering the shallow Flamingo River area when conditions allow, anchoring near Agats and transferring passengers by Zodiac or ship boat. Tide and river conditions can affect the exact landing point and timetable, so follow the arrangements announced onboard rather than assuming passengers will use the town ferry pier. Once ashore, most central sights can be reached on foot. Agats has no normal road network for cars; its streets are largely raised wooden or concrete walkways over swampy ground. Electric motorcycles are the principal local vehicle, and motorcycle taxis operate locally, but walking is normally more practical for cruise visitors staying in the center. There is no useful tourist public-transport network for reaching the surrounding Asmat communities. Villages are connected mainly by rivers and waterways, making ship-operated or locally guided boat trips the sensible option.
terminal_notes: Tide and river conditions can affect the exact landing point and timetable, so follow the arrangements announced onboard rather than assuming passengers will use the town ferry pier.

things_to_do.name: Explore Agats and the Asmat Museum
things_to_do.description: Allow about 2–3 hours. Walking through Agats is an attraction in itself, with homes, shops, government buildings and public spaces raised above the tidal wetlands. The most important stop is the Museum of Asmat Culture and Progress, whose collection includes carvings, shields, drums, ceremonial objects and other material from communities across the Asmat region. The museum is particularly worthwhile before or after a village visit because it provides context for Asmat carving, ceremonies and traditional life. It publishes daytime opening Monday through Saturday, while Sunday and holiday closure is stated; published closing times vary, so cruise visitors should confirm access with expedition staff.

things_to_do.name: Join an Asmat Village and Cultural Visit
things_to_do.description: Usually a half-day expedition activity. This is generally the most significant experience of an Agats call and is best done with the cruise line or an experienced local operator. Expedition programs commonly use Zodiacs or motorboats to travel through the Asewet River delta and surrounding waterways before visiting an Asmat community. Depending on arrangements, visits may include traditional canoes, carving, a communal Jew house, music or ceremonial performances. These are community visits rather than attractions that passengers should attempt to reach independently. River conditions, tides and local arrangements determine what is possible on a particular day.

things_to_do.name: Walk to Syuru
things_to_do.description: Allow about 1.5–2 hours from central Agats and back. Syuru lies immediately beside Agats and is one of the nearest Asmat communities accessible via the raised walkway network. Local sources describe it as roughly a 10-minute walk from the central town area. The community is associated with a traditional Jew communal house and is also used as a venue during Asmat cultural events. This is more practical than trying to arrange an independent boat to a distant village, but visitors should treat Syuru as a living community rather than an open-air attraction. A local guide is preferable, especially if entering community buildings or photographing residents.

things_to_do.name: River and Mangrove Exploration
things_to_do.description: Allow 2–4 hours depending on the ship's program. Agats is surrounded by broad muddy rivers, tidal channels, mangroves and swamp forest rather than conventional beaches. Zodiac or small-boat exploration can therefore be more rewarding than remaining entirely in town, with opportunities to observe the landscape and river-based way of life. This should normally be booked or arranged through the expedition team. Tide levels and rapidly changing weather can influence navigation, and independent boat arrangements introduce unnecessary return-to-ship risk.

things_to_do.name: Central Agats Cultural Walk
things_to_do.description: Approximate distance: 3–5 km (1.9–3.1 mi), depending on the ship's landing point and whether Syuru is included. Pure walking time: about 50–80 minutes. Recommended total time: 2.5–3.5 hours with museum and sightseeing stops. Difficulty: Easy to moderate. The route is essentially flat, but raised wooden walkways can be uneven, wet and slippery. Cruise landing point: Begin wherever the expedition team brings passengers ashore. Confirm the required final Zodiac or tender departure before leaving the landing area. Agats boardwalks: Walk through the central raised streets to see how the town functions above tidal swamp. Watch for quietly approaching electric motorcycles. Local market: Make a short stop to see everyday trading and produce from the surrounding river communities. Holy Cross Cathedral: Visit the cathedral area, long associated with the Catholic Diocese of Agats and Asmat cultural preservation. Construction of a new cathedral building was still underway in mid-2026, so access and appearance may vary. Museum of Asmat Culture and Progress: Allow at least 45–60 minutes for the collection of Asmat carvings and cultural objects. Optional Syuru extension: Continue along the walkway network into nearby Syuru if time and local arrangements permit, then return directly toward central Agats. Return to the landing: Be back well before the ship's stated final boat time; expedition operations may change with tides or weather. Passengers with limited mobility should be cautious. Even though there are no significant hills, some sections may involve narrow walkways, irregular boards, steps and surfaces that become slick after rain.

name: Agilkia Island (Philae Temple, Egypt)
summary: Agilkia Island (aka Agilika Island) is a Nile River cruise port destination located inside the Old Aswan Dam (along the river) and is the site of the Ancient Egyptian Philae temple complex. In 1902, the entire temple complex on Philae Island (downstream of Lake Nasser) was dismantled and relocated to Agilkia due to the flooding of this area to form the reservoir of the Aswan High Dam (1960-70).
description: Agilkia Island (aka Agilika Island) is a Nile River cruise port destination located inside the Old Aswan Dam (along the river) and is the site of the Ancient Egyptian Philae temple complex. In 1902, the entire temple complex on Philae Island (downstream of Lake Nasser) was dismantled and relocated to Agilkia due to the flooding of this area to form the reservoir of the Aswan High Dam (1960-70). A total of 22 Ancient Egyption monuments and architectural sites were threatened by the flooding from Lake Nasser. To preserve them was launched the UNESCO Nubia Campaign. By this grandious project were moved the Abu Simbel temples , Philae temples (Philae Island), Kalabsha temples and the Amada Temple (Nubia's oldest). Also dismantled and relocated were Debod Temple (15 km south of Aswan , moved to Madrid Spain ), Dendur Temple (given to NYC 's Metropolitan Museum of Art), Taffeh Temple (given to Leiden Holland 's Rijksmuseum van Oudheden) and Ellesyia Temple (near Qasr Ibrim, given to Turin Italy's Museo Egizio). Agilkia Island is the present-day site of the Philae temple complex near Aswan. For cruise passengers, this is not a conventional walk-off port: the island is reached only by small motorboat, normally after a road transfer from a Nile cruise mooring in Aswan to the Philae/Shellal Marina. The Temple of Isis is the main reason to visit, and the combination of road transfer, boat ride and archaeological site makes it best treated as a half-day shore visit.
getting_from_port: Most Nile cruise vessels do not berth at Agilkia itself. They normally call at Aswan, from where passengers travel by coach, private vehicle or taxi to the visitor marina near Shellal and the Aswan Low Dam. Small motorboats then carry visitors across the reservoir to the island's visitor jetty. Independent travel is possible, but it requires coordinating both the road transfer and the return boat. If arranging the boat yourself, confirm the return arrangement before leaving the marina. For cruise passengers on a tight schedule, a pre-arranged driver or organized excursion removes most of this uncertainty.

things_to_do.name: Philae Temple Complex
things_to_do.description: Allow about 1.5–2 hours on the island, or 3–4 hours including transfers from Aswan. This is the essential Agilkia visit. The principal monument is the Temple of Isis, surrounded by courtyards, pylons, smaller shrines and waterfront structures. Important highlights include the First Pylon, the birth house or Mammisi, the inner temple chambers, the Temple of Hathor and Trajan's Kiosk. The visit is practical independently if transport is arranged in advance. A guide is useful for interpreting the reliefs and temple layout, but the complex is compact enough to explore without one.

things_to_do.name: Philae and the Aswan High Dam
things_to_do.description: Allow roughly 3.5–4.5 hours. Visitors with a vehicle can combine Philae with the Aswan High Dam. This works well because both lie south of central Aswan, reducing unnecessary backtracking. The dam visit itself is relatively short, so most of the time can still be spent at Philae. Independent with planning. A hired driver can make this straightforward, although an organized excursion is convenient if the cruise schedule is tight.

things_to_do.name: Philae, the Unfinished Obelisk and Central Aswan
things_to_do.description: Allow approximately 5–6 hours. A longer call can include Philae followed by the Unfinished Obelisk and then a return to central Aswan for the Nile waterfront, Nubian Museum or a short walk around the city. This combination requires road transport between sites. Trying to add several further attractions can make the day rushed, particularly when boat queues and road traffic are taken into account.

things_to_do.name: Evening Sound and Light Visit
things_to_do.description: The Philae Sound and Light presentation can be an option for cruises staying in Aswan into the evening or overnight. Because daytime archaeological opening and evening-show arrangements are separate, this is generally more practical as an organized transfer than as a spontaneous independent visit.

things_to_do.name: Temple of Isis and Waterfront Circuit
things_to_do.description: Distance: approximately 1–1.5 km (0.6–0.9 mi), depending on detours inside the temple. Pure walking time: about 20–30 minutes. Recommended total time: 1.5–2 hours. Difficulty: Easy to moderate. Distances are short, but expect uneven stone paving, occasional steps and substantial heat exposure. Visitor jetty: Start where the motorboat drops passengers on Agilkia and follow the main approach toward the temple complex. Outer courtyard and First Pylon: Enter through the monumental approach and spend time examining the large carved reliefs. Mammisi: Visit the birth house beside the main temple route before continuing farther into the sanctuary complex. Temple of Isis: Continue through the courts, columned spaces and inner chambers toward the sanctuary. Temple of Hathor: After leaving the principal temple, follow the paths toward this smaller structure on the eastern side of the complex. Trajan's Kiosk: Finish at the distinctive columned pavilion near the water, one of the best viewpoints on the island. Return to the jetty: Follow the waterfront path back to the boat landing and allow time to locate your assigned or arranged return boat. The route is short enough for most visitors, but the exposed stone surfaces can become very hot. Allow more time than the distance suggests, especially if stopping frequently for reliefs and interior chambers.

Agios Nikolaos (port locode GRANI), also Aghios Nikolaos, is a coastal town situated on the Greek island of Crete. It lies east of island's capital Heraklion , west of the town of Sitia and north of the town of Ierapetra. In 2011, the Municipality of Agios Nikolaos, taking in part of the surrounding villages, had 27,070 inhabitants. The town of Agios Nikolaos is a municipality of Crete region. It sits partially on the ruins of the ancient city Lato pros Kamara. The total area of the municipal unit is 317.8 km2 (122.7 ml2). Agios Nikolaos was established by Dorian occupants of Lato in the late Bronze Age, at a time when the security of Lato hillfort became lesser concern and easy access to Agios Nikolaos' harbour became more important. The name of the city means Saint Nicholas. Agios Nikolaos is a common placename in Cyprus and Greece, since Saint Nicholas is patron saint of sailors and all of Greece. The archaeological site of Priniatikos Pyrgos is near the town. It was first settled in Final Neolithic, circa 3000 BC. Activity on it continued throughout Minoan Bronze Age and Classical Greek and Roman periods. Agios Nikolaos is accessible from the whole of Europe and the mainland through Nikos Kazantzakis airport, as well as the daily ferry services in Heraklion. Just a short ferry ride away from the town is Spinalonga Island, an old Venetian fortress turned ex-leper colony in the early 20th century. Agios Nikolaos is best known as a tourist town serving as a hub to the 20 or so small villages and farms which make up that part of Lassithi. Major tourist attractions include the small island Agioi Pantes, the lagoon Lake Voulismeni, the archaeological museum, local flora exhibition “Iris” and several fairs. Tourism is Western European, with the Greek tourism concentrated in mid-August, but there are a lot of Russian tourists in East Crete. The Lake Voulismeni lagoon has a small park with a trail, ducks, pigeons, traditional fishing boats, many cafes and an amphitheatre. During the 60's the modern Agios Nikolaos city became internationally recognized as it was "discovered" by renowned cinema directors (Walt Disney, Jules Dassin, etc.), BBC producers and others. The short story 'Not After Midnight' of Daphne du Maurier was set in and around Agios Nikolaos. Agios Nikolaos is one of the easier Crete ports to explore without an excursion. The cruise harbor is immediately beside the town, with Lake Voulismeni, the waterfront and central shopping streets within a short walk. For a longer day, Spinalonga, Elounda and Kritsa are realistic independent trips with advance transport planning. Independent sightseeing: Easy independently for Agios Nikolaos itself. Independent with some planning or transport for Spinalonga, Elounda and Kritsa.
getting_from_port: Agios Nikolaos is not exclusively a tender port. Cruise ships can berth at the town harbor, and recent port improvements allow vessels up to about 250 meters long to dock. The exact arrangement still depends on the ship and berth allocation, so some calls may use an offshore anchorage and tenders. Whether arriving directly at the quay or by tender, passengers normally come ashore in the central harbor area. There is no long industrial-port transfer: the town center can be reached on foot, with Lake Voulismeni roughly 5–10 minutes away. Walking: Best option for the town itself. The waterfront is mostly straightforward and paved. Taxi: Most practical for Spinalonga via Plaka, Kritsa, Panagia Kera or Ancient Lato when time ashore is limited. Public bus: KTEL services connect Agios Nikolaos with Elounda, Plaka and Kritsa. Frequencies are substantially better during the summer season, so check the timetable for the actual port-call date. Shuttle: A transfer into the center is normally unnecessary because the harbor is already beside the town.

things_to_do.name: Lake Voulismeni and Central Agios Nikolaos
things_to_do.description: Allow: 1.5–3 hours. Transport: Walk. Difficulty: Easy. The simplest port day is also a worthwhile one. Walk from the harbor to Lake Voulismeni, follow the cafés and pedestrian streets around the waterfront, continue to Kitroplateia and return along the coast. The lower waterfront is easy walking, although reaching some viewpoints above the lake involves slopes or steps. This option works especially well on a short call because almost no time is lost to transportation.

things_to_do.name: Archaeological Museum and Waterfront
things_to_do.description: Allow: 2–3 hours. Transport: Walk. Difficulty: Easy. The Archaeological Museum of Agios Nikolaos contains finds from eastern Crete and is close enough to combine with the lake and harbor on foot. It is a useful alternative to a long archaeological excursion elsewhere on Crete. State museums commonly close on Tuesdays and opening arrangements can change, so confirm before making it the focus of the day.

things_to_do.name: Spinalonga and Plaka
things_to_do.description: Allow: About 4–5 hours. Transport: Taxi, seasonal bus or organized excursion plus boat. Difficulty: Moderate because of uneven stone surfaces on Spinalonga. Spinalonga is the strongest excursion option from Agios Nikolaos. Plaka is about 16 km (9.9 mi) from town and roughly 20–30 minutes away by road. Boats make the short crossing from Plaka to the island; Elounda, about 10 km (6.2 mi) from Agios Nikolaos, is another departure point. Allow roughly 1.5–2 hours to explore the fortified island itself. Seasonal KTEL buses run from Agios Nikolaos toward Plaka and Elounda, but a taxi gives cruise passengers more control over the return journey. Boat services and archaeological-site access are seasonal, so check both before leaving the port. Independent with planning. An organized excursion becomes preferable on a short call, when tendering reduces time ashore, or if public transport timings leave little margin.
things_to_do.difficulty: Moderate because of uneven stone surfaces on Spinalonga

things_to_do.name: Kritsa, Panagia Kera and Ancient Lato
things_to_do.description: Allow: 3–4 hours. Transport: Taxi is easiest; bus works for Kritsa. Difficulty: Easy in the village, moderate at Lato. Kritsa lies about 10 km (6.2 mi) inland and is a practical alternative for passengers interested in a traditional Cretan village rather than a boat trip. The Byzantine church of Panagia Kera is about 1 km (0.6 mi) before the village. Ancient Lato lies another 3 km (1.9 mi) beyond Kritsa and is one of the best-preserved Classical-Hellenistic towns on Crete. It is about an 18-minute drive from Agios Nikolaos. Combining all three locations is easiest by taxi or arranged vehicle; walking from Kritsa to Lato takes around 45 minutes each way and is inefficient during a cruise call.
things_to_do.difficulty: Easy in the village, moderate at Lato

things_to_do.name: Harbor, Lake and Waterfront Loop
things_to_do.description: Distance: about 2.5 km (1.6 mi). Pure walking time: about 35–45 minutes. Recommended total time: 1.5–2.5 hours. Difficulty: Easy, with optional slopes and steps around the lake viewpoints. Cruise harbor or tender landing – leave the port on foot and follow the waterfront toward the center. Lake Voulismeni – walk along the lower lakeside promenade and the channel connecting the lake with the sea. Upper lake viewpoint – take the short uphill streets or steps for a higher view over the lake; skip this section if mobility is limited. Central pedestrian streets – continue through the compact shopping area behind the lake. Kitroplateia waterfront – reach the small central beach and seaside promenade; this is also suitable for a short swim in warm weather. Harbor return – follow the waterfront back toward the cruise quay. The route can easily be shortened. Passengers visiting the Archaeological Museum can add it near the beginning or end of the walk, allowing additional time for the collection.
things_to_do.difficulty: Easy, with optional slopes and steps around the lake viewpoints

name: Agropoli (Italy)
summary: Port Agropoli cruise ship schedule shows timetable calendars of all arrival and departure dates by month. The port's schedule lists all ships (in links) with cruises going to or leaving from Agropoli, Italy. To see the full itineraries (ports of call dates and arrival / departure times) and their lowest rates – just follow the corresponding ship-link.
description: Port Agropoli cruise ship schedule shows timetable calendars of all arrival and departure dates by month. The port's schedule lists all ships (in links) with cruises going to or leaving from Agropoli, Italy. To see the full itineraries (ports of call dates and arrival / departure times) and their lowest rates – just follow the corresponding ship-link. Agropoli (port locode ITAGP) is port city in Salerno province, Campania region (Italy). it is located at the beginning of Cilento coast on Tyrrhenian Sea. Agropoli is an important access port to nearby ancient site of Paestum. Established by the Greeks in 600 BC, the well-preserved site was rediscovered in 1752. Today it features the impressive Amphitheatre, Athenian Basilica, and the Temple of Poseidon. Founded by the Byzantines in the 6th century, Agropoli boasts a medieval old town that has remained intact, together with surrounding defensive walls, and a 7th-century entrance gate. Angevin-Aragonese castle, built on 6th-century Byzantine foundations, stands on top of a promontory. There is another promontory to the west of the modern tourist harbour, on which the 16th-century coastal tower of San Francesco stands next to the remains of a convent of the same name. Other main sights in Agripoli include tombs predating the Byzantine period and 16th-century Churches of Holy Mary of Constantinople, San Marco, and San Francesco. Trentova Bay beaches contribute to making the city an important seaside resort. The Municipal Antiquarian presents a collection of archaeological finds. Agropoli is a compact Cilento port where the medieval old town, castle and waterfront are practical to explore independently. Cruise ships generally anchor offshore rather than berth inside the shallow tourist harbour, so passengers should expect tender operations. The major excursion from Agropoli is Paestum, one of Italy's best-preserved Greek archaeological sites.
getting_from_port: Agropoli's harbour is primarily a marina for yachts and smaller craft, with limited depth for cruise vessels. Cruise calls therefore normally use an offshore anchorage and tenders to bring passengers into the harbour area. Once ashore, no transfer is needed for central Agropoli. The medieval quarter is less than a 10-minute walk away via the waterfront and the streets below the promontory. Taxis are available locally and are useful for Paestum or for passengers who want to avoid longer walks. The railway station is about 1.9 km (1.2 mi) from the port, making the train possible for Paestum, but the extra walk or taxi transfer to the station needs to be included in the schedule.
terminal_notes: Cruise ships generally anchor offshore rather than berth inside the shallow tourist harbour, so passengers should expect tender operations.
tender_evidence: Cruise ships generally anchor offshore rather than berth inside the shallow tourist harbour, so passengers should expect tender operations.

things_to_do.name: Explore the Old Town and Castello Angioino-Aragonese
things_to_do.description: Recommended time: 1.5–2.5 hours. Independent: Easy. From the harbour, walk toward the base of the old town and climb the Scaloni Ennio Balbo to the historic entrance. Continue through the stone gateway to Piazza Madonna di Costantinopoli, the narrow lanes of the borgo and the castle at the top of the promontory. The principal attraction is as much the setting and coastal views as the individual buildings. The climb includes steep streets and many steps, so it is less suitable for passengers with limited mobility. Castle access and opening times should be checked on the day of the visit.

things_to_do.name: Visit Paestum
things_to_do.description: Recommended time: 4–5 hours including transport. Independent: Practical with planning. Paestum is the strongest choice for passengers interested in archaeology. Its archaeological area contains three exceptionally well-preserved Greek temples together with Roman remains and a museum. By road, allow roughly 20–25 minutes each way under normal conditions. A taxi arranged for both directions is the simplest independent option. Train travel is also possible. Agropoli-Castellabate station is about 1.9 km (1.2 mi) from the port, and direct regional trains can reach Paestum in approximately 6–10 minutes. From Paestum station, the archaeological area and museum are about a 15-minute walk through Porta Sirena. Train frequencies vary, so check the current timetable before leaving the ship and identify a suitable return service in advance. For a short port call, or when tender and train timings leave little margin, an organized excursion or prearranged taxi is the safer practical choice.

things_to_do.name: Baia di Trentova
things_to_do.description: Recommended time: 2.5–4 hours. Independent: Easy with walking or a short taxi ride. Trentova Bay is the main beach and nature option close to Agropoli. The coastal walk from the port is about 2 km (1.2 mi) each way and takes approximately one hour at a relaxed pace. It follows a paved panoramic road and passes the San Francesco coastal area before reaching the bay. A taxi is preferable if the objective is simply to spend time swimming rather than use much of the port call walking. Beach facilities are most active in the warmer months.

things_to_do.name: Waterfront and Lungomare San Marco
things_to_do.description: Recommended time: 1–2 hours. Independent: Very easy. Passengers wanting a low-effort visit can remain around the marina, central streets and Lungomare San Marco. This is substantially flatter than the old town and works well for a short call, a meal or a stroll before returning to the tender.

things_to_do.name: Historic Agropoli Walk
things_to_do.description: Distance: about 2–2.5 km (1.2–1.6 mi) round trip. Pure walking time: 35–45 minutes. Recommended total time: 1.5–2 hours. Difficulty: Moderate because of the steep climb and stairs. Harbour area: Start where the tender transfer brings passengers ashore and walk along the waterfront toward the historic center. Via Cavour and Via Rupe: Continue toward the foot of the old-town promontory. Scaloni Ennio Balbo: Climb the broad staircase leading to the historic entrance. Old-town gateway: Pass through the monumental entrance into the medieval borgo. Piazza Madonna di Costantinopoli: Stop at the church and viewpoints overlooking the harbour and coast. Historic lanes: Continue uphill through the compact network of narrow streets. Castello Angioino-Aragonese: Reach the highest point of the walk for wide coastal views. Return: Descend through the same old-town entrance and continue back to the harbour. This route is straightforward without a guide, but comfortable shoes are advisable because of stone paving, stairs and steep gradients.
things_to_do.difficulty: Moderate because of the steep climb and stairs

things_to_do.name: Port to Trentova Coastal Walk
things_to_do.description: Distance: about 4 km (2.5 mi) round trip to Trentova Bay. Pure walking time: about 1.5–2 hours. Recommended total time: 3–4 hours with beach time. Difficulty: Easy to moderate. Start at Agropoli harbour. Follow the coastal road away from the town center. Pass the San Francesco coastal area and viewpoints. Continue along the panoramic road toward Trentova. Spend time at Baia di Trentova before returning by the same route or taking a taxi back to the harbour. The route is largely paved but has some gradients and limited shade. In hot summer weather, carrying water and using a taxi for one direction can make the outing considerably easier.

Aigues-Mortes is a Rhone River cruise port and town in France's Gard department (Occitanie region) with population around 9,000. The town is best-known for its perfectly preserved surrounding medieval city walls. Aigues-Mortes is located approx 90 km (56 ml) northwest of Marseille (on the French Riviera ), approx 33 km (21 ml) southwest of Nimes (Gard department's capital city) and approx 20 km (12 ml) east of Montpellier (Herault department's capital). The town is also part of France's Petite Camargue (natural region south of Arles and between Mediterranean Sea and Rhone River Delta) featuring as scenery wet plains and lakes. It is separated from Mediterranean Sea by Gulf of Lions but is also connected to the sea via Canal du Rhone a Sete that links Retang de Thau lagoons ( Sete ) with Rhone River (at Beaucaire). The canal enters the town from northwest and two branches intersect it before exiting (as a single waterway) and flowing into Mediterranean Sea. A railway from Nimes also passes through (northeast to southwest, with a train station in Aigues-Mortes) and links to the coastal terminus Le-Grau-du-Roi. This railway is used for both passenger and sea salt transportation. As cruise port, Aigues-Mortes is included in the regular schedule of the luxury hotel barge Anne Marie . The boat is owned and operated by one of Europe's largest river cruise companies - CroisiEurope . Next table shows the ports sequence of barge ship's 6-day itinerary between homeports Sete and Arles, with prices from ~USD 2000 per person (double occupancy cabin rates). Aigues-Mortes is one of the easiest cruise stops in the Camargue to explore independently. Cruise calls here are normally made by small hotel barges using the canal-side quays or marina beside the medieval town, so there is no long transfer from a seaport. The fortified center, Tour de Constance and canal excursions are all within easy walking distance.
getting_from_port: Small cruise barges normally moor on the Canal du Rhône à Sète around the Aigues-Mortes marina and Quai des Croisades. Exact berths can vary, but the port is immediately beside the fortified town. Passengers can normally walk directly from the vessel toward the Tour de Constance and city walls without a shuttle. Aigues-Mortes railway station is also close to the walls. Regional trains connect the town with Le Grau-du-Roi and Nîmes, while regional buses serve Nîmes and Montpellier. Public transport is unnecessary for local sightseeing and should only be used for a side trip after checking the return timetable carefully.

things_to_do.name: Explore the Walled Medieval Town
things_to_do.description: Allow: 1.5–2.5 hours. Independent: Very easy. Walk through the gates into the compact historic center, with Place Saint-Louis, Notre-Dame-des-Sablons church, small chapels, narrow streets and the almost complete medieval fortifications. Most sights are close together, making this the safest choice for a short call.

things_to_do.name: Walk the Ramparts and Tour de Constance
things_to_do.description: Allow: about 1.5–2 hours for the monument itself. Independent: Easy, but moderately strenuous. The complete rampart circuit is about 1.6 km (1.0 mi) and gives elevated views over the rooftops, canals, salt ponds and surrounding Camargue. The route includes roughly 100 steps, irregular surfaces and exposed sections with little shade. Access to the Tour de Constance and part of the ramparts is adapted for reduced mobility, but the complete circuit is not step-free.

things_to_do.name: Visit the Aigues-Mortes Salt Works
things_to_do.description: Allow: about 2–2.5 hours including travel and the visit. Independent: Practical with some planning. The Salin d'Aigues-Mortes visitor area is roughly 2 km (1.2 mi) from the walled center. Its salt ponds, birdlife and large salt mounds provide the most distinctive landscape around the town. A tourist train operates inside the salt works on scheduled departures and takes about 1 hour 15 minutes. Walking to the entrance is possible but can be hot and exposed; a bicycle or taxi is more comfortable. Departures are seasonal and can change because of weather or operating conditions, so booking ahead is sensible when the visit is important to your plans.

things_to_do.name: Take a Camargue Canal Cruise
things_to_do.description: Allow: 1.5–3 hours depending on the cruise selected. Independent: Very easy. Local sightseeing boats leave from the Bassin d'évolution near Avenue Tour de Constance, less than 0.5 km (0.3 mi) from the marina. Short cruises follow the Canal du Rhône à Sète through Camargue landscapes, offering an easy nature-focused alternative to additional walking. Check the departure time before committing, as schedules vary by season.

things_to_do.name: Le Grau-du-Roi and the Beach
things_to_do.description: Allow: at least 3–4 hours. Independent: Possible with planning. Le Grau-du-Roi is about 6 km (3.7 mi) from Aigues-Mortes and has a fishing harbor and Mediterranean beaches. Regional trains take about 9 minutes when the timetable fits, but services are not frequent enough to rely on without checking the return first. A dedicated cycle route also connects the two towns for about 6 km (3.7 mi) each way, largely alongside the canal and wetlands. This is a good option for an active visitor with a long call, but the medieval town and salt works are better priorities on a shorter stop.

things_to_do.name: Medieval Aigues-Mortes Circuit
things_to_do.description: Distance: up to about 4 km (2.5 mi), depending on detours. Pure walking time: about 50–60 minutes. Recommended total: 1.5–2 hours. Difficulty: Easy to moderate; mostly flat with cobbles and uneven paving. Canal-side berth / Quai des Croisades: Start beside the marina and walk toward the prominent round Tour de Constance. Tour de Constance: See the town's principal medieval tower. Enter here if you plan to visit the ramparts; otherwise continue at street level. Porte de la Gardette: Pass the historic main gateway into the fortified town. Chapelle des Pénitents Blancs: Continue through the quieter northeastern streets to this small historic chapel. Eastern and southern gates: Follow the inside of the walls toward Porte de la Reine and Porte de la Marine for views toward the salt-marsh landscape. Place Saint-Louis: Turn back into the center for the main square, statue of Saint Louis and the tourist office. Notre-Dame-des-Sablons: Visit the town's principal church, just off the square. Return to the ship: Continue through the western streets toward the Tour de Constance and canal-side marina. Passengers wanting a more demanding version can add the paid 1.6 km (1.0 mi) rampart circuit. With the tower, walls and town-center stops, allow roughly 3–4 hours rather than trying to rush the complete visit.
