Airlie Beach is a port town in Whitsunday Region (North Queensland, Australia), with population around 8,000. Port Airlie (aka Abel Point) is among the departure ports for Coral Sea cruises to Great Barrier Reef . Most regularly scheduled cruise ship calls to Airlie Beach are from Carnival Corporation -owned liners - from the fleets of Carnival Australia , P&O Australia and Princess Cruises . Airlie Beach as tourism travel destination is extremely popular among backpackers and boaters. As the beach is relatively small and the surrounding waters are teeming with box jellyfish and marine stingers, to provide a swimming zone for visitors, the town council built a medium-sized lagoon (similar to Cairns '). Airlie Beach Lagoon is sized approx 4300 m2 (46300 ft2). Whitsunday Islands were named by James Cook (1728-1779, British Royal Navy officer and cartographer). He named them in 1770 as he believed his passage through the region was on Whit Sunday (Christian festival day), without taking into account the International Date Line. Each year, local rsidents celebrate The Blessing of Fleet on Whit Sunday (Pentecost Sunday). Town's official between 1936-1987 was just Airlie. Busking (street performances) were legalized in June 2010. Most tour boat cruises from Airlie Beach to Great Barrier Reef (and the all 74x Whitsundays islands) depart from Abell Point Marina, and only a few leave out of Port Airlie. Abell Point Marina has 507 berths (moorings). Cruise ships anchor near the Marina and ferry their passengers ashore via the ship's tender boats. Abell Point Marina as facilities and amenities offers 3 restaurants (cafe bars), 1 event facility, 300 car parking lots, relaxation areas, newly developed parkland, helipad (helicopter landing area), boat maintenance facilities, services (laundry, showers, toilets, Wifi, car rental, diving, fueling, water and power supply, security, ship chandlery, waste collection). The nearest airfield is approx 30 km (19 ml) away. Abell Point Marina provides berthing even for superyachts, having 100 fixed moorings for boats with LOA length between 25-70 m (82-230 ft). Marina's max draft is 5 m (16 ft). Independent sightseeing: Independent with some planning or transport. Airlie Beach is a tender port rather than a walk-off cruise berth. Ships normally anchor offshore and passengers are brought ashore at either Port of Airlie or Shute Harbour. The landing point matters: Port of Airlie is beside the town centre, while Shute Harbour is about 10 km (6.2 mi) east of Airlie Beach and requires a bus, taxi or arranged transfer. For a short call, Airlie Beach itself is very easy to explore. For the Whitsunday Islands, Whitehaven Beach or the Great Barrier Reef, timing becomes much more important because boat trips can consume most or all of the available time ashore.
getting_from_port: This is the easiest arrival point for independent visitors. The marina terminal is only a short walk from the southern end of central Airlie Beach, with the main street reachable in roughly 5–10 minutes. The lagoon, shops, cafes and foreshore are all practical on foot. Shute Harbour Marine Terminal is about 10 km (6.2 mi) east of Airlie Beach, roughly 15 minutes by road in normal conditions. It is not practical to walk into town. Whitsunday Transit buses connect Shute Harbour with Airlie Beach, and taxis are another option. Check the same-day timetable and allow additional time for the return journey. Always confirm the day's tender landing point in the ship's information before making independent plans. The terminal used can vary by ship and call.
terminal_notes: Airlie Beach is a tender port rather than a walk-off cruise berth.
tender_evidence: Cruise ships anchor near the Marina and ferry their passengers ashore via the ship's tender boats.

things_to_do.name: Port of Airlie tender landing
things_to_do.description: This is the easiest arrival point for independent visitors. The marina terminal is only a short walk from the southern end of central Airlie Beach, with the main street reachable in roughly 5–10 minutes. The lagoon, shops, cafes and foreshore are all practical on foot.

things_to_do.name: Shute Harbour tender landing
things_to_do.description: Shute Harbour Marine Terminal is about 10 km (6.2 mi) east of Airlie Beach, roughly 15 minutes by road in normal conditions. It is not practical to walk into town. Whitsunday Transit buses connect Shute Harbour with Airlie Beach, and taxis are another option. Check the same-day timetable and allow additional time for the return journey. Always confirm the day's tender landing point in the ship's information before making independent plans. The terminal used can vary by ship and call.

things_to_do.name: Airlie Beach, Lagoon and Foreshore
things_to_do.description: Allow: 2–3 hours. Difficulty: Easy. Independent: Very practical, especially from Port of Airlie. For passengers who do not want to commit to a long excursion, central Airlie Beach is the safest use of a short call. Walk through the main street, continue to the waterfront and spend time around Airlie Beach Lagoon. The large public swimming lagoon is particularly useful in the Whitsundays because it provides swimming without exposure to marine stingers or other marine wildlife. Continue along the foreshore for views over Pioneer Bay, or extend the walk toward Coral Sea Marina before returning to the tender terminal.

things_to_do.name: Bicentennial Walkway and Coral Sea Marina
things_to_do.description: Allow: 2–4 hours depending on distance. Difficulty: Easy to moderate because of length and tropical heat. Independent: Easy. The Bicentennial Walkway follows the waterfront through the lagoon precinct, Coral Sea Marina, Shingley Beach and toward Cannonvale. Most of the route is flat and paved or boardwalk, making it one of the best independent activities in Airlie Beach. The full Lagoon-to-Cannonvale section is about 4 km (2.5 mi) each way. There is no need to complete the whole route; the lagoon-to-marina section provides the best option for passengers with limited time.
things_to_do.difficulty: Easy to moderate because of length and tropical heat

things_to_do.name: Whitehaven Beach and Hill Inlet
things_to_do.description: Allow: Usually most of the port call. Independent: Possible only with careful scheduling; organized excursion often preferable. Whitehaven Beach is the main Whitsundays excursion from Airlie Beach. Boat tours may include beach time, Hill Inlet viewpoints, snorkelling or combinations of these activities. Even products described as half-day trips can occupy around 6–7 hours from the mainland once island transfers and cruising time are included. Independent booking is realistic only when the published departure and return times fit comfortably between your actual tender arrival ashore and the ship's final tender. Passengers on shorter calls should favor a cruise-line excursion or a specifically cruise-compatible tour rather than relying on a tight independent connection.

things_to_do.name: Whitsundays and Great Barrier Reef Scenic Flight
things_to_do.description: Allow: About 2–3 hours including transfer, check-in and the flight. Independent: Practical with advance booking. A scenic flight is one of the more time-efficient ways to see the Whitsunday Islands, Whitehaven Beach, Hill Inlet and parts of the Great Barrier Reef. Some flights themselves last around one hour, although the total outing is longer once check-in and ground transfers are included. Operations are weather-dependent, so leave enough time for delays or schedule changes.

things_to_do.name: Outer Great Barrier Reef
things_to_do.description: Allow: Full day. Independent: Generally not recommended for a normal cruise call. Mainland trips to the outer reef can run for around 10 hours, with substantial cruising time each way. That makes them unsuitable for many 7–8 hour port calls. Consider an outer-reef trip only on a particularly long call or when it is offered as a ship-organized excursion with timing arranged around the vessel.

things_to_do.name: Easy: Port of Airlie to Lagoon and Coral Sea Marina
things_to_do.description: Distance: About 2.3 km (1.4 mi) one way, or roughly 4.6 km (2.9 mi) returning on foot. Pure walking time: About 30 minutes each way. Recommended total: 2–3 hours. Terrain: Mostly flat paved streets, promenade and waterfront paths. Port of Airlie: Leave the tender terminal and follow the pedestrian route toward central Airlie Beach. Airlie Beach main street: Walk through the compact shopping and dining area. Airlie Beach Lagoon: Stop for a swim or a short break beside the waterfront. Foreshore: Continue along the pedestrian path overlooking Pioneer Bay. Coral Sea Resort waterfront: Follow the coastal route toward the marina precinct. Coral Sea Marina: Turn around here, have a short refreshment stop, or return toward Port of Airlie. This is the best general-purpose walking route for cruise passengers because it stays close to town and can be shortened at almost any point. If tired or short of time, use a taxi or local bus for part of the return.

things_to_do.name: Moderate: Bicentennial Walkway to Cannonvale Beach
things_to_do.description: Distance: About 8 km (5.0 mi) return from the lagoon, plus the walk between the lagoon and your tender terminal. Pure walking time: Around 1.5–2 hours. Recommended total: 3–4 hours with stops. Terrain: Mostly flat, but the distance and tropical heat can make it tiring. Airlie Beach Lagoon: Begin on the waterfront. Coral Sea Marina: Follow the signed coastal walkway around the marina precinct. Shingley Beach: Continue along the shoreline and boardwalk sections. Waterfront lookouts: Pause for views across Pioneer Bay and the Whitsunday Islands. Cannonvale Beach: Use this as the turnaround point. Return: Walk back the same way or use local transport from Cannonvale if necessary. This route is better for passengers with at least several hours free after tendering. Avoid committing to the full return walk if the day is very hot or if your ship has an early final tender.

To see the full itineraries (ports of call dates and arrival / departure times) and their lowest rates – just follow the corresponding ship-link. Aitutaki Island (traditionally known as Ararau, Araura, Utataki) is one of Cook Islands. It is located north of Rarotonga , has population of around 2,000 and covers a total land area of approx 18 km2 (7 mi2). Aitutaki is the 2nd most of the Cook Islands. The main village (and cruise port) is Arutunga (aka Arutanga) on the west side. Aitutaki is an "almost atoll" with highest elevation 123 m (404 ft) - a hill called Maunga Pu close to the island's northernmost point. There is an area suited for land flying boats in the lagoon's southeastern part. Probably the first who settled Aitutaki were the Polynesians around AD 900. The first European contact was with Captain Bligh (1754-1817) and the crew of HMS Bounty when he discovered Aitutaki on 11 April 1789, prior to infamous mutiny. On February 10–11, 2010 the island of Aitutaki was devastated by Cyclone Pat. The high winds ripped the roofs off of most buildings and damaged other including a hospital and a school. More than 60% of houses were damaged. A few minor injuries were reported, but luckily there were no reported deaths. An army engineering team and Air Force Hercules cargo plane were provided by New Zealand with an initial US$200,000. Aitutaki Island is famous for its crystal clear central lagoon and palm-fringed beaches. A great advantage is that until today it was spared by mass tourism. An old church, which is the oldest in the Cook Islands and several gigantic Banyan trees (Ficus prolixa) are the major attractions. Tapuaetai (One Foot Island) is a small islet in the lagoon's south-east. It is often said to be the most attractive location on Aitutaki. Tapuaetai is regarded as providing tourists with the best views of Aitutaki lagoon and one can walk on a sandbank a decent distance from Tapuaetai, depending on the tide. The trip to the island is the most frequented trip on Aitutaki. In June 2008, One Foot Island was prized "Australasia's Leading Beach" at Sydney 's World Travel Awards. Air Rarotonga offers a day tour and daily flights from Rarotonga. The source of income for most locals are government jobs, followed closely by tourism. With the exposure Aitutaki Island has been given by travel programmes, tourism numbers started to climb. The addition of a newly built resort helped to increase the number of tourists. Cruise ships to Aitutaki Island dock (anchor) at Arutunga (Arutanga) on the west side. Aitutaki is primarily a lagoon destination rather than a port where passengers spend the day walking around town. Cruise ships anchor offshore and passengers come ashore by tender at Arutanga on the west coast. The immediate village is easy to explore on foot, but the lagoon, One Foot Island, Ootu Beach and the main viewpoints require a boat or land transport. Overall: Independent with some planning or transport. Arutanga is easy independently, while a pre-arranged lagoon cruise or island tour is the most practical way to see Aitutaki's main attractions. For the lagoon, a ship-organized excursion is often the simplest option because of tender timings.
getting_from_port: Cruise ships do not berth alongside a conventional cruise terminal. They anchor offshore and tender passengers into Arutanga Harbour. A new tender jetty beside the Aitutaki Fishing Club has been built specifically for cruise tenders and has been used by recent cruise calls. The main Arutanga Wharf may also be involved in port operations, so follow the ship's instructions for the day's exact landing and return point. There is no long industrial-port transfer: once ashore, passengers are already in the Arutanga area. The historic church, small shops and harbourfront are within a few minutes' walk. There is no regular public bus system for visitors on Aitutaki. Beyond Arutanga, practical choices are a pre-arranged taxi or island tour, rental car, scooter, bicycle or e-bike. Taxis and rental vehicles are limited compared with larger islands, so arranging transport before a cruise call is preferable.
tender_evidence: Cruise ships anchor offshore and passengers come ashore by tender at Arutanga on the west coast.

things_to_do.name: Aitutaki Lagoon and One Foot Island
things_to_do.description: Allow about 4–6 hours. This is the priority experience for a first visit. Lagoon trips normally combine cruising across the turquoise lagoon with snorkelling, sandbanks or small motu and, depending on the itinerary, One Foot Island. One Foot Island is accessible only by boat. Some operators offer full-day cruises, while smaller boats and private charters may provide shorter or more flexible trips suitable for a port call. Organized excursion recommended. A ship excursion provides the simplest coordination with tender operations. Independent booking is practical only when the local operator knows you are arriving by cruise ship and can arrange transport and a sufficiently early return to the tender landing.

things_to_do.name: Maungapu Viewpoint and Ootu Beach
things_to_do.description: Allow about 3–4 hours. This makes a good independent alternative for passengers who do not want a full lagoon cruise. Take a taxi, rental car or other pre-arranged transport toward Maungapu, Aitutaki's highest point. The summit is reached by a short but increasingly steep trail. Allow roughly 45–60 minutes for the climb, views and descent, longer in hot weather. The panorama over the lagoon is the main reason to make the ascent. Continue to Ootu Beach on the eastern side of the island for swimming, shallow lagoon water and a relaxed beach stop. Many local lagoon activities also operate from the Ootu area. Independent with planning. Do not rely on finding a taxi immediately when you are ready to return; arrange the return journey in advance.

things_to_do.name: Island Sightseeing by Taxi or Rental Vehicle
things_to_do.description: Allow about 2.5–4 hours. Aitutaki is compact enough for a short road tour combining Arutanga, the west-coast villages, Maungapu, Ootu and lagoon viewpoints. A taxi tour is the easiest choice if you want to concentrate on sightseeing rather than arranging a rental. A rental car or e-bike gives more flexibility. Scooters are also widely used in the Cook Islands, but visitor licensing requirements depend on the motorcycle entitlement on your home licence, which can make them less convenient during a short cruise call.

things_to_do.name: Arutanga Village
things_to_do.description: Allow about 1–1.5 hours. This is the easiest option if tendering leaves limited shore time or you prefer to remain close to the ship. The principal sight is the Arutanga Cook Islands Christian Church, built from coral limestone and regarded as the oldest church in the Cook Islands. The harbourfront, local shops and Orongo area can be combined with the church without transport. On Saturdays there may be more activity around the local market area.

things_to_do.name: Easy Harbour and Village Walk
things_to_do.description: Distance: approximately 1.2 km (0.7 mi) depending on the day's tender landing. Pure walking time: about 20 minutes. Recommended total time: 45–75 minutes. Difficulty: Easy; mostly flat village roads, with limited shade in places. Tender landing: Begin at the designated Arutanga tender jetty or wharf and take a few minutes to look across the harbour and lagoon entrance. Harbour and Orongo area: Walk through the small waterfront area used by fishermen, local boats and visiting yachts. Arutanga Cook Islands Christian Church: Continue into the village to see the coral-limestone church. If entering, dress respectfully and avoid disturbing services. Arutanga centre: Walk through the compact township around the main intersection, passing local shops and everyday island services. Waterfront return: Loop back toward the harbour and return directly to the tender point specified by the ship. This route is suitable for passengers who want a short independent look at local Aitutaki without committing to transport or an excursion. The island's major beaches and viewpoints are too far from the tender landing to include comfortably in a cruise-day walking route.

Aix-en-Provence is a Rhone River cruise port and city in southern France, located approx 30 km (19 mi) north of Marseille . The city is also in the Provence-Alpes-Cote d'Azur region, and has population around 143,000. Aix is dubbed "city of a thousand fountains", the most notable of which are the Four Dolphins (17th-century, in Quartier Mazarin) and 3 fountains located down-central Cours Mirabeau. Aix-en-Provence is an inland city, not a navigable river or seaport, so cruise ships and riverboats do not dock here. On Rhône cruise-tour itineraries that list Aix-en-Provence, including current Tauck MS Lumiere programs, the Aix visit is a land segment reached by coach after or before the actual river portion. Once passengers are dropped in central Aix, however, sightseeing is very easy to do independently.

things_to_do.name: River cruise-tour passengers
things_to_do.description: The Rhône does not run through Aix-en-Provence. Riverboats operating the Rhône and Saône use actual river ports such as Arles, Avignon and Lyon. On current Tauck MS Lumiere itineraries, the river section reaches Arles before the itinerary continues overland through Aix and the Riviera. Use the operator-provided transfer rather than trying to reach the vessel independently from Aix.

things_to_do.name: From a Marseille ocean cruise
things_to_do.description: Aix-en-Provence is about 30 km (18.6 mi) north of Marseille. Most large cruise ships use the Marseille Provence Cruise Terminal complex, which is outside central Marseille, so an independent trip to Aix involves additional ground transport from the terminal. Taxi or pre-arranged private transport is simpler than combining several public-transport stages. An organized shore excursion is preferable when the Marseille call is short or when several ships are in port. Independent travel is more practical with a long call and a generous return margin for motorway traffic and terminal access.

things_to_do.name: Old Aix and Cours Mirabeau
things_to_do.description: Allow 2–3 hours. This is the best choice for a short visit and is easy independently. Begin around the Fontaine de la Rotonde, walk along tree-lined Cours Mirabeau, explore the narrow streets of Vieil Aix and continue through the market squares to Saint-Sauveur Cathedral. The route is compact and largely pedestrian. Expect stone paving and occasional uneven surfaces rather than serious hills.

things_to_do.name: Cézanne's Aix
things_to_do.description: Allow 3–4 hours. Paul Cézanne was born and worked in Aix, and locations connected with him are scattered through the centre. Visitors with more time can continue uphill to Atelier des Lauves, his final studio. The studio has limited capacity, so advance reservation is advisable. The walk north from the historic centre is noticeably more demanding than the central sightseeing circuit, particularly in hot weather.

things_to_do.name: Musée Granet and Quartier Mazarin
things_to_do.description: Allow 2.5–4 hours. Combine the elegant streets of Quartier Mazarin and the Fontaine des Quatre Dauphins with Musée Granet, which has collections ranging from older European art to modern works and material associated with Cézanne. This works well for passengers who prefer one substantial indoor visit rather than trying to cover every landmark. Check the museum's opening day before relying on it as the main activity.

things_to_do.name: Sainte-Victoire and the Cézanne countryside
things_to_do.description: Allow at least 4–5 hours. Mont Sainte-Victoire and the countryside east of Aix are better treated as a separate excursion. Sites associated with Cézanne include viewpoints and the Bibémus area, but they are not a convenient extension of a short old-town walk. Organized excursion recommended for cruise passengers because transport and timing are more important here. Do not attempt a substantial countryside hike when your return depends on a fixed cruise transfer.

things_to_do.name: Easy: Old Aix, Fountains and Cathedral
things_to_do.description: Distance: about 3 km (1.9 mi) Pure walking time: about 45–60 minutes Recommended total time: 2.5–3.5 hours Difficulty: Easy, with some stone paving and uneven old-town streets. Fontaine de la Rotonde – Start here or at your operator's nearby central drop-off point. Cours Mirabeau – Walk the city's principal tree-lined avenue and see its fountains and historic façades. Fontaine des Quatre Dauphins – Make a short detour into Quartier Mazarin for this 17th-century fountain. Saint-Jean-de-Malte and Musée Granet – Stop outside the church or allow extra time for the museum. Place des Prêcheurs – Enter the historic centre and continue through its pedestrian streets. Place Richelme – A convenient place for a market or café stop when stalls are operating. Place de l'Hôtel de Ville – See the town hall, clock tower and surrounding square. Saint-Sauveur Cathedral – Finish at the cathedral before returning through Vieil Aix toward the Rotonde and your transfer point. This is the most practical route when passengers have only a few hours of free time. Allow additional time if entering the cathedral, shopping or stopping at a café.
things_to_do.difficulty: Easy, with some stone paving and uneven old-town streets

things_to_do.name: Moderate: Old Aix to Cézanne's Studio and Viewpoint
things_to_do.description: Distance: approximately 5.5 km (3.4 mi) round trip Pure walking time: about 80–95 minutes Recommended total time: 3.5–4.5 hours Difficulty: Moderate, with a sustained uphill section north of the old town. Fontaine de la Rotonde – Begin in the lower city centre. Cours Mirabeau – Walk through the heart of Aix. Vieil Aix – Follow the central streets toward the cathedral area. Saint-Sauveur Cathedral – A useful final central stop before beginning the climb. Atelier des Lauves – Visit Cézanne's studio if you have a reserved entry time. Jardin/Terrain des Peintres area – Continue toward the traditional viewpoint associated with Cézanne's paintings of Sainte-Victoire if time and access permit. Return to central Aix – Retrace the route downhill and aim to reach the coach meeting area well before departure. This route is less suitable during extreme summer heat or when the cruise operator gives only a short period of independent time.
things_to_do.difficulty: Moderate, with a sustained uphill section north of the old town

Ajaccio cruise port is located on the western coast of Corsica. The port city is the largest on the island and is famous with the fact that it is the birthplace of Napoleon. Ajaccio cruise port is situated in the Gulf of Ajaccio. The city covers a total area of approx 82 km2 (31,67 ml2) and has a population of around 68,600 people (2014 census). It attracts tourist with its unusual shops and amazing restaurants. Ajaccio is easily explored only on foot and has one of the most breathtaking harbours in the world. The city is French but still there is some Italian influence. Ajaccio cruise port is a tender port. Cruise ships anchor in the harbour and their passengers are transported via the ship's tender boats to the pier. The cruise terminal is located at Quai L’Herminier. On its east side is the ferry terminal and on the west side is the fishing port. Ajaccio cruise port terminal is small but modern and is known as Gare Maritime. The terminal offers booking desks, telephones, toilets and taxi services. Ajaccio International Airport is 7 km from Ajaccio cruise port terminal. The city highlights are within walking distance. You have to head left outside the terminal and continue along the road for half a kilometre to reach the heart of the city. If you want to use a taxi, be aware to negotiate the price. There is a taxi rank near Ajaccio cruise port terminal. The official language of the area is French, the currency – Euro. Independent sightseeing: Easy independently. Ajaccio is one of Corsica's simplest cruise calls to explore without an organized tour. The historic center, Napoleon-related sights, market, waterfront and Saint-François Beach are all close to the port. Transport is mainly needed for the Pointe de la Parata, the Sanguinaires coastline or excursions into the Corsican countryside. Ajaccio should not be considered a tender-only port. The commercial port has a dedicated cruise berth at the Môle Croisières, while Quai l'Herminier is also equipped for cruise tenders. Whether a particular ship docks or anchors can therefore depend on ship size, berth allocation and other traffic. Passengers arriving by tender are normally landed in the same central port area.
getting_from_port: The passenger exit is beside the Gare Maritime and Quai l'Herminier, directly on the edge of central Ajaccio. Place Foch and the entrance to the old town are roughly 0.3-0.5 km (0.2-0.3 mi) away, normally a 5-10 minute walk along the waterfront. A shuttle is not normally necessary for city sightseeing. Walking: Best for the old town, Maison Bonaparte, cathedral, Palais Fesch, market and nearby beach. Bus: Muvistrada Line 5 links the central Place de Gaulle area with the Route des Sanguinaires and Pointe de la Parata. Check the current timetable before setting out. Taxi: Useful for La Parata, beaches farther along the Sanguinaires road or a private countryside trip. Train: Ajaccio railway station is about 0.6 km (0.4 mi) from the Gare Maritime, but rail trips inland are generally less convenient than local sightseeing during a normal cruise call.
terminal_notes: Cruise ships anchor in the harbour and their passengers are transported via the ship's tender boats to the pier. The cruise terminal is located at Quai L’Herminier. On its east side is the ferry terminal and on the west side is the fishing port. Ajaccio cruise port terminal is small but modern and is known as Gare Maritime. The terminal offers booking desks, telephones, toilets and taxi services. Ajaccio International Airport is 7 km from Ajaccio cruise port terminal. You have to head left outside the terminal and continue along the road for half a kilometre to reach the heart of the city. There is a taxi rank near Ajaccio cruise port terminal. The commercial port has a dedicated cruise berth at the Môle Croisières, while Quai l'Herminier is also equipped for cruise tenders. Whether a particular ship docks or anchors can therefore depend on ship size, berth allocation and other traffic.
tender_evidence: Ajaccio cruise port is a tender port.

things_to_do.name: Old Town and Napoleon Sites
things_to_do.description: Allow 2.5-4 hours. Easy independently. This is the most practical choice for a first visit. Walk from the port through central Ajaccio to Place Foch, the narrow streets of the old Genoese quarter, Maison Bonaparte and the Cathedral of Santa Maria Assunta. Maison Bonaparte, Napoleon's birthplace, normally takes about 45 minutes to visit. Art visitors can add the Palais Fesch, whose collection usually needs another 1-1.5 hours. If your ship arrives in the morning, the Marcatu d'Aiacciu at Place Campinchi is also an easy stop; the main market operates in the morning from Tuesday to Sunday. The Citadelle Miollis is undergoing a major rehabilitation, so public access can change and it is safest to treat it primarily as an exterior sightseeing stop unless access is confirmed on the day.

things_to_do.name: Pointe de la Parata and the Sanguinaires Islands View
things_to_do.description: Allow about 3-4 hours including transport. Independent with some planning or transport. Pointe de la Parata lies about 11 km (6.8 mi) west of central Ajaccio at the end of the scenic Route des Sanguinaires. It is one of the best options if you want coastal scenery rather than museums. Muvistrada Line 5 runs from Place de Gaulle toward La Parata; a taxi is faster and easier when time ashore is limited. At the Grand Site, allow about 45 minutes for the signed walk toward the Genoese tower and viewpoints over the Sanguinaires Islands. The final approach to the tower includes fairly steep steps. Bus passengers should check the return timetable before starting the walk, as missing a service can significantly reduce the return margin.

things_to_do.name: Saint-François or Trottel Beach
things_to_do.description: Allow 2-4 hours. Easy independently. Saint-François is the easiest beach for cruise passengers, around 0.7 km (0.4 mi) from the port area beside the historic center and citadel. It works well as a swimming stop after a walking tour. Trottel Beach is farther west along the waterfront and is larger, with restaurants nearby. It can be reached on foot from central Ajaccio or by Muvistrada Lines 2 or 5. Both beaches have seasonal lifeguard coverage during July and August, but swimming conditions and supervision should always be checked locally.

things_to_do.name: Prunelli Valley and Lake Tolla
things_to_do.description: Allow roughly 4-6 hours. Organized excursion or pre-arranged transport recommended. Passengers wanting mountain scenery can head inland through the Prunelli Valley toward villages, forested gorges and Lake Tolla. The lake is about 30 km (18.6 mi) from Ajaccio and roughly 30 minutes away by road under normal conditions. This is much less convenient by public transport than central Ajaccio or La Parata. A ship excursion, private driver or carefully planned rental car is preferable, particularly because the mountain roads are slower than the distance may suggest and road delays can reduce the return margin.

things_to_do.name: Old Ajaccio, Napoleon and the Waterfront
things_to_do.description: Distance: approximately 3 km (1.9 mi). Pure walking time: about 40-45 minutes. Recommended total time: 2.5-4 hours with sightseeing stops. Difficulty: Easy. The route is mostly level, although the old town has narrow streets, paving stones and occasional uneven surfaces. Gare Maritime / cruise passenger exit: Leave the port and follow the waterfront toward central Ajaccio. Palais Fesch: See the museum and Imperial Chapel complex. Enter the museum only if you can spare about 1-1.5 hours. Place Campinchi and the market: A useful morning stop for Corsican cheese, charcuterie, produce and local specialties. The market is closed on Mondays. Place Foch: Continue into the historic center and the compact Genoese old town. Maison Bonaparte: Visit Napoleon's birthplace or simply see its exterior if time is short. Cathedral of Santa Maria Assunta: A few minutes from Maison Bonaparte and closely associated with Napoleon's early life. Citadelle Miollis and Saint-François Beach: Walk along the waterfront side of the old quarter for views of the citadel and, in warm weather, an optional beach stop. Citadel access can be restricted during the current redevelopment. Place de Gaulle and waterfront return: Finish at the broad seafront square, then walk back toward the Gare Maritime. If visiting the market, do that section early in the day. Adding both Maison Bonaparte and the full Palais Fesch visit can turn the route into a 4-hour outing; with exterior stops only, it can comfortably be completed in around 1.5-2 hours.

region: Australia - New Zealand - Pacific Ocean Islands

Akaroa Harbour (port locode NZAKA ) is located in NZ's Canterbury Region, part of Banks Peninsula. Onawe Peninsula is at the harbor's head. The Akaroa harbor is actually the crater of an extinct volcano. Cruise vessels enter Akaroa harbor to anchor there, while passengers are transported to the wharf via tenders. The small town (population under 1000) is New Zealand's oldest European settlement. In 2013 was established the Akaroa Marine Reserve. Following the February 2011's earthquake (Richter magnitude 6,3) in Lyttelton (seaport for Christchurch) , Akaroa became a substitute port for cruise ships. Akaroa NZ's cruising season runs October through April. During season 2016-2017, the cruise port had scheduled 77 ship calls. To cope with the increasing influx of cruise tourists, in 2016 was upgraded the town's water supply and mobile public toilets were added. Akaroa Civic Trust had suggested charging cruise tourists AUD 5 levy per person to help pay for the needed infrastructure. Among the most booked shore excursions are the bus tours from Akaroa to Christchurch. Akaroa is a tender cruise port, which means cruise ships anchor in the harbor and their passengers are transported via the ship's tender boats. Akaroa is one of New Zealand's easiest tender ports for independent sightseeing. Cruise ships anchor in Akaroa Harbour and passengers come ashore by tender directly beside the compact waterfront village. Most of the town's main sights, cafes and harbour activities can be reached on foot. Independent sightseeing: Easy independently for Akaroa village, the waterfront and harbour cruises. Trips into the outer Banks Peninsula require more planning, while Christchurch is far enough away that an organized excursion is usually the safer choice for cruise passengers. Akaroa is a tender port; there is no cruise berth for large ships. Tendering can be affected by wind and harbour conditions, so allow for possible delays both going ashore and returning. Akaroa's historic Main Wharf is being rebuilt during 2026-2027. During the reconstruction period, cruise tenders use nearby Drummond's Jetty, about 180 m northeast of the Main Wharf. The landing is already within Akaroa village, so no shuttle into town is necessary. From the tender landing, the waterfront, Rue Lavaud shopping area, Akaroa Museum and cafes are only a short walk away. Taxis and local tour vehicles are useful for attractions outside the village, but a car is unnecessary for a basic Akaroa visit. Construction around the Main Wharf may temporarily alter pedestrian routes and the departure points for local sightseeing boats. Most harbour operators have moved departures to Drummond's Wharf during the works, but passengers with reservations should follow the operator's current check-in instructions. This is the simplest option for a short call. Walk along Beach Road and Rue Lavaud, browse the small commercial center and visit Akaroa Museum, which occupies several heritage buildings and covers Māori, French, British and maritime history. Continue along the harbourfront toward Akaroa Lighthouse and the Garden of Tane. The central waterfront is mostly level, although paths away from the shore begin to climb.
terminal_notes: Akaroa is a tender port; there is no cruise berth for large ships.
tender_evidence: Cruise vessels enter Akaroa harbor to anchor there, while passengers are transported to the wharf via tenders.

things_to_do.name: Explore Akaroa Village and Waterfront
things_to_do.description: Allow: 2-3 hours. Transport: Walking. Difficulty: Easy. This is the simplest option for a short call. Walk along Beach Road and Rue Lavaud, browse the small commercial center and visit Akaroa Museum, which occupies several heritage buildings and covers Māori, French, British and maritime history. Continue along the harbourfront toward Akaroa Lighthouse and the Garden of Tane. The central waterfront is mostly level, although paths away from the shore begin to climb.

things_to_do.name: Take a Harbour Wildlife Cruise
things_to_do.description: Allow: About 2.5-3 hours including check-in. Transport: Walk to the departure point. Difficulty: Easy independently. Akaroa Harbour is particularly well suited to a boat trip during a cruise call. Local wildlife cruises generally spend about two hours exploring the harbour and outer coastline, with Hector's dolphins, New Zealand fur seals, seabirds and volcanic coastal scenery among the main attractions. Advance reservations are sensible on cruise-ship days. Boat operations depend on weather and sea conditions, and passengers should avoid a departure that leaves little time before the ship's final tender.

things_to_do.name: Akaroa Museum and The Giant's House
things_to_do.description: Allow: 2-3 hours. Transport: Walking. Difficulty: Easy to moderate. Combine Akaroa Museum on Rue Lavaud with The Giant's House on Rue Balguerie. The latter is a historic house surrounded by steeply terraced gardens filled with mosaics, sculptures and artwork. The Giant's House is above the main waterfront, so the walk includes an uphill section and the gardens themselves contain slopes and steps. It is therefore less suitable for passengers with limited mobility. Check its opening time for the day of your call before walking uphill, as it does not necessarily open early in the morning.

things_to_do.name: Garden of Tane and Akaroa Lighthouse
things_to_do.description: Allow: 1.5-2.5 hours. Transport: Walking. Difficulty: Easy to moderate. For a quieter alternative to shopping, walk south along the waterfront to the historic lighthouse and enter the Garden of Tane. Its network of wooded paths passes mature trees, bird habitat, viewpoints and historic cemetery areas. The waterfront approach is easy, while the garden has uneven paths and short climbs. It can be combined with the village without committing most of the port call to a longer hike.

things_to_do.name: Explore the Outer Banks Peninsula
things_to_do.description: Allow: Usually 3-5 hours. Transport: Guided vehicle tour or pre-arranged transport. Difficulty: Independent travel requires planning. The hills and outer bays around Akaroa provide excellent scenery and wildlife, but they are not practical to explore on foot during a normal cruise call. Roads away from the main highway can be steep, narrow and unsealed. Pōhatu/Flea Bay is a good example. The marine reserve lies roughly 9 km (5.6 mi) by road from Akaroa, but the final access is steep and is suitable for 4WD vehicles rather than normal sightseeing traffic. A locally operated 4WD nature or kayaking excursion is considerably more practical than trying to arrange independent transportation.

things_to_do.name: Easy Waterfront and Heritage Walk
things_to_do.description: Distance: About 3.2 km (2.0 mi). Pure walking time: 45-55 minutes. Recommended total time: 1.5-2.5 hours. Difficulty: Easy; predominantly paved and close to sea level. Drummond's Jetty – Start from the current cruise tender landing. Daly's Wharf – Walk north along the harbourfront for views back across Akaroa Harbour. Rue Lavaud – Turn through Akaroa's compact main street and heritage area. Akaroa Museum – Allow around 30-45 minutes if you want to visit the exhibitions. Beach Road waterfront – Follow the shoreline south through the central village. Main Wharf area – Pass the historic wharf location, keeping outside the construction zone during the current rebuild. Akaroa Lighthouse – Continue along the waterfront to the small wooden lighthouse. Return to Drummond's Jetty – Retrace the level waterfront route to the tender landing. This is the best choice for passengers who want a relaxed independent visit while remaining close to the ship's tender point.

things_to_do.name: Village, Giant's House and Garden of Tane Walk
things_to_do.description: Distance: About 4.5 km (2.8 mi). Pure walking time: 70-85 minutes. Recommended total time: 2.5-3.5 hours. Difficulty: Moderate because of hills, garden paths and steps. Drummond's Jetty – Leave the tender area and walk into the village. Akaroa Museum – Stop briefly or visit before continuing uphill. Rue Balguerie – Climb away from the waterfront toward The Giant's House. The Giant's House – Allow roughly an hour if visiting the terraced gardens. Rue Jolie – Descend toward the southern side of the village. Garden of Tane – Follow one of the shorter woodland paths rather than attempting a long hillside walk. Akaroa Lighthouse – Exit near the waterfront and continue to the lighthouse. Drummond's Jetty – Return north along Beach Road for the tender back to the ship. Allow additional time after rain, when woodland paths can be damp or slippery.
things_to_do.difficulty: Moderate because of hills, garden paths and steps

To see the full itineraries (ports of call dates and arrival / departure times) and their lowest rates – just follow the corresponding ship-link. Akita (Akita-shi) is the principal port and the capital city of Japan's Akita Prefecture (Honshu Island's Tohoku region), with population around 315,000. The seaport is on the Sea of Japan (to the west), while the Omono River runs through downtown. Port Akita (locode JPAXT) is officially classified as "Major Port" and has total land area approx 663 hectares (6,6 km2). During Edo/Tokugawa period (1603-1868), Akita was a major port on the coastal trade route from Osaka to Hokkaido. During the Meiji period (1868-1912) was finished a breakwater (in 1885) that was further expanded in 1902. Port Tsuchizakiko was designated as “secondary port” in 1910. When in 1941 Tsuchizaki was merged with Akita, the port was officially renamed “Akita Port”. Most of its facilities were heavily damaged during the US air raids in August 1945. After WW2 (1939-1945), the seaport was improved. Its breakwater was extended via the sinking of damaged Japanese military vessels (including the Matsu-class destroyers Take and Momo). The Japanese government classed Akita as “major port” in 1951 and as “special port” in 1962. Its Customs Office opened in 1964, allowing international shipping trade. Northern Port's extension was completed in 1970. Akita is normally a docked port call , with cruise ships using Nakajima Pier beside the Akita Cruise Terminal. The port area itself is easy to explore on foot, but central Akita is not a practical walk from the ship. For the main city sights, plan on using a local bus, taxi or any transfer provided for your particular cruise call. Overall: Independent sightseeing is practical, but it requires some transport planning. Staying around Port Tower Selion is very easy independently; central Akita is also straightforward once you reach Akita Station. Longer trips to Oga or Kakunodate need considerably more attention to transport and return times. Important: Older Akita cruise guides may mention a dedicated train between Akita Port and Akita Station. Cruise passenger trains ended after the 2025 fiscal year, and the Akita Port railway branch was abolished on July 1, 2026. Do not plan a visit around the former cruise train.
getting_from_port: Berth: Cruise ships normally use Nakajima Pier, where the Akita Cruise Terminal handles arriving passengers. Port Tower Selion: About 1 km (0.6 mi) from the cruise berth, roughly a 10–15 minute walk. This is the easiest attraction to visit directly from the ship. Akita Station and city center: Allow about 20–25 minutes by road from the port area. Public bus: Akita Chuo Kotsu's Selion Line, including route 115, connects the Selion area with Akita Station West Exit. Services are not especially frequent, particularly on weekends, so check the return timetable before relying on the bus. Taxi: The simplest independent choice when several people are traveling together or when the port call is short. Important: Older Akita cruise guides may mention a dedicated train between Akita Port and Akita Station. Cruise passenger trains ended after the 2025 fiscal year, and the Akita Port railway branch was abolished on July 1, 2026. Do not plan a visit around the former cruise train.
terminal_notes: Akita is normally a docked port call , with cruise ships using Nakajima Pier beside the Akita Cruise Terminal.

things_to_do.name: Central Akita and Senshu Park
things_to_do.description: Allow about 4–5 hours including port transfers. This is the best independent choice for a first visit. Start around Akita Station and combine Senshu Park, the former Kubota Castle grounds, Akita Museum of Art and one or two smaller cultural attractions. Senshu Park is about a 10-minute walk from Akita Station. The lower park and castle gates are easy to reach, while the climb toward the reconstructed Osumiyagura turret involves slopes and some steps. Nearby cultural stops include the Akita City Folk Performing Arts Heritage Center, commonly called Neburinagashi Kan, where the city's Kanto lantern tradition is presented, and the distinctive Red Brick Folk Museum. Independent sightseeing: Easy once in the city center. Use a taxi or the Selion bus between port and Akita Station rather than trying to walk from the ship.

things_to_do.name: Port Tower Selion and the Akita Port Area
things_to_do.description: Allow 1–2 hours. This is the simplest option for passengers who want to remain close to the ship. Port Tower Selion has a free observation level approximately 100 meters above the ground with views across the Sea of Japan, Akita and, in clear weather, the surrounding mountains and Oga Peninsula. The surrounding Michi-no-Eki Akita Port complex includes Selion Garden for regional products and the enclosed Selion Rista space. It works particularly well for a short call, poor weather or passengers who prefer minimal transport. Independent sightseeing: Very easy. The principal sights are within walking distance of the cruise terminal.

things_to_do.name: Oga Peninsula and Namahage Culture
things_to_do.description: Allow roughly 4–5 hours. The Namahage Museum on the Oga Peninsula is about a 50-minute drive from the Akita Port area. It displays the distinctive masks and traditions associated with Oga's Namahage, while the neighboring Oga Shinzan Folklore Museum presents demonstrations of the custom inside a traditional house. Public transport from the cruise terminal requires considerably more time and connections, so this is better approached by organized excursion, pre-arranged vehicle or taxi. Adding extensive sightseeing around the Oga Peninsula increases the time requirement further. Independent sightseeing: Possible with pre-arranged transport; organized excursion recommended for most cruise passengers.

things_to_do.name: Kakunodate Samurai District
things_to_do.description: Allow at least 5–6 hours and preferably a long port call. Kakunodate is a preserved castle town known for its samurai residences and historic streets. From Akita Station, the fastest Akita Shinkansen journey is about 42 minutes, followed by approximately 15–20 minutes on foot from Kakunodate Station to the main samurai district. A typical walk through Kakunodate covers about 5 km (3.1 mi), although cruise visitors can concentrate on Samurai Residence Street and shorten the route substantially. The journey can be done independently when train times line up well, but the port transfer, railway journey and waiting time consume a significant part of the day. Missing a convenient return train can quickly reduce the safety margin. Independent sightseeing: Reasonable only with careful timetable planning on a long call. Organized excursion recommended when time ashore is limited.

things_to_do.name: Easy Port Walk: Cruise Terminal to Selion
things_to_do.description: Distance: About 2 km (1.2 mi) round trip Pure walking time: About 25–30 minutes Recommended total time: 1–1.5 hours Difficulty: Easy and mostly level. Akita Cruise Terminal – leave the passenger area and follow the permitted route toward the Selion complex. Michi-no-Eki Akita Port – browse the local-products area if time permits. Port Tower Selion – take the elevator to the observation level for views over the harbor and Sea of Japan. Selion Rista – visit the glass-covered indoor green space beside the tower. Return to the cruise terminal along the same straightforward port-side route. This is the safest self-guided choice for passengers with only a short period ashore because the ship remains nearby throughout the visit.

things_to_do.name: Moderate Central Akita Walk
things_to_do.description: Start/finish: Akita Station West Exit Distance: About 4.5 km (2.8 mi) Pure walking time: About 60–70 minutes Recommended total time: 3–4 hours including sightseeing stops Difficulty: Moderate. Central streets are mostly easy, but Senshu Park has slopes and steps. Akita Station West Exit – the practical starting point after arriving from the cruise port. Akita Museum of Art – approximately 10 minutes from the station, with its large Tsuguharu Foujita mural among the principal exhibits. Senshu Park moat – cross toward the former Kubota Castle grounds. Kubota Castle Main Gate and Osumiyagura – continue uphill through the park. Skip the upper turret if you want a flatter and shorter walk. Neburinagashi Kan – learn about Akita's Kanto lantern festival and other local performing traditions. Red Brick Folk Museum – a former bank building containing regional art and craft collections. Akita Citizen's Market – near the station and useful for local food, seafood and regional products when open. Akita Station – return here for your bus, taxi or other transfer back to the ship.

Akureyri is a major cruise port and one of Iceland's oldest towns, located approx 240 km (150 mi) northeast of the country's capital city Reykjavik . Akureyri features picturesque historic houses below snowcapped peaks, several museums and botanical gardens. It is the biggest settlement outside southwest of Iceland, and one of country's largest cities. "Akureyri" means "Meadow Sandspit" in Icelandic. You can visit the villages Hauganes and Dalvik (located at the lower end of Eyjafjordur, along fjord's shore) or the islands Grimsey and Hrisey. Go inland to explore Lake Myvatn - famous bird sanctuary, with one of world's largest breeding duck colonies. En-route to Lake Myvatn, you can see amazing lava formations, craters and Grotagja fissure (former public bath). At the Godafoss Waterfall, the Nordic gods Thor and Odin watch over Iceland. Myvatn is a lush area with abundant bird and fish life. Another must-see is Krafla area and its huge lava fields. In 2017, the cruise port handled a total of 124 ship calls. This number grew to 138 in 2018 (around 130,000 passengers). Summer cruising season's most popular month is July. Most of the visiting vessels are on Iceland circumnavigation itineraries. In 2017 was inaugurated a tree-planting program, by which around 2000 trees are planted per cruise season. Also from Akureyri cruise port, tourists access one of Iceland's best-known natural attractions - Hverir (Lake Myvatn, east of Mount Namafjall). Hverir (aka Hverarond) is a barren area with high-temperature geothermal activity (hot springs). In February 2018, Port Akureyri announced an investment of EUR 5 million in building a new cruise pier (completed in 2019). The new pier has length 130 m (427 ft) and depth 9 m (20 ft). Season 2018's main highlight was the 170,000-ton cruise liner MSC Meraviglia (max passenger capacity 5386) that was scheduled for anchoring on May 24 (port stay 8 am - 7 pm). This was the largest ever ship visiting Port Akureyri. The call was part of 21-day roundtrip itinerary from homeport Hamburg Germany to ports in Norway and Iceland. In 2017, Port Akureyri's services were upgraded with a modern, high-power tugboat. The cruise berth expansion project to lengthen port's main docking pier by 100 m (328 ft) to total 270 m (886 m) was started in 2018 and completed in 2019. The facility allows berthing of cruise vessels with GT tonnage under 10,000 tons. Located just 100 m (330 ft) from downtown, another pier will be rebuilt/expanded in 2020 and ready for season 2021. Independent sightseeing: Easy. Akureyri is one of Iceland's most convenient cruise ports for exploring on foot. Most cruise ships berth close to the compact town center, generally within about a 5-10 minute walk. The main sights, waterfront, shops, cafés, Akureyri Church and Botanical Garden can all be combined without needing a tour. For passengers who want to see North Iceland's major natural attractions, Goðafoss is manageable independently with advance transport planning, while a longer Lake Mývatn itinerary is usually better suited to an organized excursion because of the distances and limited port-call time.
getting_from_port: Akureyri has several cruise berths. Larger ships commonly use Tangabryggja and Oddeyrarbryggja, while smaller vessels can use Torfunefsbryggja. The port also has anchorage and tender facilities, so the exact arrival arrangement depends on the ship and berth allocation. Most docked passengers can simply walk into central Akureyri. Hof Cultural and Conference Centre, which contains the tourist information office, is close to the harbor and is a useful orientation point. Ráðhústorg square and the main central streets are only a few minutes farther. Walking: Best option for central sightseeing. Local buses: Akureyri's municipal buses are free and can be useful for reaching the Botanical Garden, museums and residential areas farther from the waterfront. Taxis: Useful for attractions outside town and for passengers with limited mobility. Regional buses: Depart near Hof and can reach places including Goðafoss, but services and capacity are limited, making them less flexible for cruise passengers.
terminal_notes: In February 2018, Port Akureyri announced an investment of EUR 5 million in building a new cruise pier (completed in 2019). The new pier has length 130 m (427 ft) and depth 9 m (20 ft). The cruise berth expansion project to lengthen port's main docking pier by 100 m (328 ft) to total 270 m (886 m) was started in 2018 and completed in 2019. Located just 100 m (330 ft) from downtown, another pier will be rebuilt/expanded in 2020 and ready for season 2021. Most cruise ships berth close to the compact town center, generally within about a 5-10 minute walk.

things_to_do.name: Explore Central Akureyri on Foot
things_to_do.description: Allow about 2-4 hours. This is the simplest independent option. Walk from the harbor past Hof to the center, explore Hafnarstræti and Ráðhústorg, then climb to Akureyri Church. Continue through the Art Street area and, if time permits, the Botanical Garden. The center itself is compact, but Akureyri rises steeply away from the waterfront. The climb to the church and higher streets can be tiring for passengers with limited mobility.

things_to_do.name: Visit the Botanical Garden and Old Town
things_to_do.description: Allow about 3-4 hours including walking. The Akureyri Botanical Garden is a practical extension of a town walk and is accessible year-round. From there, continue south toward the older part of Akureyri, where historic wooden houses, Nonni's House and Akureyri Museum are located. The Old Town museums are roughly a 20-30 minute walk from the center. A free local bus can reduce the walking if necessary.

things_to_do.name: Goðafoss Waterfall
things_to_do.description: Allow about 2.5-3.5 hours. Goðafoss is approximately 35 km (21.7 mi) from Akureyri and normally takes around 35-45 minutes each way by road. It is one of the easiest major North Iceland attractions to fit into a cruise call. Options include cruise-oriented transfers, excursions, taxi or rental car. Regional bus Route 79 also stops near Goðafoss, but capacity is limited and schedules should be checked carefully before relying on it for a ship day. An organized transfer is safer when the port call is short.

things_to_do.name: Lake Mývatn and Volcanic Landscapes
things_to_do.description: Allow about 5-7 hours. The Lake Mývatn area is approximately 85 km (52.8 mi) from Akureyri, about an hour's drive before sightseeing stops are added. Typical itineraries combine Goðafoss with volcanic and geothermal locations such as Skútustaðagígar, Dimmuborgir and the Hverir geothermal area. Organized excursion recommended. The attractions are spread over a wide area and much of the day is spent driving. Independent rental-car touring is possible during a sufficiently long port call, but it requires careful route planning and a substantial return margin.

things_to_do.name: Whale Watching in Eyjafjörður
things_to_do.description: Allow about 3-4 hours. Whale-watching boats operate from the waterfront near Hof, making this one of the most convenient wildlife activities for cruise passengers. Humpback whales are among the species regularly encountered in Eyjafjörður, although wildlife sightings can never be guaranteed. This can be booked independently because departures are close to the cruise area, but passengers should choose a sailing that returns comfortably before all-aboard time.

things_to_do.name: Forest Lagoon
things_to_do.description: Allow about 2.5-3.5 hours. Forest Lagoon is on the opposite side of the fjord, a short drive from central Akureyri. Walking from the center takes roughly 40 minutes and is less attractive when port time is limited. A complimentary seasonal shuttle operates on selected dates between the harbor area and the lagoon, with additional city-center service at certain times. Pre-book the lagoon and verify the shuttle schedule for the specific cruise date rather than assuming that harbor transfers operate every day.

things_to_do.name: Central Akureyri and Waterfront — Easy
things_to_do.description: Distance: approximately 2-2.5 km (1.2-1.6 mi) Pure walking time: about 30-40 minutes Recommended total time: 1.5-2.5 hours Difficulty: Easy, mostly level with only minor gradients. Cruise berth: Walk toward the central waterfront. Hof Cultural and Conference Centre: Stop for tourist information, maps and orientation. Ráðhústorg: Enter the compact center and pedestrian shopping area. Hafnarstræti: Walk the main central street past cafés, shops and traditional buildings. Oddeyri waterfront: Follow part of the coastal area for views across Eyjafjörður. Return to the harbor: Follow the waterfront back toward the ship. This route is suitable for a short call, poor weather or passengers who do not want the steeper climbs found above the town center.
things_to_do.difficulty: Easy, mostly level with only minor gradients

things_to_do.name: Church, Botanical Garden and Old Town — Moderate
things_to_do.description: Distance: approximately 4.5-5 km (2.8-3.1 mi) Pure walking time: about 60-75 minutes Recommended total time: 3-4 hours with stops Difficulty: Moderate. Paved streets and paths, but with a noticeable uphill section from the center. Cruise berth and Hof: Walk into the center via the waterfront. Ráðhústorg and Hafnarstræti: Explore the main town-center streets. Akureyri Church: Climb from the center for views over the town and fjord. Art Street: Continue through Kaupvangsstræti past the Akureyri Art Museum and surrounding cultural buildings. Akureyri Botanical Garden: Walk through the landscaped garden before continuing south. Old Town: Follow the historic streets toward Nonni's House and Akureyri Museum. Return: Walk north along Aðalstræti and Hafnarstræti toward the center, then continue to the cruise berth. If the Old Town extension becomes too long, turn back from the Botanical Garden. Free city buses can also shorten the return journey.

Al Wajh (port locode SAWAJ ), aka Al Wejh/Wedjh, is a Red Sea cruise port and city in Saudi Arabia's Tabuk Province, with population around 50,000. The city is inhabited mainly by Saudis and the economy is largely based on commercial fishing. Al Wajh Airport (1984-established) serves exclusively domestic flights (by the national carrier Saudia) linking with Jeddah (Saudi Arabia's largest seaport) and Riyadh (the country's capital city). In April 2021, MSC and Cruise Saudi (fully-owned by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund) announced a partnership for launching Red Sea cruises (2021-2022 winter season) with the homeporting in Jeddah of the ship MSC Magnifica . The next table shows the 7-night/8-day itinerary (Jeddah roundtrip) as call ports and times. Prices started from ~USD 1130 (EUR 950 / GBP 816) per person with double occupancy. Al Wajh is a small Red Sea port where the most practical local sightseeing is the historic waterfront district rather than a long list of major attractions. The old town preserves coral-stone buildings, traditional wooden rawasheen windows, historic mosques and a compact harbor setting. Al Wajh is also promoted as a maritime gateway to Hegra and AlUla, but those sites require a substantial inland transfer.
getting_from_port: Do not assume the CruiseMapper map pin is the exact passenger exit. Al Wajh's harbor is primarily a working maritime and fishing area, and cruise landing arrangements can vary between ships and seasons. Larger ships have generally used tender operations rather than a conventional cruise pier. If your ship provides transport to the historic waterfront or Al Balad, independent exploration from that drop-off is straightforward. Without a transfer, pre-arranged transport is preferable to relying on a taxi appearing at the harbor. There is no well-established tourist bus network for moving cruise passengers around Al Wajh.

things_to_do.name: Explore Old Al Wajh and the Historic Harbor
things_to_do.description: Allow about 2–3 hours. This is the best choice for passengers who want to see Al Wajh itself. Walk through the Al Balad historic quarter to see traditional Red Sea architecture, including limestone and coral-stone buildings, wooden balconies and rawasheen screens. The lanes lead naturally toward the old harbor, historic mosques and Al Wajh Castle. The area is best appreciated on foot once you have reached the old town. Some heritage buildings are fragile or unrestored, so treat them as exterior sights unless access is clearly permitted.

things_to_do.name: Walk the Corniche and Waterfront
things_to_do.description: Allow about 1–2 hours. Al Wajh has a long developed waterfront, including an urban Corniche of about 2 km (1.2 mi). It is suitable for an easy sea-view walk and can be combined with the old town rather than treated as a separate excursion. Much of the wider waterfront extends well beyond the historic center, so there is little reason for cruise passengers to walk its full length. Shade can be limited, making shorter sections more practical in warm weather.

things_to_do.name: Visit Zurayb Castle
things_to_do.description: Allow about 2–3 hours including transport. Zurayb Castle stands approximately 10 km (6.2 mi) east of Al Wajh. The restored historic fortress was associated with the Egyptian pilgrimage route and contains defensive towers, a central courtyard and internal rooms. This is not a walking excursion from the port. Arrange a vehicle in advance and preferably keep the same driver for the return, as finding onward transport at an outlying heritage site may be difficult.

things_to_do.name: Hegra and AlUla
things_to_do.description: Organized excursion recommended. Cruise lines have marketed Al Wajh as a gateway to Hegra, Saudi Arabia's UNESCO-listed Nabataean site. Hegra is roughly 200 km (124.3 mi) inland by road, with transfers commonly taking around 2.5–3 hours each way depending on routing and road conditions. AlUla town is farther, at roughly 245 km (152.2 mi) by road. The journey consumes a large part of the port day, and Hegra visits use controlled visitor arrangements and timed access. Attempting this independently during an ordinary cruise call carries considerably more transport and timing risk than staying in Al Wajh. Consider it only on a long call and preferably through the ship or another fully pre-arranged excursion that coordinates entry and return transport.

Al-Minya is a Nile River cruise port and the capital city of Minya Governorate (Upper Egypt) with a population of around 260,000. The city is located approx 245 km (150 mi) south of Cairo (Egypt's capital). Nile River flows directly through the city (direction north-south). Before 3100 BC, the area formed Egypt's Oryx nome (16th out of 42 nomes/districts) and remained an independent city-state until 3200 BC when Menes unified Egypt. Being the district's capital, Minya (initially named Men'at Khufu) developed as a major trade center for import goods (mainly from Sinai and Canaan). After the Old Kingdom collapsed in 2181 BC, Oryx nome's princes became wealthy and more autonomous from the Pharaohs. Their power reached their height during Ancient Egypt's Eleventh Dynasty (2134-1998 BC) and functionally eliminated by the end of the Twelfth Dynasty (1991-1806 BC). During the Ptolemaic Kingdom (305-30 BC) the city was extensively settled by Greeks and its populations reached 40,000. Following the Antony's Civil War (32-30 BC, when Mark Antony and Cleopatra fought with Octavian Augustus), Minya became a major cotton trade hub and was inhabited by some of the wealthiest Greek and Roman traders. During the Abbasid Caliphate (750-1258 AD), the city's ruler Ibn Khasib greatly expanded it. During the Fatimid Caliphate (909-1171) Minya continued to prosper and expand by building large mosques (including EL-Lamaty and EL-Amrawy), schools, open-air markets/bazaar, public baths. The city's current-day economy is based mainly on state-run agriculture and heavy industries - like the production of cement, chemicals, fertilizers, also mining. Private businesses specialize mainly in consumer goods manufacturing (food products, furniture, metal, and woodworks). Tourism is not well developed. As cruise port, Minya is included in the regular schedule of the Movenpick Hotels and Resorts owned riverboat (hotel ship) Movenpick Darakum . The ship operates on a 10-day and 14-day cruise tour between homeports Aswan and Luxor, with included domestic flights from or to Cairo. The next table shows the 14-day itinerary as a ports sequence. Prices start from ~USD 2600 per person (double occupancy rates). Al-Minya is a Nile River cruise stop rather than a conventional seaport. The main archaeological attractions are outside the city, so the best use of a full sightseeing day is normally a guided or pre-arranged vehicle excursion. Independent exploration is practical for the Nile Corniche and central Minya, but less convenient for Beni Hassan, Tuna el-Gebel and the other desert sites. Riverboat berths can vary, so confirm the exact gangway location with the crew. Minya's main riverfront runs along the Nile Corniche, and vessels using a central mooring put passengers close to the city rather than at an isolated industrial port. The Corniche and nearby streets are practical on foot. For sites outside Minya, use the ship's excursion, a pre-arranged driver or a locally arranged taxi. Shared minibuses serve the region but are not a particularly practical choice for cruise passengers working to a fixed return time.

things_to_do.name: Beni Hassan Tombs
things_to_do.description: Best archaeological choice for a shorter call. Beni Hassan is about 22 km (13.7 mi) southeast of Minya. The Middle Kingdom tombs are cut into the limestone cliffs above the Nile Valley, with surviving painted scenes of agriculture, hunting, crafts, wrestling and everyday life. Published Nile cruise programs allow roughly 30–60 minutes each way from the Minya dock and around 1.5–2 hours at the site. Reaching the tombs involves an uphill approach and steps, with little shade. Allow about 3–4 hours overall and use arranged transport rather than attempting the trip by public transport.

things_to_do.name: Tuna el-Gebel and El-Ashmunein
things_to_do.description: Best as a guided half-day excursion. South of Minya, these two sites are commonly combined. El-Ashmunein occupies part of ancient Hermopolis Magna, while Tuna el-Gebel contains the Tomb of Petosiris, the Tomb of Isadora and extensive sacred-animal catacombs. The sites are spread across rural and desert areas and are much less straightforward to visit independently than central Minya. Nile cruise itineraries commonly schedule them as an organized morning excursion. Allow approximately 4–6 hours for the combination including road travel.

things_to_do.name: Minya Corniche and City Center
things_to_do.description: Easy independently. If you prefer not to take a long excursion, spend 1.5–2 hours along the Nile Corniche and nearby central streets. The waterfront has gardens, river views and local cafes, while historic mosques including Al-Fouly and Al-Lamty stand close to the riverfront. This is more an opportunity to experience a working Upper Egyptian city than a major sightseeing circuit. Dress modestly, and treat mosque visits primarily as exterior stops unless visitors are clearly being admitted.

things_to_do.name: Tell el-Amarna
things_to_do.description: Organized excursion recommended. Akhenaten's former capital lies roughly 58 km (36.0 mi) south of Minya and is a large archaeological landscape rather than one compact monument. Tombs, palace and temple remains are spread over a considerable area, making a vehicle essential. Many long Nile cruises do not visit Amarna by road from Minya at all: the vessel sails south and makes a separate stop near the archaeological site. Check your cruise itinerary before arranging anything independently. If your ship already calls at Amarna, there is little reason to attempt it during the Minya stop.

things_to_do.name: Easy: Nile Waterfront and Historic Mosques
things_to_do.description: Distance: approximately 2 km (1.2 mi), depending on the vessel's exact mooring. Pure walking time: about 30–40 minutes. Recommended total time: 1.5–2 hours. Difficulty: Easy; generally flat, but expect busy streets, uneven pavements and strong sun. Riverboat mooring: Start from the gangway after confirming with the crew that you can return through the same access point. Minya Corniche: Follow the riverfront for Nile views and a look at everyday city life. Al-Fouly Mosque: Pause outside this prominent mosque beside the Corniche. Al-Lamty Mosque: Continue to another of Minya's historic Islamic landmarks close to the waterfront. Central streets: Make a short diversion inland for shops and local street life rather than extending far from the river. Return along the Corniche: Retrace the waterfront to the vessel, allowing extra time to locate the correct mooring if several riverboats are berthed nearby.

name: Alang Ship Breaking Yard (India)
summary: Alang (port locode INALA) is a small "port" town in India's Gujarat State (Saurashtra Region, Bhavnagar District) with population around 20,000. Since the early 1990s, Alang has been worldwide known for its shipbreaking yard (the world's largest). There, retired marine vessels (cargo and passenger) are beached/grounded then dismantled. Some vessels (without their own power) are towed.
description: Alang (port locode INALA) is a small "port" town in India's Gujarat State (Saurashtra Region, Bhavnagar District) with population around 20,000. Since the early 1990s, Alang has been worldwide known for its shipbreaking yard (the world's largest). There, retired marine vessels (cargo and passenger) are beached/grounded then dismantled. Some vessels (without their own power) are towed. The 1983-founded Alang Yard is also officially classified as "Port Alang" and dubbed "Alang Ship Breaking Port". Here, ~50% of the world's salvaged ships have been dismantled and recycled (a total of 153 shipbreaking plots), making it the largest ship graveyard on the planet. The beaches where the vessels are broken up are on the Gulf of Khambhat, approx 50 km (31 mi) southeast of the district's capital city (Bhavnagar). Approx 175 km (110 mi) southwest of Alang is Diu Island . Approx 280 km (170 mi) to the south is Mumbai (Bombay) - direct/sea distance. At Alang's beaches are dismantled all types of vessels, including oil-gas tankers, boxships (container carriers) , bulk-cargo carriers, Ro-Ro (car ferries), passenger ships ( ferries and cruise liners ), and naval ships. The vessels are beached during high tide. When the tide recedes, hundreds of workers start to break up each ship. Most of the machinery and furniture are salvaged, and the rest is for scrap. The work is hard and dangerous, with numerous serious injuries (even deaths) happening daily. There are plans to modernize the Alang Shipyard since India and Japan signed an MoU (Memorandum of Understanding) for technology and financial help from Japan. The public-private partnership aims to upgrade Alang's shipbreaking and recycling operations according to the latest international safety-, health- and environmental regulations, as well as to make it IMO-compliant. The Yard's largest vessel so far is the supertanker "MS Seawise Giant" (oil tanker, IMO 7381154, 1979-built, 2010-scrapped as "MS Mont"). This was also the world's longest ship - with LOA length 459 m (1504 ft), draft 25 m (81 ft), GT 260941 tons, DWT 564763 tons. Note: Due to the Coronavirus crisis and IMO's new regulations (marine engine upgrades for using low-sulfur fuels and LNG ), in 2020-2021 were scrapped 15 cruise liners - an unprecedented number in comparison to previous years, and even 5-year periods. In 2020, the average ship scrap metal (DWT-deadweight tonnage) prices in Alang rose to ~USD 400 per ton (from ~$200), in Aliaga - to ~USD 300 per ton (from ~$100). EU- flagged ships' scrap values were ~USD 100-200 per ton as these vessels require dismantling at EU-certified yards. Ship scrap prices in the USA were USD 80-90 per ton. Next are listed some Alang- scrapped cruise ships and converted classic ocean liners. In brackets is the vessel's year of birth and death. Next video is the 70-min long Canadian documentary film (by Michael Kot) titled "Shipbreakers" (2004) focusing on Alang Yard's deplorable working conditions. Currently, the world's top-4 largest shipbreaking yards are Alang (India), Chittagong (Bangladesh) , Gadani (Pakistan) , Aliaga (Turkey). For CruiseMapper's collection of destroyed cruise liners see our Scrapped Cruise Ships . Alang is not a conventional cruise port. It is a specialist ship-recycling destination on the Gulf of Khambhat, where end-of-life vessels normally anchor offshore and are then beached at recycling plots. No regular cruise passenger terminal or walk-off sightseeing area is documented, and CruiseMapper currently lists no scheduled cruise calls. Independent sightseeing limited or not recommended. Any passenger landing or shore access on a special call would need to be arranged through the ship and its local agent. Once ashore, a pre-arranged car with driver is the practical way to explore the area.
getting_from_port: Cruise terminal: There is no conventional passenger cruise terminal documented at Alang. Walking: The recycling zone is an active industrial area and is not suitable for casual independent walking. Shuttles: Do not assume that a cruise shuttle will be available; arrangements for any special passenger call would be ship-specific. Road transport: A private car or taxi arranged in advance is the most practical option. Bhavnagar: approximately 50 km (31.1 mi) from Alang, normally around 45–60 minutes by road depending on traffic and the exact starting point.
terminal_notes: No regular cruise passenger terminal or walk-off sightseeing area is documented, and CruiseMapper currently lists no scheduled cruise calls.
tender_evidence: It is a specialist ship-recycling destination on the Gulf of Khambhat, where end-of-life vessels normally anchor offshore and are then beached at recycling plots.

things_to_do.name: Visit the Alang-Sosiya Ship Recycling Yard
things_to_do.description: This is the main reason to visit Alang, but it is not a normal sightseeing attraction. Gujarat Maritime Board allows visits by Indian and foreign visitors subject to permission from the Port Officer. Arrange permission before the visit rather than expecting to enter on arrival. Photography and videography inside the ship-recycling yard are prohibited for security, safety and environmental reasons. Visitors should remain with authorized escorts and follow all instructions because this is a working heavy-industrial site. Allow: roughly 2–3 hours once local transport and access arrangements are included. Best for: maritime and industrial-interest visitors. Independent visit: not suitable without prior authorization.

things_to_do.name: Bhavnagar City
things_to_do.description: For passengers who have several hours ashore, Bhavnagar provides a more conventional sightseeing option. The city is approximately 50 km (31.1 mi) from Alang, so allow about 1.5–2 hours for the return drive plus sightseeing time. Takhteshwar Temple is a practical short stop, reached by steps to a hilltop overlooking the city. Victoria Park provides a contrasting green area near Gaurishankar Lake if time permits. Allow: about 4–5 hours including transfers. Independent visit: possible with a pre-arranged driver. Avoid relying on connections between local buses during a time-limited call.

things_to_do.name: Palitana and Shatrunjaya Hill
things_to_do.description: Palitana is approximately 53 km (32.9 mi) by road from Alang. Its Shatrunjaya Hill temple complex is one of Gujarat's major sights, but reaching the principal temples requires climbing more than 3,700 stone steps. The ascent alone can take around two hours. This is a demanding full excursion rather than a quick side trip. Allow at least 5–7 hours for driving, climbing and time among the temples, and considerably more flexibility in hot weather. Difficulty: challenging. Independent visit: possible with a private driver on a long port call, but an organized or pre-arranged excursion is preferable because of the distance and substantial walking time.

summary: Port Alanya cruise ship schedule shows timetable calendars of all arrival and departure dates by month. To see the full itineraries (ports of call dates and arrival / departure times) and their lowest rates – just follow the corresponding ship-link.
