The port's schedule lists all ships (in links) with cruises going to or leaving from Alanya, Turkey. To see the full itineraries (ports of call dates and arrival / departure times) and their lowest rates – just follow the corresponding ship-link. Alanya (aka Alaiye) is a port town and a popular beach resort area located on Turkey's southern coast (Mediterranean Sea). The port is approx 138 km (86 ml) east of Antalya . Alanya's population is around 100,000. The whole district (the city and the built-up resort region) has population around 250,000 and covers a total area of around 1600 km2 (617 ml2). Because of its natural strategic position on a little peninsula into Mediterranean Sea below Taurus Mountains, Alanya has been the stronghold for a lot of Mediterranean-based empires, such as the Ptolemaic, Roman, Byzantine, Ottoman and Seleucid Empires. The greatest political importance of Alanya came during the Middle Ages, with Seljuk Sultanate of Rum under rule of Alaeddin Kayqubad I, from whom Alanya city derives its name. The building campaign of Alaeddin Kayqubad I resulted in many of the landmarks, including Alanya Castle, Kızıl Kule (Red Tower) and Tersane (Shipyard). The natural attractions, historic heritage and Mediterranean climate make Alanya a popular tourism destination, and responsible for 9% of Turkey's tourism sector and 30% of foreign purchases of real estate in the country. Since 1958 tourism has risen to become city's dominant industry, resulting in a corresponding increase in population. Cultural festivals and warm-weather sporting events take place in Alanya every year. Until about 10 years ago Alanya was just a sleepy coastal town, but today it has grown to a significant Mediterranean resort, although it has succeeded to hold on to its original character. Passengers disembark at the harbour and visit the old city with its ancient remains and castle walls. Close by the quay are located the remains of Tersane, an ancient shipyard with five linked arches. More energetic tourists should take the long steep walk to Alanya's 13th century castle above, with its miniature Byzantine basilica. Intriguing local archaelogical exhibits are featured in the Alanya Museum. There are also nice beaches and caves that are accessible by boat, such as Damlatas ("Cave of Dripping Stones"). From Alanya it's possible to vist the sites of ancient Aspendos and Perge. Easy independently. Alanya Cruise Port is beside the historic harbor and central shopping streets. The Red Tower and Seljuk Shipyard are close to the passenger exit, while Damlataş Cave, Cleopatra Beach and the castle cable car can be reached on foot across town. Most cruise calls use the central pier, although anchoring and tender operations are possible. Follow the ship’s instructions for the specific call.
getting_from_port: Passengers normally leave the terminal directly into the harbor area. A shuttle is generally unnecessary for central Alanya. On foot: Best for the harbor, Red Tower, old shopping streets, Damlataş Cave and the eastern end of Cleopatra Beach. Taxi: Useful for the upper castle, beaches farther from the center or attractions outside Alanya. Agree on the fare or confirm that the meter will be used. Local transport: City buses serve the wider resort, but routes and payment arrangements can change. For a short call, walking and taxis are usually simpler. Cable car: The lower station is beside Damlataş Cave and connects with the Ehmedek area of Alanya Castle. Operating times can vary, so check locally before relying on it for the return journey.
terminal_notes: Most cruise calls use the central pier, although anchoring and tender operations are possible.
tender_evidence: Most cruise calls use the central pier, although anchoring and tender operations are possible.

things_to_do.name: Red Tower, Shipyard and Historic Harbor
things_to_do.description: Allow 1.5–2.5 hours. This is the easiest option for a short call. Walk around the excursion-boat harbor to the 13th-century Red Tower, then continue beside the castle peninsula to the vaulted Seljuk Shipyard. The route is largely straightforward, although the shipyard approach has uneven surfaces and steps.

things_to_do.name: Alanya Castle by Cable Car
things_to_do.description: Allow 3–4 hours. Walk approximately 2 km (1.2 mi) from the port through central Alanya to Damlataş. Take the cable car to Ehmedek, then explore the walls, viewpoints and old lanes on the castle peninsula. The upper area includes slopes, stone paving and many steps. The cable car reaches part of the castle district rather than every attraction, and the main citadel requires additional uphill walking. A taxi is an easier alternative for passengers who want to reach the highest section with less walking.

things_to_do.name: Damlataş Cave and Cleopatra Beach
things_to_do.description: Allow 2.5–4 hours. Damlataş Cave is a compact limestone cave near the cable-car station and the eastern end of Cleopatra Beach. Combine a brief cave visit with swimming, a waterfront walk or time at the beach. The beach is practical independently, but the shoreline can become steep and waves may be strong. Observe local warning flags and allow time to change before returning to the ship.

things_to_do.name: Dim Cave and Dim River
things_to_do.description: Allow about 4–5 hours. Dim Cave is approximately 11 km (6.8 mi) from central Alanya, while restaurants and recreation areas are spread along the Dim River valley. A taxi with an agreed waiting arrangement or a prearranged excursion is more practical than trying to coordinate local buses during a port call.

things_to_do.name: Sapadere Canyon
things_to_do.description: Organized excursion recommended. The canyon is approximately 40 km (24.9 mi) from Alanya. Its raised walkways lead through a narrow gorge toward waterfalls and cold natural pools. Road travel consumes a substantial part of the day, so this option suits a long call with reliable round-trip transport.

things_to_do.name: Easy Harbor and Old Town Walk
things_to_do.description: Distance: approximately 3 km (1.9 mi) round trip Pure walking time: about 45–55 minutes Recommended time: 1.5–2.5 hours Difficulty: Easy to moderate, with some steps and uneven paving near the historic structures. Leave the cruise terminal and follow the harbor promenade. Walk toward the Red Tower, the prominent octagonal landmark below the castle. Continue around the base of the peninsula to the Seljuk Shipyard. Return past the Red Tower and walk through the central bazaar streets. Rejoin the waterfront and follow the harbor back to the terminal. This route remains close to the ship and can be shortened easily.
things_to_do.difficulty: Easy to moderate, with some steps and uneven paving near the historic structures

things_to_do.name: Moderate Cross-Town and Castle Route
things_to_do.description: Distance: approximately 5–7 km (3.1–4.3 mi), excluding the cable-car ride Pure walking time: about 1.5–2 hours Recommended time: 4–5 hours Difficulty: Moderate, with hills, stairs and uneven stone surfaces in the castle area. Start at the cruise terminal and walk along the harbor. Pass through central Alanya toward Damlataş Cave. Visit the cave or continue directly to the nearby cable-car station. Ride to Ehmedek and explore the castle walls, viewpoints and old lanes. Descend by cable car and stop briefly at Cleopatra Beach. Return through the center to the cruise terminal. Do not attempt the entire climb to the castle on foot unless prepared for a long, steep ascent in exposed heat. Confirm the cable car’s return operation before going up.
things_to_do.recommended_time: 4–5 hours Difficulty: Moderate, with hills, stairs and uneven stone surfaces in the castle area
things_to_do.difficulty: Moderate, with hills, stairs and uneven stone surfaces in the castle area

Albany NY (port locode USALB ) is a Hudson River cruise port and New York state's capital city with population around 100,000 (metro around 1,2 million). Albany is on Hudson River's west bank, approx 10 mi (16 km) south of its confluence with Mohawk River and approx 135 mi (220 km) north of NYC . The nearest NY cities are Troy (8 mi / 13 km to the northeast), Schenectady (19 mi / 31 km to the northwest) and Saratoga Springs (35 mi / 56 km to the north). The town (established by Dutch colonists in 1614, incorporated by the British in 1686) is well-known for its rich history, culture and architecture. The town was named after the Duke of Albany (King James II of England, Ireland and Scotland / 1633-1701). The city became the state's capital in 1797 and today is one of the oldest original settlements of the original British 13 colonies. The city developed in the late 18th- and 19th-centuries as a trade center and transportation hub, being the eastern terminus of the Erie Canal (connecting to the Great Lakes) and well-connected via the USA's main railways. Current-day city's economy is heavily based on NY state government-related employment, healthcare, education and technologies. As a cruise port, Albany NY was first included in the "Hudson River Cruises" 2018 schedule of the USA's largest river cruise company - ACL-American Cruise Lines . The next table shows the company's 7-day itinerary from homeport NYC, with prices from ~USD 4,000 per person (double occupancy). In 2019, this cruisetour itinerary was included in the schedules of the ACL riverboats American Star , American Constitution and American Independence .

Albany is a port city located in the Great Southern region of Western Australia. It is the oldest permanently settled city in Western Australia, predating Perth (state capital, situated 418 km SE) and Fremantle by more than two years. In June 2015, the estimated urban population of Albany was 33,970 making it state's 6th-largest population centre, with a total area of 297 km2 (115 mi2). The city centre lies at the northern end of Princess Royal Harbour (part of King George Sound). Albany's business district is bounded by Mount Melville to the west and Mount Clarence to the east. The city is part of the local government area of Albany City. Albany was established on December 26, 1826, as New South Wales' military outpost, which was part of a plan to prevent the ambitions of France in the region. On January 21, 1827 the outpost's commander, Major Edmund Lockyer, took possession of the continent's western third for the British Crown. Initially, the area was named Frederick Town to honour the Duke of York and Albany, Prince Frederick. The settlement was transferred to control of Swan River Colony in 1831 and renamed Albany by Sir James Stirling (Lieutenant-Governor, 1791-1865). During the last decade of 19th century, the city of Albany was served as a gateway to Eastern Goldfields. It was the only deep-water port of the colony for many years, having a place of prominence on shipping services between the Australian colonies and Britain. The opening of Fremantle Inner Harbour of 1897 saw its importance as port decline, and after that Albany's industries turned to agriculture, timber and whaling. Nowadays Albany is a major tourist destination as well as a base from which to explore state's south-west. The city is well regarded for its preservation of heritage and natural beauty. Albany is a practical port for independent sightseeing. Most cruise ships berth at Berths 1 or 2, although some vessels may anchor and tender passengers to Albany Waterfront Marina. From the berth, passengers pass through the port’s Transit Shed before continuing by shuttle, taxi, tour vehicle or on foot. Independent sightseeing: Easy in the town centre; transport or an organized excursion is recommended for the National Anzac Centre, Torndirrup National Park and the Historic Whaling Station.
getting_from_port: Free port shuttle: Normally carries cruise passengers between the port and central Albany. Confirm the final return time before leaving the shuttle. Walking: The town centre is approximately 2 km (1.2 mi) from the port, usually a 15–20-minute walk. Follow the flatter waterfront route along Princess Royal Drive and use the pedestrian overpass beside the Albany Entertainment Centre. Taxis: A limited taxi collection point operates inside the port. Demand can be high when a large ship is visiting. Private tours: Operators not contracted by the cruise line normally meet passengers in the public parking area outside the port, near the Albany Boatshed. Tender calls: Passengers normally arrive at Albany Waterfront Marina, close to the waterfront but still separated from central York Street by the railway corridor.
terminal_notes: Most cruise ships berth at Berths 1 or 2, although some vessels may anchor and tender passengers to Albany Waterfront Marina. From the berth, passengers pass through the port’s Transit Shed before continuing by shuttle, taxi, tour vehicle or on foot.
tender_evidence: Most cruise ships berth at Berths 1 or 2, although some vessels may anchor and tender passengers to Albany Waterfront Marina.

things_to_do.name: Explore Central Albany and the Waterfront
things_to_do.description: Allow 2–4 hours. This is the easiest independent option. Start around York Street, where the Albany Visitor Centre, Town Hall, shops and cafés are concentrated, then walk downhill through the historic streets to the Museum of the Great Southern, the replica brig Amity and ANZAC Peace Park. The waterfront is relatively level, but central Albany rises sharply away from the harbour. Passengers with limited mobility may prefer the shuttle for the journey between the port and York Street.

things_to_do.name: National Anzac Centre and Albany Heritage Park
things_to_do.description: Allow 3–4 hours. The National Anzac Centre stands within the Princess Royal Fortress on Mount Adelaide, approximately 3 km (1.9 mi) from central Albany. Its exhibitions, military sites and elevated views across King George Sound make it one of Albany’s most substantial attractions. This visit is possible independently by taxi. A visitor-centre shuttle may operate on some cruise days, but it does not run continuously and should be confirmed after arrival. Walking from town involves sustained uphill sections and is unsuitable for passengers with limited time or mobility.

things_to_do.name: The Gap, Natural Bridge and Torndirrup National Park
things_to_do.description: Allow 3.5–5 hours. The Gap’s cantilevered viewing platform and the nearby Natural Bridge overlook the exposed Southern Ocean coast. The lookouts have constructed paths, but the national park is outside town and cannot be reached conveniently on foot or by regular urban sightseeing transport. Organized excursion recommended. A prearranged tour or taxi is the practical choice, particularly if combining the park with additional coastal viewpoints. Conditions can be windy and wet, and visitors should remain on the designated paths. Park entry fees may apply.

things_to_do.name: Historic Whaling Station and the Southern Coast
things_to_do.description: Allow 4–5 hours. Albany’s Historic Whaling Station at Discovery Bay includes the former processing site, the restored whale chaser Cheynes IV, museum exhibits and a regional wildflower garden. It is well outside the walkable town area. Choose a ship excursion, local tour or prearranged taxi. Longer tours sometimes combine the station with Torndirrup National Park, but check how much time is allowed at each stop.

things_to_do.name: Middleton Beach
things_to_do.description: Allow 2–3 hours. Binalup/Middleton Beach is approximately 3.2 km (2.0 mi) from central Albany and has a sheltered beach, lawns and views across King George Sound. A taxi is the simplest option for a short visit. Walking is possible for active passengers, but the full return journey consumes considerable shore time and includes changes in elevation. Swimming conditions and local safety information should be checked on the day.

name: Alcoutim (Portugal)
summary: Alcoutim is a Douro River cruise port and town in southeastern Portugal, with population around 3,000. The town is located close to the border with Spain.
description: Alcoutim is a Douro River cruise port and town in southeastern Portugal, with population around 3,000. The town is located close to the border with Spain. Alcoutim municipality lies in the northeast corner of Faro District. It is Portugal's least densely populated municipality, limited on the east by Huelva Province (Spain), on the north by Mertola Municipality, on the southwest by Tavira Municipality, on the southeast by Castro Marim Municipality, and on the west by Loule and Almodovar Municipality. The municipality's administrative center is Alcoutim, which is located at the extreme eastern part on the Spanish frontier, across Guadiana River from the town of Sanlucar de Guadiana, Huelva Province in Spain. Administratively, the municipality of Alcoutim is divided into four civil parishes, including: Alcoutim e Pereiro, Gioes, Martim Longo and Vaqueiros. Alcoutim is a small river-cruise stop on the Guadiana, directly opposite Sanlúcar de Guadiana in Spain. The historic center is compact and best explored on foot. Once ashore, independent sightseeing is straightforward, although several streets and the approaches to the castle are uphill. Independent sightseeing: Independent with some planning. The town itself is easy to explore without a tour, but passengers should confirm the ship's exact landing arrangements because of current restrictions on the river pier.
getting_from_port: Alcoutim does not have a conventional ocean-cruise terminal. River cruise vessels normally approach the town via the Guadiana, with the riverfront immediately beside the historic center. Important access note: in February 2026, the port authority closed Cais de Alcoutim and several other Guadiana piers after flood damage, prohibiting vessel use until safety assessments and repairs are completed. Passengers on a scheduled Alcoutim call should therefore follow the cruise operator's current instructions regarding the actual landing point, tender or any alternative transfer. Once passengers reach central Alcoutim, almost everything of interest is within walking distance. A taxi is unnecessary for the main sights.
terminal_notes: The town itself is easy to explore without a tour, but passengers should confirm the ship's exact landing arrangements because of current restrictions on the river pier.

things_to_do.name: Explore Alcoutim Castle and the Riverside Center
things_to_do.description: Allow about 1.5–2.5 hours for the essential sights. Walk along the Guadiana waterfront, see the old quay area and Igreja Matriz, then climb through the whitewashed streets to Alcoutim Castle. The castle walls provide broad views across the river to Spain and contain an archaeological museum when open. This is the most practical choice for a short call and requires no organized excursion. The town is compact, although the climb to the castle involves slopes and some uneven surfaces.

things_to_do.name: Walk to Pego Fundo River Beach
things_to_do.description: Praia Fluvial do Pego Fundo is approximately 0.5 km (0.3 mi) from the center. It has a sandy bathing area on the Ribeira de Cadavais and is a realistic addition to a town visit, particularly in warm weather. Allow 1–2 hours if you want time for a swim or rest. Beach facilities and lifeguard coverage are seasonal, so do not assume full services outside the summer bathing period.

things_to_do.name: Cross to Sanlúcar de Guadiana
things_to_do.description: The Spanish village of Sanlúcar de Guadiana sits directly opposite Alcoutim. Small passenger boats have traditionally provided the short cross-river connection, making it possible to visit two countries during one stop. Because river-pier conditions and private boat operations can change, only attempt the crossing if the service is confirmed on the day. Allow around 1.5–2 hours for the crossing and a short walk around Sanlúcar, and return to the Portuguese side well before the ship's all-aboard time.

things_to_do.name: Take a Guadiana Boat Trip
things_to_do.description: Local operators traditionally offer short river trips as well as longer outings toward nearby Guadiana villages. A short cruise can complement a walking visit, but availability depends on river conditions and usable landing facilities. For cruise passengers, a short prearranged trip is more practical than a half-day journey. Do not make an independent boat excursion the centerpiece of a tight call unless both departure and return arrangements are confirmed.

things_to_do.name: Alcoutim Heritage and River Walk
things_to_do.description: Distance: about 4 km (2.5 mi). Pure walking time: approximately 1–1.5 hours. Recommended total time: 2.5–3 hours with sightseeing. Difficulty: Moderate, with hills and some uneven surfaces. Praça da República: Begin in the small central square after reaching the town center. Guadiana waterfront and Cais Velho: Follow the riverside promenade for views across to Sanlúcar de Guadiana. Igreja Matriz de São Salvador: See the parish church beside the old waterfront area. Alcoutim Castle: Climb to the medieval fortress for the principal viewpoint over the town and river. Ermida de Nossa Senhora da Conceição: Continue uphill to this small historic church and another elevated viewpoint. Praia Fluvial do Pego Fundo: Descend toward the river beach, approximately 0.5 km (0.3 mi) from the center. Castelo Velho area: Continue on the hillier part of the route toward the archaeological remains if time and weather permit. Return to central Alcoutim: Complete the loop back toward Praça da República and the ship's designated embarkation point. The municipality's full local walking route is hilly, reaching elevations of roughly 140 m (460 ft). Passengers who prefer an easier walk can omit Castelo Velho and simply return from Pego Fundo to the waterfront.
things_to_do.difficulty: Moderate, with hills and some uneven surfaces

Alcudia is a port town in the Spanish autonomous territory Balearic Islands. The town covers a total area of approx 60 km2 (23 mi2) and has population around 3,000. The port is located on the northern coast of Majorca Island. Alcudia is a resort town mainly popular among families. Most of its hotels are in Port d'Alcudia and Platja d'Alcudia along the 14 km (9 mi) long beach stretching to Can Picafort. The well-preserved Old Town is surrounded by a medieval wall and features many houses from the 13th-century. Outside the town walls, there are remains of a Roman town with an amphitheater. North of Alcudia is the 19th-century built bullring (bullfighting arena). The old town hosts an outdoor market on Sundays and Tuesdays. Inside the town walls are also several popular bistros and restaurants famous for their home-cooked food. Most restaurants in Port Alcudia are around the Marina and most of them are only open during the summer tourist season. Further to the north and west can be found coves and several beaches good for snorkeling, swimming, sunbathing. Alcudia is also well-known for its annual St Jaume Festival, held in early-July for 9 days. Regularly-scheduled cruiseferries link Alcudia to mainland Spain ( Barcelona ) and Menorca Island ( Ciutadella de Menorca ). The company BALEARIA serves the Alcudia-Barcelona route with 15 weekly crossings (travel time ~6 hours) and the Alcudia-Ciutadella route with 4 daily crossings (travel time ~1 hour). A second large ferry company ( TRASMEDITERRANEA ) serves the Alcudia-Ciutadella route with 12 weekly crossings (~2 hours travel time). Alcúdia is a good port for independent sightseeing. The medieval old town, Roman remains, Port d'Alcúdia waterfront and a long sandy beach are all close enough for a normal cruise call. More distant sights such as Formentor and s'Albufera are also possible, but require transport and more attention to timing.
getting_from_port: Alcúdia does not have the predictable cruise-terminal setup found in Palma. Cruise calls are relatively infrequent, and ships can use the anchorage rather than berth alongside the ferry facilities. Tender passengers should therefore check where their ship is landing before planning a walking route. The commercial passenger terminal, Estació Marítima , is on the Port d'Alcúdia waterfront. In the summer season, TIB bus line 323 serves the maritime station and connects it with Alcúdia town and Alcanada. The main Port d'Alcúdia bus stops have additional routes serving the old town, beaches and other parts of northern Mallorca. A taxi is the simplest option for the old town and normally avoids spending valuable port time waiting for a bus. Do not assume that a cruise-line shuttle will operate unless your ship specifically announces one.

things_to_do.name: Alcúdia Old Town and Roman Pol·lèntia
things_to_do.description: Allow about 2.5–3.5 hours. This is the best all-round choice for a first visit and is easy to arrange independently. Take a taxi or local bus to the historic centre, then explore the medieval gates, narrow streets, Plaça de la Constitució, Sant Jaume Church and sections of the city walls. The archaeological remains of Roman Pol·lèntia lie immediately south of the medieval centre. The site includes residential remains, the forum area and a Roman theatre, making it easy to combine Roman and medieval Alcúdia without another transfer.

things_to_do.name: Port d'Alcúdia and Alcúdia Beach
things_to_do.description: Allow about 2–4 hours. This is the easiest relaxed option, especially when tenders land near the Port d'Alcúdia waterfront. Walk around the marina and waterfront before continuing to the sandy beach. Alcúdia Beach extends for more than 7 km (4.3 mi) along the bay, with shallow water and a developed resort section near the port. There is no reason for cruise passengers to travel far along the beach unless they specifically want a quieter section.

things_to_do.name: Alcanada Coast
things_to_do.description: Allow about 2–3 hours. Alcanada lies east of the commercial port and provides a quieter alternative to the main resort beach. The coast is rocky and pebbly rather than a broad sandy strand, with pine trees and views toward the small island and Alcanada lighthouse. Seasonal TIB line 323 links the maritime station with Alcanada, or it is a short taxi ride. Walking is also possible for reasonably fit passengers and is most convenient if the ship's landing point is near the commercial port.

things_to_do.name: S'Albufera de Mallorca Natural Park
things_to_do.description: Allow about 3–4 hours. This is a worthwhile independent option for birdwatchers and nature enthusiasts. The main entrance at Pont dels Anglesos is around 6 km (3.7 mi) from Alcúdia town and is served by TIB routes along the Alcúdia–Can Picafort corridor. Visitors enter on foot or by bicycle, and the information centre is about 1 km (0.6 mi) inside the park. A free visitor permit is obtained at the information centre. Because a proper visit involves additional walking to hides and observation areas, this is better for passengers who have at least several hours ashore after allowing for transport.

things_to_do.name: Formentor Peninsula
things_to_do.description: Allow about 4–6 hours. Formentor offers one of northern Mallorca's principal scenic excursions, with Port de Pollença, Mirador del Colomer, Formentor Beach and the lighthouse among the possible stops. Independent travel is possible with seasonal TIB line 334 from Alcúdia, but services and access arrangements should be checked on the day. Road access to the peninsula is regulated during the busy season, and private-vehicle restrictions can apply. For a short cruise call, a ship or organized excursion is usually the safer choice because it removes the risk of waiting for buses or dealing with seasonal traffic controls.

things_to_do.name: Easy to Moderate: Alcúdia Old Town and Pol·lèntia
things_to_do.description: Start: Alcúdia Centre Històric or Pol·lèntia bus stop after transferring from the port. Enter through Porta de Mallorca and look at the medieval walls and moat. Follow the old streets toward Plaça de la Constitució . Continue through the historic centre to Porta del Moll, or Xara Gate . Walk along the wall perimeter toward Sant Jaume Church . Visit the nearby Pol·lèntia archaeological area . If time permits, continue through the Roman site toward the Roman Theatre before returning to the old town bus stop or taxi rank. Distance: about 2.5 km (1.6 mi), depending on how much of Pol·lèntia is included. Pure walking time: about 45–55 minutes. Recommended total time: 2–3 hours with sightseeing stops. Difficulty: Easy to moderate. Mostly level, but expect cobbles, uneven paving and occasional steps.

things_to_do.name: Moderate: Port to Alcanada Coastal Walk
things_to_do.description: Start: Estació Marítima or the eastern side of Port d'Alcúdia. Leave the passenger-terminal area toward the fishing harbour . Continue east along the port roads toward Camí d'Alcanada . Pass the area around Torre Major , the old coastal watchtower. Continue through the residential area to Cala Poncet . Finish at Alcanada Beach for views across to the lighthouse island. Return by the same route, or use seasonal bus line 323 if its timetable suits your ship. Distance: roughly 5 km (3.1 mi) round trip from the commercial port area. Pure walking time: about 1 hour 15 minutes. Recommended total time: 2–3 hours. Difficulty: Moderate. Mostly easy surfaces with a few inclines, but the route is exposed to the sun and some sections follow roads rather than a continuous seafront promenade.

summary: Port Aldabra Atoll Seychelles cruise ship schedule shows timetable calendars of all arrival and departure dates by month. The port's schedule lists all ships (in links) with cruises going to or leaving from Aldabra Atoll Seychelles. To see the full itineraries (ports of call dates and arrival / departure times) and their lowest rates – just follow the corresponding ship-link.
description: Port Aldabra Atoll Seychelles cruise ship schedule shows timetable calendars of all arrival and departure dates by month. The port's schedule lists all ships (in links) with cruises going to or leaving from Aldabra Atoll Seychelles. To see the full itineraries (ports of call dates and arrival / departure times) and their lowest rates – just follow the corresponding ship-link. Aldabra Atoll is the world's second-largest coral atoll - after Kiritimati (Christmas Island) . It is part of the Outer Islands (Seychelles) in the Indian Ocean. Aldabra Island is located 1120 km (700 mi) southwest of Victoria (Mahe Island) . The Aldabra Atoll has 4 larger islands, plus 40 smaller ones, all inside its lagoon. There are also a few very small islets located between Grand-Terre Island and Picard Islands. A scientific research station of SIF (Seychelles Islands Foundation) is based at La Gigi village, Picard Island. The permanent staff of 12 people conduct research to study the biodiversity of Aldabra. Aldabra is not easy to access. No helipads, landing jetties or airstrips, have been permitted to be constructed on the atoll. The closest airfield on Assumption is 50 km (31 ml) south-east of Picard. Supply ships that operate from Mahe provide food and other essentials to the scientists and staff at the station once per 2 months. Cruises are operated by several cruise lines along with dive boats that may call on Aldabra Atoll on expedition tours. Visits by people other than SIF scientists and staff are strictly controlled. Only guided tours are offered with prior permission and current numbers indicate that an average of 900 tourists are able to see the atoll per year. Within Aldabra, paved walking paths exist from La Gigi village which leads to premonitory from where views of the mangrove species and the large lagoon (during low tides) are seen. Aldabra is not a conventional cruise port. There is no cruise terminal, harbour, jetty, road network or independent tourist infrastructure. Expedition ships visit this remote UNESCO-listed nature reserve under prior authorisation from the Seychelles Islands Foundation (SIF), normally anchoring in the designated area off Picard Island. Passengers go ashore or join water activities in the ship's expedition boats or Zodiacs. Independent sightseeing is not permitted. Access is limited to designated visitor areas, and activities are supervised by SIF staff. For cruise passengers, the practical approach is to participate in the ship's organised expedition programme rather than attempt to arrange anything independently. Visiting vessels use a designated anchorage near the SIF Research Station on Picard Island. There is no dock, so passengers transfer by small expedition craft. Settlement Beach in front of the research station is the normal landing point. If conditions there are unsuitable, La Gigi in the West Channels may be used instead. Picard cannot normally be reached by boat around low tide because the fringing reef becomes too shallow. Landing schedules are therefore planned around the local tide, and the day's programme can change at short notice because of currents, wind or sea conditions. Passengers going ashore also undergo strict biosecurity procedures. Clothing, footwear and equipment must be clean and free of seeds, soil and other material that could introduce invasive species.
terminal_notes: There is no cruise terminal, harbour, jetty, road network or independent tourist infrastructure.

things_to_do.name: Guided Nature Walk on Picard Island
things_to_do.description: This is the main land-based experience and the best opportunity to see Aldabra's giant tortoises, seabirds, unusual vegetation and raised-coral landscape. All routes begin near the Research Station and are guided. La Gigi walk: About 1 hour round trip. A relatively short coastal walk on a sandy path toward the lagoon, with views across Passe Femme and opportunities to watch frigatebirds, boobies and other seabirds. Historical walk: Up to about 1 hour 30 minutes. Follows the coast toward the remains of the former settlement, including old buildings, water tanks, a church and cemetery. Backpath walk: About 1 hour. A more natural route behind the station through vegetation and across exposed fossil coral. The terrain is rougher and the walk is considered moderately difficult. Picard and the Research Station area are the only terrestrial parts of the atoll normally open to visitors. Landing elsewhere is prohibited.

things_to_do.name: Zodiac Cruise Through the Lagoon
things_to_do.description: A lagoon cruise is one of the most practical ways to experience Aldabra because much of the wildlife and landscape is best viewed from the water. Trips are timed around high tide and follow approved routes with SIF staff aboard. The shorter West Channels cruise generally takes about 1–2 hours, passing mangroves, coral islets and narrow tidal channels. A longer trip between the Main Channel and West Channels may take around 2–3 hours and can provide sightings of turtles, rays, sharks, wading birds, boobies and frigatebirds.

things_to_do.name: Snorkelling
things_to_do.description: Snorkelling may be offered on the outer reef or in selected tidal channels. Some locations are used for drift snorkelling, so this is a controlled expedition activity rather than independent swimming from shore. Currents can be strong and vary rapidly with the tide. Expedition staff and SIF personnel assess conditions before guests enter the water, and channel snorkels are normally arranged so the current carries swimmers toward the lagoon rather than out to sea. Participation requirements depend on conditions and the expedition team's safety assessment.

things_to_do.name: Beach Swimming near the Research Station
things_to_do.description: When conditions allow, passengers may spend some time on Settlement Beach and swim close to shore under supervision. Blacktip reef sharks are frequently present in the shallows and are one of the notable wildlife sightings here. Swimmers must remain within the area specified by expedition and SIF staff.

things_to_do.name: Scuba Diving
things_to_do.description: Some expedition vessels arrange diving in designated areas including Settlement, Anse Var and selected channels. Diving must be organised in advance with SIF and requires qualified expedition dive staff as well as SIF supervision. Currents are a significant factor. Main Channel is particularly demanding and is reserved for experienced divers with the appropriate certification and skills. Diving should therefore be considered an expedition activity rather than something passengers can arrange locally after arrival.

To see the full itineraries (ports of call dates and arrival / departure times) and their lowest rates – just follow the corresponding ship-link. Alderney is the most northerly located of the Channel Islands. It is part of Bailiwick of Guernsey, British Crown dependency. Alderney Island is 5 km (3 miles) long and 2.4 km (1 1⁄2 miles) wide. Its area is 8 km2 (3 sq.miles), making it the 3rd-largest of the Channel Islands, and the 2nd largest in Bailiwick. Alderney is around 15 km (10 miles) to the west of La Hague on Cotentin Peninsula, Normandy (France), 30 km (20 miles) to the north-east of Guernsey , 100 km (60 miles) from the south coast of Great Britain. Alderney is the closest of Channel Islands to both the United Kingdom and France. It is separated by the dangerous Alderney Race from Cap de la Hague. Cruise ships to Alderney Island Channel Islands dock (anchor) at St Anne - port town on the northern coast. Alderney is small enough for a rewarding independent port day, but the arrival is by tender and much of the island is hilly. Braye Harbour, St Anne and nearby coastal sights are practical on foot; reaching the eastern beaches, lighthouse and more distant fortifications is easier by pre-booked taxi, bicycle or tour.
getting_from_port: Ship tenders use the passenger landing pontoon at Braye Harbour, close to the Harbour Master's Office. Passengers step directly into the working harbour area, with Braye Beach and the lower end of Braye Road nearby. St Anne is uphill from the harbour. The walk is short enough for most passengers, but the climb is noticeable and some streets in town are cobbled. Allow approximately 15–20 minutes each way between the harbour and central Victoria Street. Alderney does not have the frequent public transport normally found at larger cruise ports. Licensed taxis are available but supply is limited, so relying on finding one immediately at the harbour is not advisable. Bicycle and e-bike hire can be useful for passengers wanting to cover more of the island. The Alderney Railway runs between Braye and Mannez on selected days, normally including Saturdays during the main summer season. Its limited timetable makes it an attraction rather than dependable cruise-day transport, so check the operating schedule for the date of the call.
tender_evidence: Alderney is small enough for a rewarding independent port day, but the arrival is by tender and much of the island is hilly.

things_to_do.name: St Anne and the Historic Town Center
things_to_do.description: Allow: 2–3 hours. Independent: Easy, provided you are comfortable with the uphill approach. Walk from Braye Harbour into St Anne and explore Victoria Street, St Anne's Church, the older lanes around Le Bourgage and the central streets. The Alderney Museum is a worthwhile addition for passengers interested in the island's evacuation, occupation, fortifications and local history. This is the most straightforward choice for a short call because no transport is necessary and the route can easily be shortened if tender operations or weather change.

things_to_do.name: Braye Harbour and Beach
things_to_do.description: Allow: 1–2 hours. Independent: Very easy. Passengers wanting a relaxed visit can remain close to the tender landing. Braye Beach is only a few minutes away and is sheltered by the harbour breakwater. Combine the beach with a walk around the harbour, Braye Common and views toward the surrounding coastal defenses. This is also the safest option when the call is short or tendering conditions appear uncertain because you remain close to the return point.

things_to_do.name: Fort Albert, Bibette Head and the North Coast
things_to_do.description: Allow: About 2.5–3 hours with sightseeing stops. Independent: Practical for reasonably fit walkers. The official Fort Albert and Bibette Head walking route covers approximately 5.3 km (3.3 mi). It passes Braye Common, viewpoints above Braye Bay, the Fort Albert area and well-preserved German defenses at Bibette Head before continuing through the northern coastal landscape. The route includes hills, tracks and exposed sections. Walking shoes and a windproof or waterproof layer are advisable even when conditions at the harbour appear calm.

things_to_do.name: Longis Bay, Roman Fort and Mannez
things_to_do.description: Allow: 3–4 hours. Independent: Best with a bicycle or pre-arranged taxi. The eastern side of Alderney combines Longis Bay, nature areas, the Roman Fort and the coast around Mannez. Longis has the island's longest sandy beach and is also useful when northerly winds make the north-coast beaches less comfortable. Trying to include all of these sights entirely on foot can consume too much of a normal port call. Cycling works well on Alderney's relatively quiet roads, while a taxi or local tour gives more time at each stop.

things_to_do.name: Wildlife or Island Boat Trip
things_to_do.description: Allow: Usually around 2.5–3 hours depending on the operator and conditions. Organized excursion recommended. Local boat trips can explore Alderney's cliffs, forts and offshore seabird areas, including the gannet colony around Les Etacs and, seasonally, wildlife around Burhou. These trips are strongly dependent on weather and sea conditions and should be reserved in advance rather than treated as an activity that can always be arranged after landing.

things_to_do.name: Braye Harbour and Beach Walk — Easy
things_to_do.description: Distance: Approximately 2 km (1.2 mi) return. Pure walking time: About 30–40 minutes. Recommended time: 1–1.5 hours. Difficulty: Easy and mostly level. Start at the passenger landing pontoon beside the Harbour Master's Office. Walk through the harbour area and look across Braye Harbour toward the Victorian breakwater. Continue to Braye Beach. Follow the shore toward Braye Common. Pass Braye Station, the western terminus of the Alderney Railway. Return along the harbour side to the tender pontoon. This route keeps you close to the ship and is useful for passengers with a short visit or when changing weather makes a longer walk undesirable.

things_to_do.name: Braye Harbour and St Anne — Moderate
things_to_do.description: Distance: Approximately 4 km (2.5 mi) including a circuit of central St Anne. Pure walking time: About 60–75 minutes. Recommended time: 2–3 hours. Difficulty: Moderate because of the sustained climb from Braye and some cobbled streets. Start at the Braye Harbour passenger landing pontoon. Walk inland and follow Braye Road uphill toward St Anne. Reach Victoria Street and the Visitor Information Centre area. Visit St Anne's Church. Continue through the old streets around Connaught Square and Le Bourgage. Pass the Alderney Museum if time permits. Return to Victoria Street and walk downhill along Braye Road. Finish back at the passenger landing pontoon. The town portion follows the same compact area covered by Alderney's official self-guided St Anne walk. Allow additional time if visiting the church or museum.
things_to_do.difficulty: Moderate because of the sustained climb from Braye and some cobbled streets

To see the full itineraries (ports of call dates and arrival / departure times) and their lowest rates – just follow the corresponding ship-link. Alert Bay BC is cruise port and village on Cormorant Island (BC Canada) with population around 1500. Over 1/2 of the residents are First Nations (indigenous) people. Two Indian Reserves take up the rest Cormorant Island - Alert Bay 1 (eastern part) and Alert Bay 1A (western part). Alert Bay has museums, drug and alcohol rehab center, hospital, dental clinic, post office, drugstore, grocery store, 3 restaurants, pub, retail shops, liquor store. The town is served by Alert Bay Airport and Alert Bay Water Aerodrome. There is also a harbour marina (for yachts and boats) and BC Ferries terminal with regularly scheduled ferry service to British Columbia's Port McNeill (Vancouver Island) and Sointula (Malcolm Island). Alert Bay also has a campground and ecological park with a cedar swamp and old-growth trees. In Alert Bay is also world's tallest totem pole. In 1921, Canada's Government, in an effort to cease the potlatch custom of song, dance and wealth distribution under 116th Section of Indian Act, confiscated plenty of items including copper shields, dance regalia and wooden masks. During the 1970s-1980s, the Kwakwakawakw Indians regained their possessions after hard negotiations. The returned artifacts are now displayed at Umista Cultural Centre (museum). Alert Bay is a compact cultural and nature-focused port on Cormorant Island. The main sights are concentrated around the waterfront and can be explored on foot, although the village becomes hilly away from the shore. The strongest independent plan is to combine the U'mista Cultural Centre, waterfront totem poles and the 'Namgis Big House area, adding the Ecological Park if time and walking ability allow.
getting_from_port: Alert Bay does not have a conventional cruise terminal. Tender ports are normal for larger ships, while some small expedition vessels have used the Government Dock. The exact landing arrangement depends on the vessel, so passengers should follow the ship's instructions rather than assuming the BC Ferries terminal is the cruise landing point. The waterfront landing area is close to the village centre. The Visitor Centre, shops and waterfront are reached quickly on foot, and most of Alert Bay's important visitor attractions are within a few kilometres. There is little reason to arrange a vehicle for a normal cruise call unless mobility is limited. The BC Ferries terminal also sits in the village, but its scheduled ferries to Port McNeill and Sointula are primarily useful for local transportation. Taking an independent ferry off Cormorant Island during a short cruise call adds unnecessary schedule risk unless the port stay is unusually long.
terminal_notes: There is also a harbour marina (for yachts and boats) and BC Ferries terminal with regularly scheduled ferry service to British Columbia's Port McNeill (Vancouver Island) and Sointula (Malcolm Island).

things_to_do.name: U'mista Cultural Centre
things_to_do.description: Allow about 1.5–2 hours including the walk. This is the priority attraction for most first-time visitors. The centre's Potlatch Collection includes ceremonial regalia that was confiscated during Canada's potlatch prohibition and later returned to the Kwakwaka'wakw community. Permanent and temporary exhibits provide useful context for the culture seen around Alert Bay. U'mista is on Front Street and can be reached independently along the waterfront. During the main summer cruise season it normally opens daily, but passengers should check the current day's hours before relying on an early-morning visit. Guided cultural tours and other programs may also be offered on selected dates.

things_to_do.name: Waterfront, Totem Poles and 'Namgis Big House
things_to_do.description: Allow 1.5–2 hours. Walking through the village provides a good introduction to Alert Bay even without entering a museum. Stops can include the waterfront, memorial totem poles, the exterior of the 'Namgis Traditional Big House and the very tall totem pole beside it. The Original 'Namgis Burial Grounds contain important memorial poles but are not a sightseeing area to enter. View them respectfully from the public road and observe any posted photography or access restrictions. The Big House is also not normally open simply for casual entry; public access is generally associated with scheduled cultural performances or special programs.

things_to_do.name: Alert Bay Ecological Park
things_to_do.description: Allow about 1–1.5 hours from the village centre. Also known locally as Gator Gardens, the park protects a flooded forest and wetland environment with boardwalks and several short forest trails. The Village of Alert Bay describes the walk through the park's boardwalk and trails as roughly 25 minutes, but additional time should be allowed to reach it from the waterfront and for wildlife watching. This is a good addition for passengers who have already visited U'mista or who prefer nature to museums. The route rises away from the waterfront, and damp boardwalks or forest surfaces can be slippery after rain.

things_to_do.name: Cultural Performance or Guided Experience
things_to_do.description: Allow roughly 1–2 hours plus walking time. Seasonal Kwakwaka'wakw dance performances are sometimes presented at the 'Namgis Big House, particularly during summer. U'mista also offers guided cultural visits and may arrange demonstrations or totem-pole talks. These experiences are more schedule-dependent than ordinary sightseeing. If a performance or guided program coincides with the ship's call, it can be one of the most worthwhile ways to spend the visit, but passengers should confirm the current date and time rather than assuming a performance takes place every cruise day.

things_to_do.name: Whale Watching or Wildlife by Boat
things_to_do.description: Usually several hours. Local operators use the waters around the Broughton Archipelago and Johnstone Strait for whale and wildlife trips. These excursions can be excellent on a long port call, but they are less suitable for improvised independent sightseeing because departure times, weather and sea conditions all matter. A ship-arranged or firmly pre-booked local excursion is preferable when the boat trip occupies a large part of the port stay. Confirm the expected return time and leave additional margin for tendering back to the cruise ship.

things_to_do.name: Waterfront and Cultural Walk
things_to_do.description: Distance: approximately 4 km (2.5 mi) round trip. Pure walking time: about 55–65 minutes. Recommended total time: 2.5–3.5 hours with U'mista and sightseeing stops. Difficulty: Easy to moderate, with some uphill sections. Cruise landing or Government Dock area: Begin at the passenger landing designated by the ship and orient yourself along the waterfront. Alert Bay Visitor Centre: Pick up a current village or totem-pole map if the centre is open. Original 'Namgis Burial Grounds: View the memorial poles respectfully from the public road; do not enter the burial grounds. Waterfront boardwalk: Continue along the shoreline toward the cultural area, watching for additional carvings, poles and views across the channel. U'mista Cultural Centre: Allow roughly an hour or more for the exhibits. 'Namgis Traditional Big House: Walk to the exterior of the ceremonial house and the tall totem pole beside it. Expect some uphill walking. Return to the waterfront: Retrace the route toward the cruise landing, allowing additional time if tender queues are forming.
things_to_do.difficulty: Easy to moderate, with some uphill sections

things_to_do.name: Ecological Park Detour
things_to_do.description: Distance: approximately 2.5–3 km (1.6–1.9 mi), depending on the cruise landing and trails used. Pure walking time: about 45–55 minutes including the short park trails. Recommended total time: 1.5–2 hours. Difficulty: Moderate because of hills and potentially wet boardwalks. Start from the cruise landing and walk through the village toward the Visitor Centre. Continue uphill toward Alert Bay Ecological Park. Follow the boardwalk through the flooded forest and use one or more of the short nature trails. Return downhill to the waterfront. If time remains, add the Visitor Centre, nearby shops or a short section of the waterfront before returning to the ship.
things_to_do.difficulty: Moderate because of hills and potentially wet boardwalks

description: Port Alesund cruise ship schedule shows timetable calendars of all arrival and departure dates by month. The port's schedule lists all ships (in links) with cruises going to or leaving from Alesund, Norway. To see the full itineraries (ports of call dates and arrival / departure times) and their lowest rates – just follow the corresponding ship-link. Alesund is a major cruise port and one of Norway's most picturesque fishing towns. It is located at the mouth of Stor Fjord and is actually on two islands connected by bridges. Cruise ships dock close to downtown, so shopping and city touring can be done on foot. Alesund is one of the "Express Route" ferry ports visited regularly as part of the government-subsidized passenger and cargo shipping service in Norway. The cruiseferry itinerary is between two homeports - Bergen (southmost) and Kirkenes (northmost) and connects a total of 34 ports, which are Norwegian communities without any road or air access. Independant tour operators offer from Alesund guided tours to Hjorundfjorden . In June 2022, Enova SF (Norwegian state-owned enterprise) provided grants for installing shore power connectivity at several Norwegian cruise ports (including Alesund), scheduled for completion and inauguration in 2023. Between 2016-2022, Enova granted a total of NOK 842 million for 119 such projects. The technology allows the berthed cruise ship to shut down its diesel engines and instead use the city-grid electricity for the onboard hotel operations and services, thus saving fuel and reducing emissions. Enova SF (2001-founded government enterprise) is owned by Norway's Ministry of Petroleum and Energy and managed by the Ministry of Climate and Environment. From Alesund, cruise tourists can take the 400 steps up to Kniven Overlook (Mt Aksla) for a spectacular panoramic view of the bay surrounded by offshore islands and mountains. The town was rebuilt with stone (instead of wood) following a devastating fire in 1904. The modern city is rich in art nouveau architecture (turrets, towers, medieval facades). Further out is the outdoor Sunnmore Museum where guests can see a collection of boats and traditional farmhouses and the Medieval Museum which features a recreation of a 10th-century village. The Atlantic Ocean Marine Park is also on the outskirts with massive seascape tanks created into the coastline. Cruisers can also visit the Giske islands (burial mounds) and Godoy (lighthouse). Alesund is a starting point for touring the hills of the Sunnmore region, Norang Valley, Oye Glaciers, Runde Island. As a settlement, Alesund was established in the 9th century when the Viking Rollo/Rolf (850-930/Normandy's first ruler between 911-928) built a castle nearby. The village received town status in 1848. Alesund is one of the ferry ports along the "Express Route" - Norway's Government subsidized "Norwegian Coastal Express". This is a regularly scheduled passenger and cargo shipping service in Norway. The "ferry and cruise" itinerary is between two turnaround ports - Bergen (southmost) and Kirkenes (northmost). It connects a total of 34 ports, which are Norwegian communities without any road or air access. Since January 2021, Norway's coastal ferry service is operated by two companies - Hurtigruten (7 ships) and Havila (4 ships). The Norwegian Government's annual subsidy for the ferry service is around USD 100 million. The list of all ports along the northbound "Norwegian Coastal Express" itinerary includes Bergen (turnaround port), Alesund, Floro , Geiranger (Stranda) , Maloy (Vagsoy) , Molde , Torvik (Heroy, Leinoya Island) , Kristiansund , Rorvik (Vikna) , Trondheim , Bodo , Bronnoysund (Bronnoy) , Nesna , Ornes (Meloy) , Sandnessjoen (Alstahaug) , Stamsund (Vestvagoy Island) , Svolvaer (Vagan, Austvagoya Island) , Trollfjorden (Hadsel) , Finnsnes (Lenvik) , Harstad (Hinnoya Island) , Risoyhamn (Andoy Island) , Skjervoy , Sortland (Langoya Island) , Stokmarknes (Hadseloya Island) , Tromso , Berlevag , Hammerfest , Honningsvag (Mageroya Island , Nordkapp / North Cape ), Kjollefjord (Lebesby) , Mehamn (Gamvik) , Oksfjord (Loppa) , Batsfjord , Vardo (Vardoya Island) , Kirkenes (turnaround port). Ålesund is one of the easiest Norwegian cruise ports to explore independently. Ships normally berth directly beside the compact city centre, putting the Art Nouveau district, Brosundet waterfront and the foot of Mount Aksla within walking distance. A cruise call can therefore work well without an organized excursion, while taxis, local buses and cruise-day sightseeing services make the aquarium and surrounding islands practical alternatives.
getting_from_port: The main cruise berths are immediately beside central Ålesund. Passengers can normally leave the secure quay area and continue into town on foot without a shuttle transfer. Brosundet, Jugendstilsenteret, Ålesund Church and the entrance to the Mount Aksla steps can generally be reached within about 20 minutes from the ship. Port security fencing may alter the exact pedestrian exit when ships are alongside, and parts of the quay or the movable bridge at Brosundet can be closed during cruise operations. Follow the signed passenger route rather than assuming the shortest route visible from the ship is open. Local FRAM buses serve destinations outside the centre. Cruise-day sightseeing buses and the Ålesund city train also operate seasonally; the city train makes a circuit of about 70 minutes including a stop at the Fjellstua viewpoint. Taxis are normally available around cruise calls.
terminal_notes: Ships normally berth directly beside the compact city centre, putting the Art Nouveau district, Brosundet waterfront and the foot of Mount Aksla within walking distance.
tender_evidence: Cruise ships dock close to downtown, so shopping and city touring can be done on foot.

things_to_do.name: Art Nouveau Centre, Brosundet and Mount Aksla
things_to_do.description: Allow about 2.5–4 hours. This is the most practical first visit and requires no transport. Walk through the Art Nouveau centre, cross Hellebroa for views along Brosundet, and visit Jugendstilsenteret if you want more context on the rebuilding of Ålesund after the 1904 fire. Continue to Byparken and climb the 418 steps to Fjellstua on Mount Aksla. The climb is steep, with viewpoints along the way, and the tourist office recommends allowing roughly 30–40 minutes for the journey uphill on foot. Passengers who do not want the stair climb can use a taxi or a sightseeing service that drives to the upper viewpoint.

things_to_do.name: Atlanterhavsparken Aquarium
things_to_do.description: Allow about 3–4 hours including transport. Atlanterhavsparken is approximately 3.6 km (2.2 mi) from central Ålesund and is a good choice for families or poor-weather days. The aquarium combines large saltwater displays with outdoor areas for seals and otters. Local bus number 1 toward Hessa can be used from central Ålesund. Get off at Tuenesvegen and allow another 10–15 minutes on foot. A taxi is simpler when port time is limited; the drive from downtown is normally only several minutes. Check current feeding times and opening arrangements before setting out.

things_to_do.name: Alnes Lighthouse and Giske
things_to_do.description: Best treated as a half-day trip. Alnes on Godøya offers open-ocean scenery and a lighthouse visitor centre, while nearby Giske has its medieval church. Reaching the islands involves road travel through the island and tunnel network, so this is less convenient than sightseeing in central Ålesund. A pre-arranged sightseeing tour is the simplest option for cruise passengers and commonly combines Alnes, Giske and a stop at Mount Aksla. Independent travel is possible with sufficient planning, but check transport connections carefully and leave a larger return margin than for city sightseeing.

things_to_do.name: Fjord or Coastal Boat Trip
things_to_do.description: Ålesund is also a practical departure point for boat trips into the surrounding fjords and archipelago. Options can include Hjørundfjord sightseeing or shorter coastal wildlife and RIB trips. These are worthwhile when the sailing fits comfortably inside the ship's port call. Check the actual departure point and confirmed return time before booking independently. Longer trips toward distant fjord destinations consume a substantial part of the day and are better suited to long port calls or excursions specifically timed for cruise passengers.

things_to_do.name: Central Ålesund and Mount Aksla
things_to_do.description: Difficulty: Moderate. Distance: roughly 4 km (2.5 mi), depending on the berth and small detours. Pure walking time: about 60–75 minutes, plus the 418-step climb. Recommended total time: 2.5–3.5 hours with viewpoints and sightseeing stops. Cruise terminal exit: Leave the secure quay and follow the signed pedestrian route toward the city centre. Byparken: Walk to the city park at the foot of Mount Aksla. Mount Aksla and Fjellstua: Climb the 418 steps, stopping at the intermediate viewpoints before reaching the main panorama over Ålesund, the islands and surrounding mountains. Kongens gate: Descend the same steps and continue through the central Art Nouveau streets. Brosundet and Hellebroa: Cross the bridge and pause for the classic view along the narrow harbour channel. Jugendstilsenteret: See the former pharmacy building and surrounding early-20th-century architecture. Add museum time if your schedule allows. Molja waterfront: Continue toward the harbour entrance and Molja Lighthouse for another waterside viewpoint. Return to the ship: Follow the central waterfront back toward the signed cruise-terminal entrance. The central sections are straightforward, but the Aksla stairs make this route unsuitable for passengers with limited mobility. In wet weather the steps and cobbled streets can be slippery. For an easier version, omit Aksla and concentrate on Brosundet, the Art Nouveau quarter and the waterfront.

The port's schedule lists all ships (in links) with cruises going to or leaving from Aleutian Islands, Alaska. To see the full itineraries (ports of call dates and arrival / departure times) and their lowest rates – just follow the corresponding ship-link. The Aleutian Islands in the Northern Pacific Ocean are a chain/archipelago of 14 large islands plus 55 smaller-sized isles. Some belong to the USA and some to Russia. The group's total land area is 6821 mi2 (17666 km2). It extends approx 1200 mi (1900 km) westward from Alaska toward Kamchatka Russia . They also mark the dividing line between Bering Sea (north) and Pacific Ocean (south). As a cruise destination, the Aleutians are visited mainly by smaller-sized ships and superyachts from the fleets of ultra-luxury travel brands like Seabourn , Silversea , Hapag-Lloyd , Ponant , Crystal , Windstar , Azamara . The Aleutian archipelago contains the USA's westernmost territory (Attu Island) and Russia's easternmost territory (Semisopochnoi Island). While nearly all Aleutians are part of the Alaska State, at the extreme west, the Commander Islands are Russian. The Aleutians' westernmost island is Attu, with Russia's Commander Islands located approx 208 mi (335 km) to the west. Attu is ~1100 mi (1800 km) from mainland Alaska, ~750 mi (1210 km) northeast of the Kuril Islands (Russia), and ~4800 mi (7700 km) from Washington DC . The Aleutians are also part of the Pacific Ring of Fire (its northern part), with 57 active volcanoes. Sadly, the Aleutians are best known for the battles there during WW2 (1939-1945). The air-bombing of Dutch Harbor (Amaknak Island, Unalaska) in June 1942 was one of only two attacks on US territories - preceded by the attack on Pearl Harbor ( Oahu Island, Hawaii) in December 1941. The Aleutians comprise of 5 archipelagos, listed next (east to west) and in brackets - the names of their largest islands (also east to west). Among the largest Fox Islands (Attu, Unalaska, Umnak, Unimak), the largest one is Unimak (4070 km2 / 1571 mi2), followed by Unalaska (2720 km2 / 1051 mi2). The Aleutians form a curved island chain similar to the Kuril Islands (Russia), Japan, and the Philippines. All these arcs are located at the Pacific Plate's edge and experience seismic activity. The Aleutians are located between the tectonic plates of the Pacific Ocean and North America. Their elevation is greatest in the eastern and least in the western islands. Their coastlines are rocky and approaching them is exceedingly dangerous. The land (steep mountains) rises immediately from their coasts, reaching heights of 6200 ft (1900 m). The plant growing season is 130+ days (early-May through late-September). Due to the strong winds, the Aleutian conifers rarely reach a height of 10 ft (3 m), with many of them being less than 5 ft (1,5 m) tall. Instead of trees, these islands are covered with dense growth of shrubs and herbage (berries, grasses, sedges, low-flowering plants, Aleutian shield fern). The islands' fauna is represented by large colonies of breeding seabirds and some Asiatic birds. Radioactivity is present after the nuclear weapon testing on Amchitka Island (1971). Today, most of the Aleutians are protected wilderness areas as part of the Alaska Maritime Wildlife Refuge (total area 4,9 million acres / 20,000 km2, of which the wilderness area is 2,64 million acres / 10700 km2) and the Aleutian Islands Wilderness(total area 1,3 million acres / 5300 km2). On the less mountainous Aleutian Islands, the economy used to be raising sheep, reindeer, bisons, even some llamas (on Unalaska). The islands' current economy is based primarily on fishing, and the US military presence in the archipelago. As transportation, there are air- and ferry services, plus the Alaska Marine Highway passing through most of the Alaskan islands. In the "USA top 10" largest Alaskan islands are Kodiak , Prince of Wales, Chichagof , St Lawrence, Admiralty , Nunivak, Unimak, Baranof Island . Adak Island's largest settlement is the port town Adak (population around 400). Adak is the USA's westernmost and Alaska's southernmost island, with length 34 mi (55 km), width 22 mi (35 km). By total land area (approx 275 mi2 / 711 km2) it is ranked USA's 25th largest island. In Aleutian, the word adak (adaq) means "father". The island's vegetation is at lower elevations only and mostly tundra (no trees) - low-lying flowering plants, berries, grasses, mosses. The weather is harsh - strong winds (gusts in excess of 120 mph / 190 kph), cold temperatures (20-60 F / -7 to 16 C), extensive fogs, frequent clouds, cyclonic storms and rains (260+ rainy days per year). Island's highest elevation point is Mt Moffett (northwest end) - 3924 ft (1196 m). In the 18th century, Russian explorers visited for the first time the island but didn't establish permanent settlements. During WW2, the Japanese Imperial Army took control of the Aleutian Islands Attu and Kiska, from where they air-bombed the US base at Dutch Harbor (Amaknak Island, Unalaska) . In response, the USA started a military campaign that required the construction of bases to launch operations from the western Aleutian Islands. Adak was the island chosen for building an airfield (today Adak Airport). Flight operations started in September 1942. In May 1943, American soldiers landed on and conquered Attu Island (2300 Japanese and 550 Americans died in the battle). When US soldiers landed on Kiska Island (August 1943), they found that the Japanese were evacuated by their navy, right after the Adak battle. During WW2, Adak was populated by approx 6000 US military personnel. Adak Town is on Kuluk Bay, located approx 1200 mi (1930 km) southwest of Anchorage AK and approx 450 mi (724 km) west of Dutch Harbor AK. Flight time from Adak to Anchorage is 3+ hours (depending on weather). Adak is on the same latitude as Vancouver Island (BC Canada). Adak Airport (state-owned, west of Adak Town) is one of the Aleutians' largest and most sophisticated. It was built by the US Navy and used mainly for Naval air transportation. It has two runways with lengths 2,4 km (7800 ft) and 2,3 km (7600 ft). Adak Airport currently serves regularly scheduled flights (by Alaska Airlines) linking to Anchorage AK (Ted Stevens Airport). Attu Island is the USA's westernmost point. Attu has length 35 mi (56 km) and width 20 mi (30 km). By land area (345 mi2 / 893 km2) it is ranked the USA's 23rd largest island. Attu is uninhabited since 2010 when the Attu Station (USCG Station LORAN) was permanently closed/decommissioned and its personnel (20 people) left the island. The Aleut people were the island's inhabitants prior to WW2. On June 7, 1942, the Japanese landed on Attu (without opposition) after landing on Kiska Island (June 6th). in response to the invasion, the Alaskan authorities conducted a mandatory evacuation of ~900 Aleuts from the Aleutians. When the Japanese landed, Attu's population (45 Aleuts and 2 Americans) were captured and imprisoned in a camp near Otaru Japan. In September 1942, the Japanese Attu Island garrison was transferred to Kiska, leaving Attu essentially unoccupied. In October 1942, the Japanese re-established their Attu base (at Holtz Bay) with about 2300 troops (by March 1943). In May 1943 started the US operation to recapture Attu. The following battles resulted in 3929 US casualties (including 1200 with severe cold injuries). At the end of May, the Japanese troops were finally defeated in Massacre Valley (2351 dead) where the Americans built later the "Navy Town". In August 1943, the Japanese forces evacuated Kiska. Kiska Island has length 22 mi (35 km), width 1,5-6 mi (2,5-10 km), total land area 107 mi2 (278 km2) and is part of the Aleutians' Wilderness Park, meaning special permissions to visit are required. Kiska was discovered in 1741 by the Russian explorer Vitus Bering (1681-1741). Starting 1775, the island (along with mainland Alaska) became one of Imperial Russia's fur trading outposts. In 1867, the USA negotiated the purchase of Alaska from the Russian Empire, with Kiska included in the deal. Kiska has an active volcano (on the northern end). In January 1962 there was an explosive eruption with lava extrusion. A second eruption with lava flow was reported in March 1964. During WW2 ((on June 6, 1942) the Japanese military forces landed at Kiska, and on June 7th captured Attu Island. During winter 1942-1943, they reinforced and fortified both islands. The US Navy started operations to cut Kiska Island's supply. In October 1942, US forces bombed the island 5 times. Following winter 1942-1943, Attu was liberated and Kiska bombed once more before a larger US force (including 95 warships and 168 aircraft) defeated the Japanese garrison on Kiska in August 1943. However, after the loss of Attu Island (in May) and the impending arrival of the Allied forces, in July the Japanese removed all their troops without being noticed. Atka Island has length 65 mi (105 km), width 2-20 mi (3-30 km) and total area approx 405 mi2 (1048 km2), ranking it USA's 22nd largest island. In its northeastern part is located the Korovin Volcano (height 5030 ft / 1533 m). Atka's westernmost point is Cape Kigun, approx 3,4 mi (5,5 km) from Oglodak Island. Port Atka AK is on the eastern coast and has population around 100. Unga Island is the largest of Shumagin Islands (just off mainland Alaska/Alaskan Peninsula). The island has total area approx 171 mi2 (442 km2), ranking it the USA's 35th largest. Unga is currently uninhabited. It was previously named Grekodelarovskoe Ostrov - after Evstratii Ivanovich Delarov (1740-1806) - Greece-born skipper who served the Russian-American Company (fur trading company) in Alaska, which was then called Russian America. In the 19th century, Unga Island's economy was based on mining and cod fishing. With the decline of these industries, its population departed, leaving a ghost town in its place. Puffins, kittiwakes, cormorants, sea otters and peregrine falcons are prominent among the cliffs of this picturesque island. Seguam Island is uninhabited and mountainous, with total area 80 mi2 (207 km2), length 16 mi (26 km), width 7 mi (11 km), highest elevation point (Pyre Peak) 1054 m (3458 ft). It consists of several composite/conical volcanoes and contains 2 calderas/volcanic craters. The last (explosive) eruption was reported in 1993 (at Pyre Peak/the western caldera) that produced lava flows. Chagulak Island is round-shaped (diameter 1,9 mi / 3,1 km) and consists of a single cone stratovolcano (height 3747 ft / 1142 m). Chagulak is separated from Amukta Island via a sea channel (width 4,3 mi / 7 km). The Aleutian Islands listing represents a vast archipelago rather than a single cruise terminal. Most visits are made by small expedition ships, with activities determined by the specific island, sea conditions, wildlife and local access rules. Organized excursion recommended: On remote islands, passengers normally go ashore by Zodiac or tender and explore with the ship’s expedition team. Independent sightseeing is generally limited to community calls such as Unalaska/Dutch Harbor or Adak.
terminal_notes: The Aleutian Islands listing represents a vast archipelago rather than a single cruise terminal.
tender_evidence: Organized excursion recommended: On remote islands, passengers normally go ashore by Zodiac or tender and explore with the ship’s expedition team.

things_to_do.name: Guided Wildlife Landing
things_to_do.description: Join the expedition team for birding and shoreline wildlife observation. Depending on the island and season, possible sightings include puffins, auklets, murres, bald eagles, sea otters, seals, sea lions and whales. Wildlife is never guaranteed, and visitors should remain with their assigned group.

things_to_do.name: Expedition Hike
things_to_do.description: Some landings include guided walks across treeless tundra, volcanic slopes or coastal valleys. Routes are selected on the day and can range from short nature walks to demanding hikes over wet, uneven ground. Walking poles and waterproof boots are useful.

things_to_do.name: Zodiac Cruise or Kayaking
things_to_do.description: Where landing is unsuitable, the ship may offer small-boat exploration along sea cliffs, kelp beds and sheltered bays. Kayaking should be attempted only through the ship’s supervised program because cold water, wind, swell and rocky shores make independent paddling impractical.

things_to_do.name: Unangan Culture and Remote Communities
things_to_do.description: Some itineraries visit inhabited communities such as Unalaska, Akutan, Atka or Adak. Activities may include cultural presentations, local museums, churches and walks through the settlement. Respect local guidance, private property and any restrictions on photography.

things_to_do.name: World War II Sites
things_to_do.description: The archipelago contains military remains from the Aleutian campaign, including bunkers, gun positions and abandoned installations. These are best visited with a guide because structures may be unstable and unexploded ordnance or other hazardous debris can remain in remote areas.

things_to_do.name: Local Heritage Circuit
things_to_do.description: A practical visit can combine the Museum of the Aleutians, the Aleutian World War II National Historic Area Visitor Center and the Holy Ascension Cathedral. These attractions are spread between the Dutch Harbor and Unalaska sides of the community, so a ship shuttle, local tour or prearranged transport is more practical than attempting the entire circuit on foot.

things_to_do.name: Hiking and Scenic Viewpoints
things_to_do.description: Bunker Hill and Mount Ballyhoo offer scenery and military remains, but access may require a recreation permit because much of the surrounding land is privately owned by the Ounalashka Corporation. Conditions can be muddy, exposed and windy. Arrange permits and transport before committing to a hike.

name: Alexandria (Egypt, Cairo)
summary: Port Alexandria cruise ship schedule shows timetable calendars of all arrival and departure dates by month.
